quam a divinis vacent colloquii: sed in ter opera manuī. in corde meditatio fer ueat scripturaruz:que postea quam in ar dorez spiritus mentez perdurere: non in orationem deuotissimaz comuuetur. Sit ergo monachus christi nules ficuti ani mal dei munduz quod ruminat: habens semp in ore cordis sui. sanctarum pabula scripturarum: ne vanis z perniciosis cogitationibus mens pateat: aut verbuz ex ore loquentis turpe sine ociolum erupat. Memor sit semper inter operandum scri pturae dicentis: Beatus vir qui in lege do mini meditatur die ac nocte. Omnis eni qui dominii iesum in veritace diligit: do crinam simul et passionem eius in corde suo cui lachrymis z orationibus quotidie renoluit. Verus namqz dei amator non est: qui mandatoriz eius vel ad momenti obluuiscitur. Enimvero sicut ait scriptura: q diligunt dominu requirunt que bene placta sunt illi: z qui timent nomen sanctum eius: replebuntur lege ipsins. Hinc quidam sanctozz dicit ad dominuz. In corde meo abscondi eloquia tua: vt non peccez tibi. Excitandus ergo semper animus: z stimulis spiritualibus quotidiere nouādus: ne vel ignavia torpeat: vel incerti ocio languescat. Labozi monastice in sticutionis exercitium: lectionis z oratio nis studium: z diligens custodia vigilia ru: vera sunt incitamenta virtut. Aibil autem sancto proposito monachi perniciolius oció: quoniam z carneí excitat: in libidine: z mentis omnem eneruat virtu tem extinguitz spiritus feruozem. Omni niú em fomes z nutrimenti malorum in clauistro est ociz. Ubicungzigitur fueris sive in agro sive in clauistro semper ociz z perniciosissimam anime pestem fugito mentez ornans z exercitans vel orazione vel meditazione scripturarum. Cu bonis z studiosis dei amatorizbus conversare li benter: negligentes vero z salutis pro prie contempto: es devita. Qui enim piceem contingit inquinabitur ab ea: z sol citum se facit peccatozum: non erit immu nis a scelere. Sermones tuos diligenter considera: vt nulli detrahas omnino: nec alium auscultes detrahentem: quoniam detractozsimul z libes auditoz. Vterg de moni famulatur: alter loquendo alter ve ro auscultando. Laboza sicut bonus mi les christi ielu: z diligenter operare mani bus quodcunqz tibi ex obedientia inium gitur: nec tibi du rum videatur alterius o bedire imperio, pro quo spiritu tuo coroz na etern efelicitas preparatur in celo. Un de nullus laboz grauis, nullum tempus longum. nulla monacho dura videri ob seruantia debet: quibus gloria eterne bea ticudinis acquiritur. Brevitatem huius vite fratres mei perpendite z agite bon quamdiu licet: quoniam qui nunc parce leminat: post mozez quoqz parce z metez z pro suo vnusquizc operc mieredem co dignaz recepturus est: no pro alieno. La bozandi tempus brevissimum est: mercedes vero que bonis debetur operibus se piternum. Considerate fratres mei homines mundo implicatos z omnes huius seculi amatores quam fontes sunt in rebo terrenis atez caducis: in celestibus vero debiles z infirmi: vt vos intantii deo pl cere curetis: quantum illi vt mundo divi tes appareat z gloriozi continue laborat. Nam pro temporali gloria. multi vsez ad moziez desundare non refugiuue: sed pro spe future felicitatis etiam parum vel age re vel sustinere contennuit. Pro terrenis lucris quaslibetiniurias pacientissime tolerant: z pro celesti mercede sustinere vt te nuissini verbi continueliaz recusant. Re gi terreno principi vel indici toto die fo/ tes possunt assistere: in oratione autem co ram omnipotent domino ad vnus boze spaciuz nequeunt perdurare. Multa pro acquirendis perituriis divitizs aduersa li benter tolerant: superna vero bona quere re tanto magis negligent: quato in amo re rerrestrium delectabilius occupantur. Horum vos conversatio fratres charissi ni admoneat omnes huius nudi curas tanto amplius fugere: quanto iam vobis licet minus terrenarum rerum negotia p tractare. Omnez sollicitudinem vestram z curam pro acquisitione celestium bonorum semper impendite: z pro mercede fu ture beatitudinis omni tempore diligen tissime laborate. Hazsicut scriptura testatur militia est vita vestra super terram: et quecuz homo seminauerit: hec z metez. Scitote quia mozs quotidie properat: et singulis momentis pars vite non ampl us reuersura extinguitur. Vigilate igitur fratres mei charissimi vigilate. quia nesci tis quando dominus deus nostre ad iudi ciu mortis vniuscuiusqz venturus sicero

...that they may be free for divine converse; but amid the works of the hands let meditation on the Scriptures burn in the heart; and after it has brought the mind into the ardor of the spirit, let it be moved into most devout prayer. Therefore let the monk, Christ’s soldier, be like the clean animal of God that chews the cud, always having in the mouth of his heart the fodder of the holy Scriptures, lest the mind lie open to vain and pernicious thoughts, or a foul or idle word burst from the speaker’s mouth. Let him always remember, while working, the Scripture that says: Blessed is the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night. For everyone who loves the Lord Jesus in truth daily turns over in his heart, with tears and prayers, both his teaching and his passion. For he is not a true lover of God who forgets his commandments even for a moment. Indeed, as Scripture says: Those who love the Lord seek the things that are pleasing to him, and those who fear his holy name shall be filled with his law. Hence one of the saints says to the Lord: In my heart I have hidden your words, that I may not sin against you. The spirit, therefore, must always be stirred up and renewed daily by spiritual goads, lest it grow numb through sloth or languish in uncertain idleness. The labor of monastic discipline, the practice of reading and prayer, and the diligent keeping of vigils are true incitements to virtue. Nothing, however, is more harmful to the holy purpose of the monk than idleness, since it both excites the flesh to lust and weakens every strength of the mind and extinguishes the fervor of the spirit. For idleness in the cloister is the tinder and nourishment of all evils. Wherever, therefore, you may be, whether in the field or in the cloister, always flee idleness as the most pernicious plague of the soul, adorning and exercising the mind either with prayer or with meditation on the Scriptures. Converse gladly with the good and zealous lovers of God; but avoid the negligent and the despisers of their own salvation. For he who touches pitch will be defiled by it, and he who makes himself a companion of sinners will not be free from crime. Consider your words carefully, so that you detract from no one at all, nor listen to another who is detracting, since both the detractor and the willing hearer serve the demon: the one by speaking, the other by listening. Labor like a good soldier of Christ Jesus, and diligently do with your hands whatever is enjoined upon you by obedience; nor let it seem hard to you to obey another’s command, for which eternal happiness, a crown for your spirit, is prepared in heaven. Therefore no labor, no length of time, no observance ought to seem hard to a monk, by which the glory of eternal blessedness is acquired. Consider, my brothers, the brevity of this life and do good while it is permitted, since he who now sows sparingly will also after death reap sparingly, and each one will receive a fitting reward for his own work, not for another’s. The time for laboring is very brief, but the recompense that is owed to good works is everlasting. Consider, my brothers, men entangled in the world, and all lovers of this age, how strong they are in earthly and perishable matters, but weak and feeble in heavenly things; so that you may take care to please God as much as they labor continually to appear rich and glorious to the world. For for temporal glory many have not refused to sweat even unto death; but for the hope of future happiness they despise even doing or enduring a little. For earthly gains they most patiently tolerate all sorts of injuries; and for a heavenly reward they refuse to endure the insult of even a very slight word. They can stand all day before an earthly king, prince, or judge; but in prayer before the almighty Lord they cannot continue for the space of one hour. They gladly tolerate many adversities for the acquisition of perishable riches; but they neglect the more to seek heavenly goods, the more pleasantly they are occupied in love of earthly things. Let their way of life, dearest brothers, admonish you all the more to flee all the cares of this world, inasmuch as you are now permitted to handle fewer of the affairs of earthly things. Always devote all your solicitude and care to the acquisition of heavenly goods, and labor most diligently at all times for the reward of future blessedness. For, as Scripture testifies, your life upon earth is a warfare, and whatever a man has sown, this he shall also reap. Know that death hastens daily, and at every moment a part of life, never to return, is extinguished. Watch, therefore, my dearest brothers, watch, for you do not know when the Lord our God will come to the judgment of each one’s death

Om̄ia VIII. an media nocte/ an gallicātu: an māene cū venerit repēte īueniat vos dormiētes. Uigilate itaqꝫ omni tempore orantes: vt digni habeamini fugere mala omnia qͣ futura sunt et stare cuꝫ fiducia ante cōspe ctum filij dei omnia iudicantis. Omnes enim diuo testante christophilo stabimus ante tribunal christi: vt referat vnusquisqꝫ propria corporis prout gessit. Siue bonuꝫ siue malũ. Beatus ille monachus quem inuenerit dominꝰ in bonis operibus vigilantem: qui se ad nuptias agni celestis in vera puritate cordis preparauerit: qui occurrere iudici non formidabit. Semper sit illud ī cordibꝰ vestris memorabile verbũ diui hieronymi super euangelium cata matheuꝫ dicentis. Siue comedam siue bibam. siue aliud quid faciam: semper vox illa videtur sonare in auribus meis. Surgite mortui et venite ad iudicium. Quoniens diem illū cogito futuri examinis. totꝰ corde et corpore cõtremisco. Unde si qua presc̃tis vite est leticia frẽs mei. ita agenda est: vt amaritudo illius tremēdi judicij nũquam recedat a memoria. O dies illa magna terribilis tremēda nimii et amara valde: in qua sol et luna obscura buntur: non diminutione luminis sed cōparatione maiestatis: vbi cessabit omne argumentũ excusationis: vbi omnia erũt manifesta: nihilqꝫ latere iudicem poterit. quoniam qui nouit occultas cognitiōes mentiũ tunc palaz iudicabit. qui nec gratia preuenitur. nec misericordia flectitur: muneribus et donis non corrũpitur: pręcibꝰ non mitigabitur: nec satisfactione iaꝫ deinceps aliqua placabit᷑. In hac igit̉ vita positi fratres agat vnusquisqꝫ vestrũ pro anima sua quantũ potest: qm̄ penitenzia peccatorum hic facta soluꝫ est vtilis et fructuosa: quam diu locus est venie et sententia adhuc differtur iusticie. Qui bene facere ac penitentiā agere differt vsqꝫ ad mortẽ damnationi est ꝓximꝰ: quoniam bonuꝫ quod sanus et incolumis negligit raro infirmus et iam moriturus instaura bit. Dicit enĩz sanctꝰ papa gregoriꝰ. Quis quis penitentie fructus differre vsqꝫ ad mortis horam non metuit: ipse sibi testis est quod penitere veraciter nũquaꝫ in eiꝰ mente fuit. Nunc ergo cōuertite vos ad dominũ nostrũ intoto corde vestro penientiã agentes coram illo: et sic viuite precor vt cum hinc migranduꝫ fuerit, appa Fo.XVII. rere ante faciem eius non timeatis. Quod sine intermissione sit orandũ. Om̄ia.viiij. DOminus ac saluator noster iesus christus in euāgelio fratres cata lucam volens nos cõtinuos es se in orationibus ita premonuit dicens. Oportꝫ semper orare et nunquam deficere. Hoc domini consilium pre cũctis mortalibus maxime decet monachos et om̃es in qua cũqꝫ religione claustrales: quo rū omnis actio et tota vita īmo quicquid faciūt aut oratio esse debet aut saltem orationi conforme. Dicuntur enim non absqꝫ ratione spirituales quicũqꝫ militiā profitētur monasticā: quatenus ipso moneantur vocabulo carnis voluptates pro dei amore cōtēnere: et per verā charitateꝫ in ardore spiritus ambulare. Dicit namqꝫ sanctꝰ christi apostolꝰ. Qui in carne sunt deo place re non possunt: quoniã si secunduꝫ carnem vixeritis moriemini: si autē spiritu facta carnis mortificauerit᷑ viuetis. Sciēs aūt sine orationis instantia feruorem spiritus diu in nobis non posse subsistere. ite rū ad thessalonicenses ait. Semper gaudete: sine intermissione orate: in omnibus gratias agite: quoniā hec est volūtas dei in christo iesu in omnibus vobis. Quis autem sit modus orandi salvator nos dociuit in euangelio dicens. Tu autē cũ oraueris intra in cubiculum tuum. et clauso ostio. ora patrem tuũ in abscondito: et pater ter tuus qui videt in absc̃ondito reddet tibi. Et in alio loco dixit ad mulierē samentanā. Mulier crede mihi qͥa veniet horam pater tales querit qui adorent eum. Spiritus est deus: et eos qui adorant eum. in spīritu et veritate oportet adorare. Orati onem esse cordis potius quam sermoneꝫ oris prolixum ex christi doctrina constat manifestum: quia cum deus sit spūs: non aliter quā intimo feruore spūs venit adorandus. Orationis enĩz cordis in feruore spiritus magna est virtus: multiplica tionis ꝑo sermonū sine attentione mentꝭ c iij [unclear]

Homily VIII.

whether at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning, lest, when he comes suddenly, he find you sleeping. Therefore watch at every time, praying that you may be accounted worthy to escape all the evils that are to come, and to stand with confidence before the sight of the Son of God, who judges all things. For, as the divine lover of Christ bears witness, we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive the things proper to the body, according as he has done, whether good or evil.

Blessed is that monk whom the Lord shall find watching in good works, who has prepared himself for the wedding of the heavenly Lamb in true purity of heart, who will not fear to meet the judge. Let that memorable saying of divine Jerome on the Gospel according to Matthew always be in your hearts, when he says: Whether I eat or drink, or do anything else, that voice always seems to sound in my ears: Rise, dead, and come to judgment.

As often as I think of that day of the future examination, I tremble with my whole heart and body. Therefore, if there is any joy in the present life, my brothers, it must be so conducted that the bitterness of that dreadful judgment never withdraw from memory. O that great, terrible, dreadful, exceeding and very bitter day, on which the sun and moon will be darkened, not by diminution of light but by comparison with majesty; where every argument of excuse will cease; where all things will be manifest, and nothing will be able to lie hidden from the judge, because he who knows the hidden thoughts of minds will then judge openly; who is neither anticipated by favor, nor bent by mercy; is not corrupted by gifts and presents; will not be softened by prayers; nor thereafter will he be appeased by any satisfaction.

Therefore, brothers, while you are placed in this life, let each of you do as much as he can for his soul, because penance for sins done here alone is useful and fruitful, so long as there is room for pardon and the sentence of justice is still delayed. He who postpones doing good and performing penance until death is very near to damnation, because the good that he neglects when healthy and unharmed he will rarely restore when sick and already about to die. For holy Pope Gregory says: Whoever does not fear to defer the fruits of penance until the hour of death is himself a witness against himself that true repentance was never in his mind. Now therefore turn yourselves to our Lord with your whole heart, doing penance before him, and live, I pray, in such a way that, when you must depart from here, you may not fear to appear before his face.

That one must pray without ceasing. Homily IX.

Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, brothers, in the Gospel according to Luke, wishing us to be continual in prayers, admonished us thus, saying: It is necessary always to pray and never to fail. This counsel of the Lord befits, before all mortals, monks most of all, and all cloistered persons in whatever religious life, whose every action and whole life, indeed whatever they do, ought either to be prayer or at least conformed to prayer. For all who profess the monastic service are called spiritual, not without reason, in order that they may be admonished by the very word to despise the pleasures of the flesh for the love of God, and to walk through true charity in the ardor of the spirit.

For the holy apostle of Christ says: Those who are in the flesh cannot please God; for if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, you will live. Knowing, however, that without constancy in prayer the fervor of the spirit cannot long endure in us, he likewise says to the Thessalonians: Always rejoice; pray without ceasing; in all things give thanks, because this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for all of you.

But what the manner of praying is, the Savior taught us in the Gospel, saying: But you, when you pray, enter into your chamber, and with the door shut, pray to your Father in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you. And in another place he said to the Samaritan woman: Woman, believe me, because the hour will come [unclear] the Father seeks such as will adore him. God is spirit, and those who adore him must adore in spirit and truth. It is manifest from Christ’s teaching that prayer is of the heart rather than a lengthy speech of the mouth, because, since God is spirit, he must be adored in no other way than by the innermost fervor of the spirit. For the prayer of the heart in the fervor of the spirit has great power; but the multiplication of words without attention of mind

That one must pray without interruption.

...no usefulness at all. Hence Saint Jerome says: God is to be prayed to not in words only, but with the heart. Therefore the chanting of five psalms with purity of heart, serenity, and spiritual cheerfulness is better than the singing of the whole psalter with anxiety and sadness of heart. And the holy pope Gregory says: True petition is not in the sounds of the mouth, but in the voices of the heart, that is, in holy thoughts. For it is not words but desires that make the stronger voices in the ears of God.

Except, therefore, for those prayers which we are bound to say either by decree of the Church or by the institution of the monastic order, [prolixity?] in the rest and multiplication of words contribute nothing, or little, to true and inward devotion of the mind, since where there is no fervent desire in the love of God, an excessive extension of speech is introduced in vain. For sacred Augustine says: Let much speaking in prayer be absent, but let fervent attention persevere; for to speak much in praying is to handle a necessary matter with superfluous words. For prayer embraces many things in few words, so that the simplicity of faith might quickly learn the sufficiency of its salvation, and the prudence of the ingenious might stand amazed at the depth of the mysteries.

But for those in whom, because of hardness of heart, the compunction of inward fervor has been lacking, when they prostrate themselves in prayer there is need of more extended speech, shouting, and tears, so that by long exercise of the mind they may at last strike forth within themselves the burning fire of divine love, until they rise in the affection of holy prayer in the Spirit of God. But afterward, when the fervor of divine love and compunction has penetrated the mind, there is thereafter no need for the exercise of words, but the continuation of spiritual nourishment is required, lest the fervor of the spiritual fire be extinguished. To this end our most holy father wished prayer in the assembly to be shortened, so that if anyone wished to pray apart in the spirit, he could do so.

There are, however, some who are so hard of heart that while praying they find little or nothing of spiritual compunction; for them freedom brings ruin, and solitude often brings despair. Attend, I pray you, dearest brothers, to what I say to you, and consider how greatly you are bound to pray without interruption. It is not enough for a monk, striving toward perfection in the school of Christ the eternal king, to discharge the canonical prayers; nor is it sufficient for a man solemnly dedicated to God by vow to fulfill the common prayers of the order in the convent, since one who is commanded always to pray without interruption is bound beyond verbal prayers also to spiritual prayers. For prayers instituted by the Church or by the order fall under the merit of obedience, and under the law of necessity by reason of a precept; but that manner of praying which is called spiritual is strengthened in the freedom of the spirit as useful and necessary for a monk at every time for perfection.

Hence it must be noted that for prayers which are by precept of the Church or the order, the utterance of words is required as a matter of necessity, together with the intention of satisfying the statute by which anyone is bound to pray. Let those see how they satisfy the command of the Church who do not express the seven canonical prayers by the utterance of words, but with closed mouth run through the sequence of prayers by thought alone, with their eyes assisting. But in those prayers which we undertake to say not by command but by our own will and from devotion alone, the fervor of the mind toward God suffices without the utterance of words, because, as we have said, God requires such worshippers as adore in spirit and truth. But the canonical prayers, which they call the hours, we are bound to say, and not merely to think. In both cases devotion of mind toward God is useful; without it no prayers are believed to be effective.

And so, my brothers, when we stand for prayer, we ought to watch with the greatest zeal and attend to the prayers which we pour forth, lest we pray without the fruit of inward compunction. Therefore let every thought of the flesh depart far away; let no occupation with household affairs hinder the mind; nor let the soul then think anything else at all except this alone which is being said. Therefore also the priest, after the preface has customarily been sent before the sacrifice, prepares the minds of the brothers, saying, Lift up your hearts, so that when the people answer, We have them with the Lord, he may admonish them that they ought to think of nothing other than the very God whom they invoke. Let the breast therefore be closed against the adversary and lie open to the Lord alone; and in the time of holy prayer let no one admit any occupation of the world at all.

Great is the usefulness of pure prayer, which, like a faithful messenger, carries out the command of the fervent mind, and, flying, ascends into heaven, where flesh does not reach. For prayer is sustained by two wings, so that it may fly up into heaven; one of these is called fasting, and the other is named almsgiving. Hence Saint John Chrysostom says: Nothing is more powerful than a person praying, who prays with

Homily VIII. Fol. xviii.

[fasting?]: because it has two wings, and neither strays nor grows sluggish. Let us therefore pray in the highest fervor of spirit, and let us live with as much purity of conscience as we can, because that prayer is perfect and pleasing to God whose cause and tongue alike cry out, whose deeds and speech agree with its supplication, whose life and thought lend patronage to its petitions. For without the justice of truth every prayer will be fruitless, because we know that God does not hear sinners, and that salvation is far from sinners, as Scripture says: “He who turns away his ears so as not to hear the laws, his prayer will be abominable.” The holy prophet also says in the psalm: “If I have regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me.” For just as in a wound no medicine is of any benefit unless the iron is first drawn out, so the prayer of that man is of no benefit while deceit still remains in his mind or hatred in his breast.

But in order that God may hear your prayer, first of all the conscience must be cleansed from every stain of mortal sin, and the mind must take on a true purpose of amendment. To pray much and at the same time offend in many things: what else is this than to mock God? For in two ways prayer is hindered, so that it is not heard by the Lord: one, when the one praying still commits evil by sinning; the other, if he has not, for God’s sake, forgiven his debtor the debt. Therefore you who desire to have the fruit of your prayers, who wish to come with the penitent to God’s mercy, take care that you do nothing evil against God’s will, and diligently see to it that you truly forgive from the heart all things committed against you by men. For you know that the Lord said: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven.”

But after you have cleansed your conscience from evil and forgiven every offense to your neighbor, then you will be ready to entreat the Lord, casting yourself humbly down in his sight; and pray with purity of heart and fervor of spirit, nor cease from prayer as long as you live in the flesh. Let your prayer be pure, simple, clear, and manifest; let it be full of gravity and weight, and adorned with the beauty of true humility. Do not ask anything in prayer contrary to the salvation of the soul, nor pray too importunately for a temporal thing, because it is shamelessness to ask riches from God, which furnish the greatest occasion for pride and often defile Christian purity. It is not shamelessness if you ask for daily bread, because it is one thing to ask for material by which you may become proud, and another to ask for necessary nourishment by which you may live.

Do not justify yourself when praying, lest like the Pharisee you go away condemned; nor ask anything from the Lord as if by debt owed to your merits, but humble yourself in all things, so that you may deserve to receive grace. Remember the humility of the publican, and pray with such humility that you may find with him pardon for sins and justification of the soul. For God’s grace is more abundant than the prayer of the suppliant, and he grants us more when we pray than we ask. You will not pray with a cry of the voice to him who knows the hidden things of the heart, but in the fervor of spirit and the inward cry of the mind strike the ears of the divine majesty. Nor should you draw out a length of words before him who is spirit, because God will be appeased not by much speaking but by the devout mind of the one praying.

At the time of prayer cast away from yourself every malice and unrest of heart, and, as we often say, forgive if you have anything against your neighbor. For unless for love of the Savior you forgive your neighbor every debt, you will obtain nothing from the Lord by your prayers. It is said that there is a certain kind of serpent which, when it wishes to go into the water to drink, first vomits out all its poison. You also, monk, imitate this serpent in this respect: vomit out all the poison of anger and bitterness, forgiving your brother a hundred denarii, so that the Lord may forgive you ten thousand talents. As you desire the Lord to be toward you, so also show yourself toward your fellow servant. Call upon the Lord with your whole heart and you will find him; let your prayer be ardent and most pure, so that your mind may be joined to him in most holy love.

Strive for this throughout your whole life: that you may offer pure prayer to the Lord God at all times. He does not act with levity, nor is his judgment easily moved; what he promised is fixed. If you pray earnestly, you will see a miracle. Remember that you stand beneath the gaze of God, who understands all the secrets of hearts and knows the hidden things of minds. Therefore stand watchfully in the sight of him who knows all things, and pray with as much fervor of spirit as you can, that [unclear] liij

Quod sine intermissione sit orandum. misericordiam consequi merearis. Nam oratione sancta mundatur conscientia pe- nitentis: et qui cor isuum in vera puritate ad dominū erigit: eius oratio vacua non redit. O si sciretis fratres charissimi quā grate sint deo pure mentis orationes: et quantā anime cōferant vtilitatē: nullum transire tēpus sine precibꝰ sineretis. Ora- tio enim nostra si pura fuerit et ardens in feruore spiritus. nūcius est fidelissimus ad deū: pro nobis deo loquitur: et omnia que saluti nostre sūt necessaria obtinet dū p̄catur Quo circa vos admoneo et in ve- ra charitate exhortor vt sine intermissiōe oretis: nec a sancti spiritꝰ feruore vnquaꝫ cessetis. Non sit vobis vlluꝫ tempus va cuū vel in torpore mentis ociosum. In ti- more domini semper queso vigiles et solli citi estote: quatenus temptationes immi- nentes fortiter possitis vincere ac supera- re. Hoc vt cogitationes sordide menteꝫ pulsare ceperint. ad studium orationis re- currite: et minime vobis poterunt preuale- re. Oratio nanqꝫ grandis munitio est ani- me: in cuiꝰ presentia deficiūt omnes ma- chinationes partis aduerse. Per oratiōes em purissimas omnia nobis a deo tribu- untur vtilia: et cuncta procul effugantur aduersa. Mens orationibꝰ puris in amo- re dei valenter accenditur: et quicquid oc- currerit leuioris macule orando purgat̉. Orationibus sanctis et continuis mūdꝰ vincitur: anime pestes deuotis precibus sanantur: lachrymis et fletu superatur dia- bolus: et cui mille cohortes ad pugnādū non sufficiūt: vnius oratione pauperis in- firmatur. Quemadmodū a facie ignis ce- ra liquescens resoluit̉: sic ad orationis pu- re feruorem omnis demonū potentia con- trita eneruat̉. Si cogitatio turpis animo tuo ꝑ demones immissa fuerit: impresso mox frōti signo crucis dicitio. Salua me iesu christe: mediator dei et hominū: et cun- ctaꝫ a me hostis antiqui depelle nequitīa per tuam innocentissimā passionē. Quid hac oratione breuius: quid ve potentius esse potest? Nam statim vt contra demo- nū vel presentiā vel sugestionē cuꝫ feruo- re mentis prolata fuerit: omnis iniquita- tis machinatio recedit. Orationis enim pure virtus est maxima: quoniam et celuꝫ penetrat: et sua constantia debellat aerias potestates. Oratio mente illuminat: affe- ctū purificat: veniaꝫ delictoruꝫ impetrat: spiritum in dei amore contra omnes ad- uersarios confortat. Fihil sic mentem a terrenis ad celestiuꝫ amorem eleuat: nihil carnis voluptates tam cito et valenter ex- terminat: nihil adeo illustrat intellectum: nihil quoqꝫ intantuꝫ veritatis confundit aduersariū: sicut oratio pura que cū feruo- re diuini amoris ad deū funditur: et bone testimonio conscientie decorat̉. Si denio nibus cupis esse terribilis: si dei vis esse amicus: conscientiaꝫ habeto puram. et spi- ritualem nūquam intermittas orationeꝫ Omnia enim deuota potest oratio: si recti- tudine fidei et vite puritate oco retur. Ora- tio demones fugat: virtutem malignan- tiuꝫ eneruat: languescentem in tepiditate animā sanat: ac debilem et infirmū in dei timore spiritū cōfirmat. Oratio pura deo facit proximū: et eum quem acceperat ser- uuꝫ. dei facit esse amicuꝫ. Oratio pura et feruens in amore dei celum penetrat: in- tellectum orantis mirabiliter illuminat. infernu claudit: paradysū a perit: animas fidelium introducit. Ueritas eniꝫ nō me- titur: que in sancto euāgelio promittit di- cens. Petite et dabiur vobis: q̄rite et in- uenietis: pulsate et aperietur vobis. Om- nis eniꝫ qui petit accipit: et qui querit inue- nit: et pulsanti aperietur. Quis vestros in toto corde suo conuersus ad dominū ora- uit vnquam et non est ex auditus? Aut qͥs inuocauit domini: qui amalech confidenteꝫ in virtute sua. non ferro pugnando sed preci- bus sanctis orando deiecit. Multum em̄ yalet de precatio iusti assidua: et oratio hu- miliantis se penetrat nubes. Helias ho- mo erat similis nobis passibilis: et oꝛavit oratione vt non plueret super terram et non pluit annos tres et mēses sex. Et rufum oranit et celum dedit plurium: et terra dedit fructum suum. Oratione et la- chrymis rex ezechias quindecim annos vitē lōgioris obtinuit: et ꝓphete sententiā precibus mutauit. Orationibus viri san- cti claruerunt miraculis: et supplicantes ad dominum mortuos reuocarunt ad vi- tam. Orationis etiam puritati subiecta sunt omnia: et nihil est in nobis tam diffi- cile: quod oratio deuota et feruidan eque

That one must pray without ceasing.

...that you may deserve to obtain mercy. For by holy prayer the conscience of the penitent is cleansed; and he who raises his heart to the Lord in true purity, his prayer does not return empty. O, if you knew, dearest brothers, how pleasing to God are the prayers of a pure mind, and how much benefit they confer upon the soul, you would allow no time to pass without prayers. For our prayer, if it is pure and burning in the fervor of the spirit, is a most faithful messenger to God; it speaks to God on our behalf, and obtains all things that are necessary for our salvation while it prays.

Therefore I admonish you and exhort you in true charity to pray without ceasing, and never to cease from the fervor of the Holy Spirit. Let there be no time for you empty or idle in sluggishness of mind. In the fear of the Lord, I beg you, always be watchful and attentive, so that you may be able bravely to conquer and overcome the temptations that threaten. As soon as foul thoughts begin to knock at the mind, run back to the practice of prayer, and they will be in no way able to prevail against you. For prayer is a great fortification of the soul; in its presence all the contrivances of the opposing side fail. For through the purest prayers all useful things are granted to us by God, and all adversities are driven far away.

The mind is powerfully kindled in the love of God by pure prayers, and whatever occurs of a lighter stain is cleansed by praying. By holy and continual prayers the world is conquered; the plagues of the soul are healed by devout petitions; by tears and weeping the devil is overcome; and he for whom a thousand cohorts are not sufficient for battle is weakened by the prayer of one poor man. Just as wax, melting before the face of fire, is dissolved, so at the fervor of pure prayer all the power of demons, crushed, is enervated.

If a base thought has been cast into your mind by demons, then at once, with the sign of the cross impressed upon your forehead, say: Save me, Jesus Christ, mediator of God and men, and drive away from me all the wickedness of the ancient enemy through your most innocent passion. What can be briefer than this prayer, or more powerful? For as soon as it has been uttered with fervor of mind against the presence or suggestion of demons, every contrivance of iniquity withdraws. For the power of pure prayer is very great, since it both penetrates heaven and by its steadfastness overthrows the powers of the air.

Prayer illuminates the mind, purifies the affection, obtains pardon for sins, and strengthens the spirit in the love of God against all adversaries. Nothing so raises the mind from earthly things to the love of heavenly things; nothing so quickly and powerfully destroys the pleasures of the flesh; nothing so illumines the understanding; nothing likewise so greatly confounds the adversary of truth, as pure prayer, which is poured out to God with the fervor of divine love and is adorned by the testimony of a good conscience. If you desire to be terrible to demons, if you wish to be a friend of God, have a pure conscience and never interrupt spiritual prayer.

For devout prayer can do all things, if it is [offered?] with uprightness of faith and purity of life. Prayer puts demons to flight, enervates the power of the malign, heals the soul languishing in tepidity, and strengthens the spirit that is weak and infirm in the fear of God. Pure prayer makes one near to God, and him whom it had received as a servant it makes to be a friend of God. Pure prayer, fervent in the love of God, penetrates heaven, wonderfully illuminates the understanding of the one praying, closes hell, opens paradise, and brings in the souls of the faithful.

For Truth does not lie, who in the holy Gospel promises, saying: Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and he who seeks finds, and to the one knocking it shall be opened. Which of you has ever turned to the Lord with his whole heart and prayed, and has not been heard? Or who has called upon the Lord, who cast down Amalek, trusting in his own strength, not by fighting with iron but by praying with holy prayers? For the continual supplication of the just man avails much, and the prayer of one humbling himself penetrates the clouds.

Elijah was a man subject to suffering like us; and he prayed with prayer that it should not rain upon the earth, and it did not rain for three years and six months. And again he prayed, and heaven gave [rain?], and the earth gave its fruit. By prayer and tears King Hezekiah obtained fifteen years of longer life, and by prayers changed the prophet’s sentence. By prayers holy men shone with miracles, and, supplicating the Lord, recalled the dead to life. To the purity of prayer also all things are subject, and there is nothing in us so difficult that devout and fervent prayer

Omēlia.VIII. Fo.XIX. at impetrare.Tunc autē orantes fiduciā impetrandi quod postulamus a domino accipimus:cū precibus nostris vite pra- uitas nulla contradicit.Naꝫ iuste precis exauditor est dominus.quando videlic̄z orationem vite cōmendat integritas:et re atus conscientie nullus besitare facit oꝛā tem.Inter dissimiles non stabit amicicia et inter deū et peccatoꝛem non poterit esse cōmunio.Si vis exaudiꝛi orans:cura in primis vt a dei voluntate non discoꝛdes. Uine spiritu persimilis ꝺeo:et nullam pa tieris in oratione repulsaꝫ.Enimuero cō scientie puritas in feruoꝛe ꝺiuini amoꝛis hominem ꝺeo facit intellectu persimilem similitudo causat amorem:amoꝛ vero in- troduct familiaritatē:familiaritas confi dentiam:et confidentia petitionis conse- quitur facilem impetrationem. Nā sicut inter dissimilia non fit vnio:ita inter deuꝫ et hominem malum nihil proficit oꝛatio. Quicunque igitur vestrum orationum sua rum consequi ꝺesiderat effectum:in pri- mis per veram penitentiaꝫ coꝛdis sui ꝺo- micilium ab omni mundet delicto:ꝺein- de sancte compunctionis semetip̄m stuꝺ at inflāmare exercicio:postea mentem cō- tinue pascat in dei amoꝛis studio:quate- nus bonū quod incboaẗ:nullo ꝺinceps tempore intermittat.Postea vero quam crescente semper in eo ꝺiuini amoꝛis ꝺeisi derio.sācte puritatꝭ exercitiū lōgo studio ꝑduxerit in cōsuetudineꝫ et mens in bono ꝓposito necessariā cōceperit firmitatē:tūc primū similitudo ꝺiuine cōmuniōis pau latiꝫ introduicitur:et ad statū debitum oꝛa tio formatur.Nā quāto mēs in ꝺei amo re amplius excitata profecerit:tanto citiꝰ oratio quod postulat a domino impetra- bit.Solus etenim ꝺei amoꝛ facit oratio- ne esse potentem:m̄ quo mens quanto fer uentius arserit:tanto facilius petitionuꝫ suarū consequetur effectuꝫ.Nam si mul- tū amas:multum potes.Deus enim cha ritas est:et qui manet in charitate in ꝺeo manet:et deus in eo.Jn quo vero manet deus:nihil est illo foꝛtiuis:nisi ꝺeus ip̄e so lus. Sūt inter vos quidam infirmi et de biles animo q; se iam foꝛtes in via ꝺomi- ni existimant atque perfectos:quorū est et rara et hoꝛaria ꝺeuotio:qui sine veste nu- ptiali regno se apꝓpinquasse gloriantur ce lorum.cum tamē adhuc longe in inferio- ribus iaceant.His ego quod sepius dixi iterum ꝺico:quoniaꝫ nemo repente fit sū- mus:et nisi monachus omnes passiones suas animales per carnis macerationeꝫ ꝺomuerit:ad montē ꝺiuine contēplatio- nis altissimū non pertingit.Quisquis eī in cenobio sub potestate et obedientia cō- stitutus.voluntatem suā contra monasti cā institutioneꝫ sequitur:dignus non est vt in suis orationibus a domino exaudia tur.Isti auteꝫ ꝺ̄ qui bus loquimur in ocu lis suis magni sint et sapientes:qui pro- priaꝫ voluntatē diligētes ad omnia mur murāt:et quicquid ipsi non oꝛdinauerint. male factū putant.Actus fratrū suoꝛum curiosa inquisitione ꝺiscutiunt:suas vero ꝺiscernere negligentias contentunt.Jn moꝛibns sūt dissoluti et incōpositi:i n ver- bis leues et clamosi:ad obedientiā inuo- luntarij.et semper in bonis operibus tar- di et accidia pleni.Communia oꝛdinis ex ercitia negligunt:priua tis iuxta volunta tem pꝛopꝛie inten dunt.Et quam ꝺiu ī sua te meritate permanent:ad verum ꝺei amorem non consurgunt.Audiant quid ꝺominus ꝺicat:monachi pꝛopꝛie volūta tis amatoꝛes.Non veni vt faciam volun tateꝫ meam:sed eius qui misit me patris Hunc fratres preceptoꝛem attendite:ad cuius imitationem nisi vixeritis:sine fru- ctu orabitis.Eius namque orationem libē ter exaudit ꝺn̄s:q̇ mādata eius in verita- te custodit.Qui vero ꝺei mandatū trans- gredit.q; carnis voluptates et mūdi sola- tia cuꝫ ꝺesiderio sequitur:eius oꝛatio non ex auditur.Deus namque iustus et rectus tunc orationem tuā libenter exaudire cre ditur:quādo mens et vita bona simul ꝺe precantur.Cuius autem cōuersatio ꝺeo ꝺisplicet:oꝛatio eius quo modo placebit? Deus enim spiritus est:et homo q̇ non in spū sed in carne ambulat:certe ad ꝺeum minime apꝓpinquat.Tu itaque monache q̇ ad puritatē euāgelij et regule nō ambu- las:q̇ pꝛopꝛiaꝫ non dei voluntatē amas. scito qm̄ oꝛationū tuarū nō senties effica ciam:nisi priꝰ emendaueris vitā.Nisi em̄ cōuersatio tue concor dauerit oꝛatiōi: non impetrabis quod precaris. Homily VIII.

Folio XIX.

to obtain. Then, when we pray, we receive confidence of obtaining from the Lord what we ask, when no perversity of life contradicts our prayers. For the Lord is the hearer of a righteous prayer, namely when integrity of life commends the prayer, and no guilt of conscience makes the one who prays hesitate. Friendship will not stand between those unlike each other, and between God and a sinner there can be no communion. If you wish to be heard when you pray, take care first that you do not differ from the will of God. Live in the spirit most like to God, and you will suffer no rejection in prayer. For indeed purity of conscience, in the fervor of divine love, makes a man like to God in understanding; likeness causes love; love introduces familiarity; familiarity, confidence; and upon confidence there follows the easy obtaining of one’s petition. For just as there is no union among things unlike, so between God and an evil man prayer avails nothing.

Therefore whoever among you desires to obtain the effect of his prayers, let him first, through true penitence, cleanse the dwelling-place of his heart from every fault; then let him strive to inflame himself by the exercise of holy compunction; afterward let him continually feed his mind in the pursuit of the love of God, so that the good which he begins he may thereafter at no time interrupt. But afterward, when, with the desire of divine love always increasing in him, he has by long effort brought the exercise of holy purity into habit, and the mind has conceived the necessary firmness in its good purpose, then for the first time the likeness of divine communion is gradually introduced, and prayer is formed to its due state. For the more the mind, stirred up in the love of God, has advanced, the more quickly will prayer obtain from the Lord what it asks. For the love of God alone makes one powerful in prayer; and in it, the more fervently the mind has burned, the more easily it will obtain the effect of its petitions. For if you love much, you can do much. For God is charity, and he who remains in charity remains in God, and God in him. But in him in whom God remains, there is nothing stronger than he, except God himself alone.

There are among you certain men weak and feeble in spirit, who already consider themselves strong and perfect in the way of the Lord; their devotion is both rare and fleeting, and they boast that without the wedding garment they have approached the kingdom of heaven, although they still lie far off in the lower places. To these I say again what I have often said: that no one suddenly becomes the highest, and unless a monk has subdued all his animal passions through the mortification of the flesh, he does not reach the very high mountain of divine contemplation. For whoever, placed in a monastery under authority and obedience, follows his own will against monastic discipline, is not worthy to be heard by the Lord in his prayers.

But those of whom we speak are great and wise in their own eyes: loving their own will, they murmur at everything, and whatever they themselves have not arranged they think badly done. They examine the actions of their brothers with curious inquiry, but are content to neglect discerning their own negligences. In their morals they are lax and disorderly; in words frivolous and loud; unwilling toward obedience, and always slow in good works and full of sloth. They neglect the common exercises of the order and attend to private ones according to their own will. And as long as they remain in their own rashness, they do not rise up to the true love of God. Let monks who love their own will hear what the Lord says: “I came not to do my own will, but that of the Father who sent me.” Brothers, attend to this teacher; unless you live in imitation of him, you will pray without fruit. For the Lord gladly hears the prayer of him who keeps his commandments in truth. But he who transgresses the commandment of God, who follows with desire the pleasures of the flesh and the consolations of the world, his prayer is not heard.

For God, just and upright, is believed then gladly to hear your prayer when a good mind and a good life make supplication together. But if a man’s conduct displeases God, how will his prayer please him? For God is spirit, and a man who walks not in the spirit but in the flesh certainly does not approach God at all. Therefore you, monk, who do not walk according to the purity of the Gospel and the Rule, who love your own will and not God’s, know that you will not feel the efficacy of your prayers unless you first amend your life. For unless your conduct agrees with your prayer, you will not obtain what you ask. Then you cry to the Lord with one great voice, when even with the tongue silent you cry out with good works. For good prayers and evil conduct merit nothing good. Therefore do what a certain wise man advised: and if you have sinned, do not cast yourself away again, but pray also concerning your former sins, that

38
tibi dimittantur. Ante orationes prepara animā tuaꝫ: et noli esse quasi homo qͥ tenꝑat deuꝫ. Sit mēs pura et ardēs in amo re domini: sit cōscīa mundā et in sancte cō uersationis proposito roborata: et erit ora tio diuinis auribꝰ grata. Si aliter oraue¬ ris:nihil impetrabis. Bene orat qui bene viuit: et facile impetrati qui sanctis operibus orat:Denciqꝫ oratio multuꝫ redditur efficax et grata ī cōspectu dei: si fuerit om ni tempore cōsonans passiōi domini no- stri iesu christi. Christus enim deus est et homo mediator inter deuꝫ et nos: per quē tutuꝫ a ccessuꝫ habemus ad patreꝫ: sicut ipse testatur in sancto euangelio. Nemo inquit venit ad patrem nisi per me. Unde nulla pretereat dies in qua christo ad mi nus semel orando gratias non agas: qui snorū dolore vulneruꝫ anime tue sana uit languores: qͥ sanguineꝫ pro te suū effudit et moꝛte sua innocentissima de mortis ꝑ petue interitu te miseruꝫ redemit: Homo certe ingratissimus est et christiano voca¬ bulo indignus: qui tantorū beneficiorum christi vsqꝫ adeo fuerit obliuiosus: vt nō quotidie vel semel ad minus gratiarū illi referat actiones. Monachus aut̄ qui se- culo mortuus deo soli viuere iubetur: do¬ minice passionis memoriaꝫ in suo pectore iugiter portet: semper gratias agēs suo redemptori: semper benedicēs: semp ado¬ rans: et quotidie īmo quantuꝫ fieri potest singulis momētis amaritudinē vulnerū christi cū lachrymis cōpaciēdo reuoluat Omni die post orationes singulas regu lares quas greci appellāt canonicas: fie¬ xis genibus et elevata mente in celū dicat Gracias ago tibi et benedicēs adoro te o mediator dei et hominū christe iesu dulcis sime deus et homo: pro incarnatione tua sanctissima. pro natiuitate tua ex virgine. pro circūcisione. pro fuga in egyptum et se ptenni in exilio quod pro nobis sustinui- sti. Adoro te domine saluator iesu christe pro laboribus tuis. pro fame et siti. frigo¬ re ac nuditate: pro itineribus tuis. pro do ctrina et predicatione tua: pro miraculis tuis pro vocatōe gentiū: et pro iustificatio ne peccatoruꝫ. Ago tibi gratias domine fili dei viui. pro dolore vulnerū tuorum: bendico te pro effusione sanctissimi sang uinis tui: adoro te pro morte tua quam in nocentissime sustinuisti: et rogo te per om nem passionē tuā pietatem et clementiam miserere mei nunc et in hora moꝛtis mee. Hāc breuissimā orationē in die ad minꝰ septies deuotus monachus perorabit: vt quotiēs coraꝫ imagine crucifixi trāsierit simili modo cum feruore mentis christū adorabit. Qui verus christi amator est: christū semper cogitat: christū loquitur et veneratur: christum sibi nō dubitat vbiqꝫ esse presentem. Eius memorie passio chri- sti nunquaꝫ deest. et pre amoris magnitu dine seip̄m obliui scitur: et in christo mēte et desiderio totus occupat̉. In amore chri sti quisqͥs feruet animo, terrena contēnit. carnē vincit sola celestia cōcupiscit. Chri- stum vigilans semp cū desiderio cogitat dormiēs christum somniat: et continue su spirans. cum diuo ignacio clamat Am or meus crucifixus est. Suspirij s coniūgit suspiria: et iesuꝫ queꝫ toto corde suo diligit non oculis sed spiritu presente cernit. Ur gente amoris desiderio quotiens crucifi¬ xum intuetur. mox in lachrymas resoluit̉ et estuans charitatis incēdio vociferatur. O amor cunctis fortitudinibus for tior. quā dulciter ardet qͥ christi d̓siderio inflā matur. Recte locutꝰ est qui dixit Fortis est vt mors dilectio. Quid enīqꝫ fortius es se potest amore christi: cuius ardore sācti martyres tot milia genera mortis contē- nentes superauerunt? O amor crucifixe meꝰ miserere mei da mihi eam de qua lo quoꝛ dilectionis tue sentire dulcedineꝫ: vt semper in coꝛde meo circumferam tuam amarissimā passionem Scio fratres mei scio quod non est effica cioꝛ modus oran di. nec vtilior nobis qui adhuc sumus in firmi: quaꝫ in memora et virtute passiōis domini nostri iesu christi Unde cum sit manifestum quod sine mediatore non est ascensus mentis ad deum: omne opꝰ bo num in christi nomine est inchoandū: qͥa tunc preces ad deuꝫ vtiliter effundimus cum purificata conscientia per eius vni¬ genitum filium oramus. De custodia et origi- ne cogitationum: Omelia nona. Salomon rex il le quondaꝫ sapientissimus in libro quem prouerbio¬ rum prenotauit filium

…may be forgiven you. Before [your] prayers, prepare your soul, and be not as a man who tempts God. Let the mind be pure and ardent in the love of the Lord; let the conscience be clean and strengthened in the purpose of a holy way of life; and the prayer will be pleasing to the divine ears. If you pray otherwise, you will obtain nothing. He prays well who lives well; and he easily obtains who prays with holy works. Finally, prayer is rendered much effective and pleasing in the sight of God, if it be at all times consonant with the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ. For Christ is God and man, the mediator between God and us, through whom we have safe access to the Father, as he himself testifies in the holy Gospel: "No one," he says, "comes to the Father but through me." Whence let no day pass on which you do not at least once give thanks to Christ by praying—who by the pain of his wounds healed the languors of your soul, who shed his blood for you, and by his most innocent death redeemed you, wretched, from the destruction of perpetual death. Truly a man is most ungrateful, and unworthy of the Christian name, who is so far forgetful of Christ's so great benefits that he does not daily, or at least once, render thanksgivings to him. But let the monk—who, dead to the world, is bidden to live for God alone—carry continually in his breast the memory of the Lord's passion, always giving thanks to his Redeemer, always blessing, always adoring; and daily—nay, as much as can be done, in every single moment—let him with tears, compassionating, turn over [in his mind] the bitterness of Christ's wounds. Every day, after the several regular prayers which the Greeks call canonical, with knees bent and mind raised to heaven let him say: "I give thanks to you, and blessing [you] I adore you, O mediator of God and men, Christ Jesus, most sweet God and man, for your most holy incarnation, for your nativity from the Virgin, for [your] circumcision, for the flight into Egypt and the seven years in exile which you endured for us. I adore you, Lord Savior Jesus Christ, for your labors, for [your] hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness; for your journeys, for your teaching and preaching, for your miracles, for the calling of the nations, and for the justification of sinners. I give you thanks, Lord, Son of the living God, for the pain of your wounds; I bless you for the shedding of your most holy blood; I adore you for your death which you most innocently endured; and I beseech you, by your whole passion, [your] piety and clemency, have mercy on me now and in the hour of my death." This most brief prayer the devout monk will recite at least seven times a day, so that as often as he passes before the image of the Crucified, in like manner, with fervor of mind, he may adore Christ. He who is a true lover of Christ always thinks of Christ, speaks of and venerates Christ, [and] does not doubt that Christ is everywhere present to him. The passion of Christ is never absent from his memory; and through the greatness of love he forgets himself, and in Christ is wholly occupied in mind and desire. Whoever is fervent in soul in the love of Christ despises earthly things, conquers the flesh, [and] desires only heavenly things. Waking, he ever thinks of Christ with desire; sleeping, he dreams of Christ; and, continually sighing, with the divine Ignatius he cries: "My love is crucified." He joins sighs to sighs, and Jesus—whom he loves with his whole heart—he discerns present, not with his eyes but with his spirit. With the desire of love urging [him], as often as he gazes on the Crucified, he soon dissolves into tears, and, glowing with the fire of charity, cries out: "O love stronger than all strengths! How sweetly he burns who is inflamed with the desire of Christ!" Rightly did he speak who said: "Love is strong as death." For what can be stronger than the love of Christ, by whose ardor the holy martyrs, despising so many thousand kinds of death, overcame [them]? O my crucified love, have mercy on me; grant me to feel that sweetness of your love of which I speak, that I may always carry about in my heart your most bitter passion. I know, my brothers, I know that there is no more effective mode of praying, nor more useful to us who are still weak, than to be in the memory and power of the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ. Whence, since it is manifest that without a mediator there is no ascent of the mind to God, every good work must be begun in the name of Christ; for then we usefully pour out prayers to God, when with purified conscience we pray through his only-begotten Son.

Om̄ia .IX. Fo.xx. ad veram cohortatus sapientiam. inter cetera dixit. Fili mi attēde sapiensiā meā et prudentie mee inclina aurem tuam: vt custodias cogitationes: et disciplinam la bia tua conseruent. Non enĩz minima sa pientie pars est fratres charissimi. si sciat monachus cogitationes suas prudenter dicernere: et earum motus omni tempo re sollicite custodire. Magnares est nihil cogitare mali: sed non minoris prudẽ tie malas ab exordio cogitationes posse repellere. Humani etenim cordis profũ da sententia. mobilis. varia. multiplex et instabilis semper: cuius obseruare princi pia et refrenare motus: summa prudẽtia est: et magnuꝫ sapientie signum. Holam si dixerō perpetuo motu agitatam cor hominis averitate non oberraui: maxime siquis eius inquietudinem examinissim pe̓ siculare voluerit. Quid naꝫ aliud est cor humanum quam mola quedam in mo cū semper conterens aliquid? Nunquaꝫ est ociosum cor humianum: nunquam sine motu quiescit: sed agit semper aliquid et sicut mola semetipsam consumit vacua motu proprio: ita cor hominis a semetip so turpiter defluit: dum boni cogita tio non constringit. Semper mouetur in aliquod obiectum cum amoris sui de siderio: semper molit: semper agit. semper circa aliquid occupatur delectabile. siue bonum fit siue malum. Sicut corpus nõ mouetur sine anima: sic mẽs hominis nõ manet fixa in bono nisi continue restricta fuerit per sancta exercitia. Propterea di exit in ecclesiastico vir sapiens. Iocũditas cordis hec est vita hoīs: et thesaurꝰ sine d̓ fectione sanctitatis: et exultatio viri est lō genitas. Diserere anime tue placẽs deo et contine. et congrega cor tuuꝫ in sanctitate eius: et tristiciā longe expelle a te. Quid est cõgregatio cordis: nisi diligens custo dia cogitationis? Cor etenĩz suum in san ctitate domini congregat: qui motus co gitationuꝫ suarū in timore dei iugiter ob seruat. Et ideo scriptura dicit. Omni cu stodia serua cor tuum: quoniam ex ipso vi ta procedit Sumunt auteꝫ cogitationes motuū suorum principia ex his que offe runtur a sensibus: que tanto euagãtur ꝑ siculosius: quanto minus iudicio ratiōis ab exordio considerantur. Quisquis igiti cogitationum suarũ vigilans esse deside rat: quisquis congregare cor suum in san ctitate domini optat: sensus suos exteriores in primis diligentissime custodiat: et frenũ prudentie singulis imponat. Hinc de auditu et visu scriptura sic p̄cipit Se pi aures tuas spinis. et linguam nequam noli audire: et ori tuo facito ostia: et seras auribus tuis. Beatꝰ homo qui obturat aures suas ne audiat sanguinem: et claudit oculos suos ne videat malum. In sā cto quoqƺ iob sic legimus Pepigi fedus cum oculis meis: vt ne cogitarem quidẽ de virgine. In eos vero qui ministerio sē suum corruerunt in foueam peccatorum sic dominus contestatur per prophetam hieremiam. Quia ascendit mors per fene stras vestras: ingressa est domos vestras disperdere paruulos deforis: et iuuenes de plateis. Mors per fenestras domos nostras ingreditur: quotiens iniqua co gitatio per ministerium visus vel auditꝰ ad mentem intromittitur. Domus enim conscientia est: de qua scriptura dicit Nisi te instanter tenueris in timore domini: cito subuertetur domus tua. qđ custodit eaꝫ Timore igit̉ domini munienda est domꝰ cõscientie: sensus quoqƺ diligentissime re frenandi sunt: qƺ custodire cogitationes suas nō sufficit: qui aures et oculos ab oc casiōe mali non auertit. Itaqƺ si vis cogitationũ tuaruꝫ custos esse prudẽs et verꝰ cõgregator cordis in sanctitate dn̄i: sepiaures tuas spinis cõpunctionis timoris dei ne audiãt malū: et oculos auerte tuoꝫ ne ꝑ visum introducāt pctm̄. Quod tibi nō licet concupiscere: noli cuꝫ desiderio videre: et quod habere nō expedit: noli cogitare. Multi perierũt ministerio sensuum et qđ videre incaute pergunt externa: sepiꝰ īteriora sua turpiter amiserũt. Qui nō timet periculuꝫ iaꝫ certe p̃pe interituꝫ est: et qui de sua p̄tute p̄sumit ad ruinam peccati festinanter currit Qui oculum vibrat in choruscationeꝫ fulguris excecabitur ad horaꝫ: et qđ considerat specieꝫ mulieres. nō erit īmunis a periculo. Illiꝰ laudo prudentiā monachi qđ in medio turbarũ est solꝰ. et sēsibꝰ suis p̄ponit cẽsorem: ne quid intromittat mali ad dominaꝫ. Stattuit iuxta portam custodes: qui gladio et fuste repellãt īcõposite irruētes Timor ei Om̄ia .IX. Fo.xx. De custodia et origine cogitationum

Works, IX. Fol. xx.

...having exhorted him to true wisdom. Among other things he said: “My son, attend to my wisdom, and incline your ear to my prudence, that you may guard your thoughts, and that your lips may preserve discipline.” For it is no small part of wisdom, dearly beloved brothers, if a monk knows how to discern his thoughts prudently and to guard their movements carefully at all times. It is a great thing to think nothing evil, but it is not a lesser mark of prudence to be able to repel evil thoughts from their very beginning. For the deep reflection of the human heart is ever shifting, varied, manifold, and unstable; to observe its beginnings and restrain its movements is the height of prudence and a great sign of wisdom. If I have called the heart of man a mill, driven by perpetual motion, I have not strayed from the truth, especially if anyone should wish to examine its restlessness most closely. For what else is the human heart than a kind of mill, always in motion, always grinding something? The human heart is never idle, never rests without movement, but is always doing something; and just as an empty mill consumes itself by its own motion, so the heart of man shamefully runs down from itself when thought of the good does not constrain it. It is always moved toward some object with the desire of its love; it is always grinding, always acting, always occupied with something delightful, whether it be good or evil. As the body is not moved without the soul, so the mind of man does not remain fixed in the good unless it has been continually restrained by holy exercises. Therefore the wise man said in Ecclesiasticus: “Joyfulness of heart is the life of man, and the treasure of holiness without failing; and the exultation of a man is length of days. Delight your soul in what is pleasing to God, and hold it in, and gather your heart in his holiness, and drive sorrow far from you.” What is the gathering of the heart, if not the diligent guarding of thought? For he gathers his heart in the holiness of the Lord who continually observes, in the fear of God, the movements of his thoughts. And therefore Scripture says: “With all custody guard your heart, because from it life proceeds.” But thoughts take the beginnings of their movements from those things which are presented by the senses; these wander the more dangerously the less they are examined from the outset by the judgment of reason. Therefore whoever desires to be watchful over his thoughts, whoever wishes to gather his heart in the holiness of the Lord, should first of all guard his outward senses with the greatest diligence, and set the bridle of prudence upon each of them. Hence Scripture commands thus concerning hearing and sight: “Hedge your ears with thorns, and do not listen to a wicked tongue; and make doors for your mouth, and bars for your ears.” “Blessed is the man who stops his ears lest he hear bloodshed, and closes his eyes lest he see evil.” We also read thus in holy Job: “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think of a virgin.” But against those who have fallen into the pit of sins through the service of their senses, the Lord thus bears witness through the prophet Jeremiah: “Because death has climbed in through your windows; it has entered your houses to destroy the little ones outside, and the young men from the streets.” Death enters our houses through the windows whenever a wicked thought is let into the mind through the service of sight or hearing. For the house is conscience, of which Scripture says: “Unless you hold yourself constantly in the fear of the Lord, your house will quickly be overthrown.” [unclear] guards it. Therefore the house of conscience must be fortified by the fear of the Lord; the senses too must be restrained with the greatest diligence, because he does not sufficiently guard his thoughts who does not turn his ears and eyes away from the occasion of evil. And so, if you wish to be a prudent guardian of your thoughts and a true gatherer of the heart in the holiness of the Lord, hedge your ears with the thorns of compunction and of the fear of God, lest they hear evil; and turn away your eyes, lest they introduce sin through sight. What it is not lawful for you to desire, do not look upon with desire; and what it is not expedient to have, do not think upon. Many have perished through the service of the senses, and because they proceed incautiously to see outward things, they have often shamefully lost their inner goods. He who does not fear danger is already surely near destruction; and he who presumes on his own virtue runs hastily toward the ruin of sin. He who flashes his eye into the brilliance of lightning will be blinded for the moment; and he who gazes upon the beauty of women will not be free from danger. I praise the prudence of that monk who is alone in the midst of crowds, and sets a censor over his senses, lest he admit anything evil to his lady. He sets guards beside the gate, who with sword and club repel those who rush in disorderly. Fear [unclear]

Propterea fra tres considerate sermones vestros: z ner mo loquatur verbum ad reni non pertis nens vel inuste vtilitatis:vel necessarie ra Omelia. IX. Fo. XXI.

The holy fear of the Lord never deserts the mind of a wise man; but, just as a strong and ever-watchful champion always stands at the prince’s side, so it guards the [house?] of the heart. He turns his ears away from all scurrility of words, and closes his eyes lest they see evil. He always walks according to the twelfth degree of humility, with his gaze fixed upon the ground, praying to the Lord with the prophet: “Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity; in your way give me life, O Lord.”

Go, I admonish you, brothers: direct your senses in the fear of the Lord, so that you may always be able to keep the dwelling of the heart clean and inviolate. Remember the Scripture, which says: “Be clean, you who carry the vessels of the Lord.” Consider, I pray, with how great a cleanliness and purity of mind you ought to shine, you who not only, by reason of the priestly order, carry the vessels of the Lord, but, what is more, are even yourselves the vessels of the Lord. For the holy lover of Christ, Paul, says: “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?” And again he says: “Or do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God, and you are not your own?” And elsewhere: “For the temple of God is holy, which you are.” And concerning that same Paul, in the Acts of the Apostles, the Lord said to Ananias: “Go, for this man is a vessel of election for me.”

The monk who performs priestly office in the Church of God is bound by a double reason to the observance of most holy purity. For the soldier of Christ, because of the vow which he made to God, must be pure, holy, and continually tireless in good works; and by reason of the priestly ministry, circumspect and most diligently watchful. For it is written: “Cursed is the man who does the work of God negligently.” You are ministers of almighty God, who daily sacrifice his Son at the altar; his work is entrusted into your hands, and therefore great purity of mind and body is demanded in your manner of life.

Therefore, in order that the chaste purity of the mind may remain, the instability of thought must be restrained. The senses must be guarded at all times, for through them the integrity of the mind is corrupted. For you are dead to the world and have now begun to live for Christ; it is not lawful for you to think anything except what is holy, nor is it fitting for you, ministers of God, to love anything earthly. For it is God whom you serve, O monks; it is the Almighty whom you minister to, my brothers. Live pure, holy, and innocent, because it is not fitting for you to be occupied with the business of the world, you who have been called to the soldiery of God.

Let love of God and purity of heart grow in you with time, so that the longer you live in this world, the holier you may become. Always turn yourselves away from every evil, so that you may be able to persevere without failing in good thoughts. Always raise the eyes of your mind to heaven, and do not occupy the sight of the flesh with perishable things. Also always close your hearing to every useless, vain, and foolish speech, and always think with fear on the future judgment of God. Do not pollute your hands with the unlawful and shameful touch of any things whatever, so that you may be able to sacrifice the Son of God with a clean body and a pure conscience.

In food and drink it is not the part of monks to distinguish flavors, nor is it fitting for the soldiers of Christ to love bodily delights. Nature requires few things, and rustic foods by which it may be nourished; appetite, however, unless it is restrained by the command of reason, is dragged toward unlawful things, through which the simplicity of nature is violated. Therefore flee excess in all things, and observe regular moderation in your way of living. Let none of you patiently listen to one who detracts from his brothers or speaks evil of his neighbor. Let each one of you restrain his tongue from useless speech, and let good monks blush to speak evil of any Christians.

Never let that warning of the Lord depart from your memory, spoken in the holy Gospel: “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. A good man from a good treasure brings forth good things, and an evil man from an evil treasure brings forth evil things. But I say to you that every idle word which men shall have spoken, they shall render an account for it on the day of judgment.” O sentence too greatly to be feared. If an account is demanded for idle speech, what do detraction, scurrility, and filthy speech deserve? Or if a useless word is judged guilty under the strict reckoning of examination, what will he answer who so readily speaks what is evil and harmful? An idle word is every utterance of men which has been spoken without just usefulness and lacks the reason of lawful necessity. Therefore, brothers, consider your words, and let no one speak a word not pertinent to the matter, or to just usefulness, or to necessary [unclear].

Scurrilitates: verba ociosia: & risum mouentia:eterna clausura in omnibus locis dānamus: & ad tale eloquium discipulů aperire os non permitimus. Triahic verborum genera sanctus pater Benedictus monachis interdictit: et eterna clausura in omnibus locis dānauit. Scurrilia videlicet ociosa: et risum mouentia Quid autem si scurrilitas: grammatico et nobis interpretatio declarauit. Est enim scurrilitatis vitius urbanitati et modestie oppositum: & iocularitas quedaz lasciva ritum pronocans auditorum sine verecū dia vel honestate inmoderatuz per verba et gestus qui non congruunt rationi nec virum decent bonum nec sapienti co ueniunt. Dicitur autem scurrilitas a scurr ra qui domos sequitur divitium lascivis et inhonestis verbis et gestibus auditores praenij vel stipis gratia pronocans adri sum. Et hoc genus verborum monachis unus pater Benedictus interdictit: & pe ritus dānauit: quoniam qui deo servit et merito abstine in conspectu eius p petuo a verbis turpibus et inhonestis in/ bentur. Inter scurrilitatem vero et multi loquium hoc interesse videtur: quod illa exceditratione inhonestatis: & ista causa superfluitatis. Illa est turpis et inhon/ estatis vero sine virtute superflua. Sut riloquium his recte coniungitur: quoniam non solum monachis verum etiam omnibus interdictis christianis. Vinc sanctus christi apostolus dicit. Fornicatio antem et omnis immunditia aut avaritia nec no minetur in vobis sicur decet sanctos: aut auripitudo: aut stultiloquium: aut scurrili tas que ad rem non pertinere: sed magis gratiarum actio. Verba ociosuz similiter monachis cunctis interdictur: quoniam a domino sicue auditis in sancto euange lio prohibetur. Risum quogz mouentia verba non decent homines christianos: & multominus conueniunt claustralibus Monachus em qui mortuus est mudo sua novissima semper cogitare precipit: risum vero et omnem presentis vite insole tiam pro dei amore vbicq locorum contē nere inebetur. of [unclear]. For you have heard the fearful sentence of the Lord, and you are not unaware of the command of our holy lawgiver, who says in the Rule: “Buffooneries, idle words, and words that provoke laughter we condemn to perpetual exclusion in all places, and we do not permit the disciple to open his mouth for such speech.”

Here holy father Benedict forbade three kinds of words to monks, and condemned them to perpetual exclusion in all places: namely, buffoonish, idle, and laughter-provoking words. What buffoonery is, the interpretation of the grammarians has declared to us. For the vice of buffoonery is opposed to refinement and modesty, and is a certain wanton jocularity provoking the laughter of hearers, without shame or honor, immoderate in words and gestures, which do not accord with reason, do not befit a good man, and are not suitable for a wise man. Buffoonery is so called from a buffoon, who follows the houses of the rich, provoking his hearers to laughter by wanton and dishonorable words and gestures for the sake of a reward or a coin.

And this kind of words holy father Benedict forbade to monks and condemned utterly, because those who serve God are rightly commanded to abstain perpetually, in his sight, from foul and dishonorable words. Between buffoonery and much-speaking there seems to be this difference: the former exceeds by reason of dishonor, the latter by reason of excess. The former is foul and dishonorable; the latter is superfluous without virtue.

Foolish talk is rightly joined with these, since it is forbidden not only to monks but also to all Christians. Hence the holy apostle of Christ says: “But fornication and all uncleanness or covetousness, let it not even be named among you, as befits saints; nor filthiness, nor foolish talk, nor buffoonery, which are not to the purpose, but rather thanksgiving.” Idle words are likewise forbidden to all monks, because they are prohibited by the Lord, as you have heard, in the holy Gospel. Words that provoke laughter also do not befit Christian people, and much less are they suitable for cloistered men. For the monk, who is dead to the world, is commanded always to think on his last things; but he is bound everywhere, for love of God, to despise laughter and every insolence of the present life. Laughter is a confused voice, declaring the inward joy of the mind with immoderate cheerfulness. But nothing

Dū vero cōsue tudini male tēpus concedit̉: quedā moꝑ

[unclear] humility, reverence, and subjection are required, lest anyone seem to speak more than is fitting. A man is known from his words, and he who multiplies utterances in his mouth is foolish in heart. A man’s speech is the witness of his conscience, and for one who loves modesty and innocence of heart, his words ought to be modest and without vanity. For you are ministers of the living God, my brothers: let no vain, useless, and idle word go out from your mouth, but only what is good for the edification of the hearers, so that it may increase charity in their minds, toward the illumination of the heart in the knowledge and love of the highest truth. Precious is the tongue of the monk that speaks nothing at all except what is holy, and worthy of blessing is the mouth from which nothing is brought forth except what is divine. Let each one keep his heart clean from every wicked thought, since he who is good in heart does not speak an evil word, and he who truly loves God does not utter idle speech. Apply every care and consideration to your thoughts, since evil must be watched there with principal attention, where it takes the beginning of its proceedings, so that as soon as it has begun to arise it may be cut off by the roots. For there is no thought of evil so weak that it does not grow with time, if it is nourished by the consent of the thinker. Therefore evil, while still weak, must be conquered immediately at the beginning, because when delay intervenes, even a very small evil gains strength, though in the beginning it may seem [unclear]. A great fire often arises from a small spark, and from a lesser thought a great sin sometimes rises up. When thought gives birth to delight, it is accustomed soon to burst into consent, and consequently into deed also, if it can cast itself headlong. But when the will, through delight, has granted consent to an evil thought for the deed, even if what the soul desires is not completed, nevertheless the sin has already been consummated before God. But what does Scripture say? Sin, when it has been consummated, brings forth death. For almighty God regards the will of man, whether he wills good or evil. Therefore he says in the holy Gospel: Whoever has looked at a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. God reckons the will as the deed whenever a person cannot bring into effect what he wished. Therefore again and again I admonish you, brothers, and with as much diligence as I can I solemnly urge you, that according to the holy Apostle you walk cautiously, not as fools, redeeming the time, because the days are evil. Watch most cautiously for the snares of the evil demon, and resist evil and unclean thoughts immediately from the beginning, because remedy is considered far too late when the disease has gained strength through long time. Accustom yourselves at all times to dwell upon good and holy thoughts, and you will easily be able to overcome the insolence of evil ones. For just as vessels filled with good liquids receive no external corruption, so minds filled with good thoughts do not admit the intemperance of evil ones. Since the eye of the heart is that by which God is seen, and through purity of conscience one arrives at the glory of eternal happiness. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: Blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God. A clean heart is the dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit, and where evil thought is not admitted, God without doubt abides. A clean heart is the seat of wisdom, and where purity of mind is guarded, no perils of adversity will harm. Be mindful of Scripture saying: Perverse thoughts separate from God, but tested virtue corrects the foolish. For wisdom will not enter a malicious soul, nor will it dwell in a body subject to sins. For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee the deceitful, and will withdraw himself from thoughts that are without understanding. But a perverse thought is any thought admitted that is contrary to evangelical purity; by commerce with it the mind of the thinker is defiled, whenever by thinking about and turning over those things that are opposed to God it takes delight in them. And those perverse thoughts separate the mind of the thinker from God and little by little cast it down into the depth of evils. For an evil and perverse thought, when it has penetrated, first poisons through the venom of delight; then it clouds reason; afterward it draws the will into consenting to the evil suggestion; finally it consummates sin in deed. From then on, an evil once presumed is practiced more freely, and all shame or fear is removed through habit. Sin is joined to sin, and little by little the habit of doing evil is strengthened. But when time is granted to an evil habit, a certain
