Om̄ia .xv. Fo. xxxv. ac nutabūdā eā reddit omīqꝫ integritatis ac puritatis contemplatione omnino de spoliat. Propterea magna discretiōe opꝰ est: vt et corpori cibus duntaxat impēdat̉ ad vite sustentationē necessarius: et nullꝰ indulgētie fiat excessus. Hinc ait diuus papa gregorius. Magnus discretionis labor est exactori ciboruꝫ corpori et aliqͥs impendere: et aliquid denegare: et nō dan do gulā restringere: et dando naturā enu trire. Per abstinentiā quippe vicia extin guenda sunt nō caro: et per cibū corpus alendū est non peccata. Sic ergo necesse est vt artē cōtinentie monachus in victu teneat: quatenus nō carnē: sed vicia occi- dat. Sepe em̄ dū in carne hostem ꝑsequi mur: spiritū deuotionis quē diligimus ꝑ īmoderatā abstinentiā seuere trucidamꝰ Sepius etiā dumarniiniū compatiē tes quasi conciui parcimus: ad preliū cō tra nos hostē enutrimus. Domināte aūt gule vicio: om̄e qd̓ homines fortiter ege- runt perdunt: qꝛ dū venter non restringit̉ simul onnes virtutes obruintur. Nā ad conflictū spiritualis agonis nō assurgit̉: si nō intra nos meripos positꝰ hostis: gu- le videlicet appetitꝰ: per nos iuuante deo prius edomet̉: qm̄ nisi ea que nobis sunt viciniora superauerimus: inaniter ad ea que sunt lōgius positā pugnaturi festina mus. Incassum nanqꝫ contra extraneos inimicos bellū in campo geritur: si intra orbis menia ciuis insidians habeat̉. De- monū insultus nunqͣꝫ vincimus: nisi gu- lam prius in nobismetipsis superemus. Nemo se fratres inani persuasione sedu cat: vt inter fabas et olera credat non esse peccatū: si animus nimia laxet voluptate percipiendi appetitū. Nam vbiqꝫ pōt in sumendo esseratus: dū vltra nature nor mā extendit̉ appetitus. Ecce carneꝫ siue in monasterio siue extra nūqͣꝫ comedimꝰ: pisces hic in rure campestri rarissime vi- demus: nemo inter nos vnqͣꝫ lautiora vi- dit cibaria: delicata habere nec possumꝰ nec quidē debemꝰ esculenta. Cibaria aūt nostra sunt ordeū: auena: fabe: pisa et ole- ra: lac qͥꝫ cascus et oua. Ex his vite nostre quotidiana ꝑcipimus sustentacula: quo- rū ne cōsurgat fastidiū: fames incitat ap- petitū. Pisces extra tempus ieiunij qua- drageusalis nobis vsqꝫ adeo sunt rari: vt vix in mẽse semel pauci afferant̉ ex na bo fluxmine atqꝫ minutissimi. Nullū est in tota burffeldenium reformatione ceno/ biu: minus in pisciū necessitate prouisum Sed nunquid ꝓpterea nō possimus gu- le viciū incidere: qm̄ lautiora cibaria non possumus inuenire? Enimuero cũ nō ci- bus in vicio sit sicutiam dictū est sed ap- petitus: nō minus pisorū aut fabarū co- mestor in edendo pōt delinquere: quā il- le qui cibos lautissimos et exquisitos con- fueuit mauducare. Non facit nos inopia penitus: nō minus pisorū aut fabarū comē- testor in edendo pōt destinat simplicē et rusticaruꝫ quo vtuncqꝫ sustentet̉ natura: hoc precor fratres mei curemus: ne in illo qd̓ nause am delictatis generat: cōscientia nostra  excessum polluat̉. Sumamus cũ pacien tia et gratiarū actione de eo quod dn̄s do- nauit quantū necessitas ipsa requirit: nec putemus diaboli nobis nō posse nocere insidias: qui primos in paradyso homīes nō lautiora cibo: sed modico et vili pomõ supplantauit. Non em̄ in cibo viciū est sʒ in appetitu: cũ aut interdicta nobis cōcu- piscimus: aut cōcessis auide inhibātes ali- ter utimur quā debemus. Nec minē plus decet abstinentia qͣ monachū: qui cuꝫ sit ad christi militiā specialiter vocatus: nō conuenit eius professioni quibuslibet va care delicijs. Paupertas nostra abstinen tie nobis quandā necessitatē indicit: qꝛ tā to nos facilius ad temperantiā possumꝰ restrīgere: quāto nos quo defluamur cibarijs: eo purius in sanctitate animi ie- innemus. Facilium em̄ in paupertate ser uat̉ temperantia, que in diuisijs quidē pe ricilitat̉ cicius. Qualis aūt debeat esse ci bus monachorū: beatus manifestat hic/ ronymus dicens in epl'a quadā ad pauli nū. Sit vilis et vespertinꝰ tibi cibus: ho lera videlicet et legumina: interdūqꝫ pisci culos edere paucos: ꝓ sũmis ducas de licijˢ. Qui christi desiderat: et illo celesti pane vescitur: non querit magnopere qͣꝫ de preciosis cibis stercus cōficiat. Ama tor christi abstinētiā diligit: ieiuniū vt vni cũ anime corporisque remediū colit: sũmo cauet studio: ne cor eius graue ē a crapu la: nec plus sumit ciborū: qͣꝫ cōtenta pau cis expostulat natura. Monachus aūt qͥ ieiiunium abijcit: qui nutriceꝫ virtutū absti- f iij De abstinentia et ieiunio monacho.

and renders it wavering, and strips it entirely of all contemplation of integrity and purity. Therefore great discretion is needed, so that food necessary for the support of life alone is supplied to the body, and no excess of indulgence occurs. Hence the holy Pope Gregory says: “It is a great labor of discretion to give something to the demanding body and to deny it something; by not giving, to restrain gluttony, and by giving, to nourish nature.” For through abstinence vices are to be extinguished, not the flesh; and through food the body is to be nourished, not sins. Thus, then, it is necessary that the monk maintain the art of continence in his diet, so that he kills not the flesh but vices. For often, while we pursue the enemy in the flesh, we severely slaughter, through immoderate abstinence, the spirit of devotion which we love. More often also, while we have compassion on the [unclear], as though sparing a fellow-citizen, we nourish an enemy for battle against us. But when the vice of gluttony rules, men lose everything they have done bravely; for when the belly is not restrained, all the virtues are overthrown together. For one does not rise up to the conflict of spiritual combat if the enemy placed very near within us, namely the appetite of gluttony, is not first subdued by us, with God’s help; because unless we overcome the things that are nearer to us, we hasten in vain to fight against those placed farther away. For war is waged in vain in the field against foreign enemies if within the walls of the city there is a citizen lying in ambush. We never overcome the assaults of demons unless we first overcome gluttony in ourselves.

Let no one, brothers, deceive himself by empty persuasion, so as to believe that there is no sin among beans and vegetables, if the mind loosens too far the appetite of receiving by excessive pleasure. For in taking food one can everywhere be [unclear], when appetite is extended beyond the rule of nature. See, we never eat meat either in the monastery or outside it; here in this open countryside we see fish very rarely; no one among us has ever seen more sumptuous foods; we neither can nor indeed ought to have delicate fare. Our foods are barley, oats, beans, peas and vegetables, milk also, cheese and eggs. From these we receive the daily supports of our life; and hunger stirs appetite so that disgust for them may not arise. Outside the time of the Lenten fast, fish are so rare for us that scarcely once in a month a few are brought from the river Nahe, and those very small. In the whole Bursfelde reform there is no monastery less provided with the necessity of fish. But can we therefore not fall into the vice of gluttony, because we cannot find more sumptuous foods? Indeed, since the vice is not in the food, as has already been said, but in the appetite, the eater of peas or beans can sin no less in eating than he who is accustomed to eat the most sumptuous and choice foods. Poverty does not make us wholly [unclear]; [unclear] simple and rustic [foods], by which nature may somehow be sustained. This, my brothers, I pray, let us take care of: that in that which produces loathing of delicacy our conscience not be polluted by excess. Let us take with patience and thanksgiving, from what the Lord has given, as much as necessity itself requires; and let us not think that the snares of the devil cannot harm us, since he overthrew the first men in paradise not by more sumptuous food, but by a small and common apple. For the vice is not in the food but in the appetite, when either we desire things forbidden to us, or, eagerly gaping after permitted things, we use them otherwise than we ought.

Nor does abstinence befit anyone more than a monk, who, since he has been specially called to the soldiery of Christ, ought not by his profession to have leisure for any delicacies. Our poverty imposes upon us a certain necessity of abstinence; for we can restrain ourselves to temperance all the more easily, since the less we overflow with foods, the more purely we fast in holiness of mind. For temperance is more easily preserved in poverty, but in riches it is indeed more quickly endangered. What the food of monks ought to be, blessed Jerome makes clear, saying in a certain letter to Paulinus: “Let your food be cheap and taken in the evening: namely vegetables and legumes; and sometimes consider it the height of delicacy to eat a few little fish. He who desires Christ and feeds on that heavenly bread does not greatly seek what dung he may make from precious foods. The lover of Christ loves abstinence; he cultivates fasting as the one remedy of soul and body; he takes the greatest care that his heart not be weighed down by surfeiting, nor does he take more food than nature, content with little, demands.” But the monk who rejects fasting, who [rejects] abstinence, the nurse of virtues—

On abstinence and fasting for the monk.

rentis odi: qui cibos cui aviditate ingurgitati: qui vinum aut siceram et quicquid in ebriare potest ad saciaret: quid potat: ipso monachi nomine indignus est: ercbisti non potest esse discipulus. Ve tempore: nolitris: in quibus iam clerici et monachi coplures virtutis abstinentie turpiter abiecerunt: qui populo dei nó minus exemplum quam verbo iter salutis premonstrare debuerant: comestationibus decliti: continuisque potationibus et voluptatibus: contra omnem honestatem: clericorum immersi: eum in perditionem eternae moris precedere festinant. Dicit autem scriptrura: Inicium vite hominis: panis et aqua. At nunc monachi et claustrales nostrí quicquid preciosius venditur: quicquid lautiús inueniunt: sibi magniúsum pribus comparant: suis ventribus ingurgitando sepeliunt: animam simúl et corpus per intemperantiam coarum punt. Inter epulas de ieiunio disputant et cum inebriati fuerint temperantiam laudant. Ibi vnlusquie victorem se gloriatur vicio: cum a gula et ebrieitate iam fuerit superatus. Videte inquit dominus noster iesus christus in sancto euangelio secundum Lucam: ne grauen tur corda vestra in crapula. Non decet hominem deo dicatum ad saciaretam co/medere vel bibere nec licet monacho pl9 quam natura exigit manducare. Magno discretionis mode/ramine omes vtamur claustrales opor quatenus ita corpus nutriat esculentis et pociulis: vt spiritui subseruiens possi vi/ nere: nó autur incrassati contra mentis imperiú incipiat lascivire. Procul semp absit sacieras: qm nihil sic inflamát cor/ pus et concitat membra genitalia sicut in digestus cibus et venter estuás vino sive ceruisia. Sponla christi vinuz fugiat pro veneno: qm aduersus adolescéntiá arma sunt vi/ nú et ipfa iuuent?: proclúvior ad gulá. Nó fic avaricia quatit adolescéntiá: nec inflat superbia: nec delectat ambitio: sic uetilla que nobis videntur concreta voluptatis

[unclear]: he who gulps down foods with greed, who drinks wine or strong drink and whatever can intoxicate to satiety, is unworthy of the very name of monk; he cannot be a disciple of Christ. Woe to our times, in which already very many clerics and monks have shamefully cast away the virtue of abstinence, who ought to have shown the people of God the way of salvation no less by example than by word. Given over to gluttonies, and immersed in continual drinkings and pleasures, contrary to all clerical propriety, they hasten to go before [unclear] into the perdition of eternal death. Scripture says: The beginning of a man’s life is bread and water. But now our monks and cloistered men buy for themselves at great cost whatever is sold more dearly, whatever they find more sumptuous; by gorging their bellies they bury it, and through intemperance corrupt soul and body alike. Amid banquets they debate fasting, and when they have become drunk they praise temperance. There each one boasts that he is victorious over vice, although he has already been conquered by gluttony and drunkenness. Our Lord Jesus Christ says in the holy Gospel according to Luke: See that your hearts are not weighed down in excess. It does not befit a man dedicated to God to eat or drink to satiety; nor is it lawful for a monk to eat more than nature requires. Let eating still hunger; let it not induce fullness. Let belches be far away, which satiety is accustomed to produce at feasts; let vomiting and undigested [unclear] not be heard among monks. It is necessary that all of us cloistered men use great moderation of discretion, so that one nourishes the body with foods and drinks in such a way that, serving the spirit, it may be able to live, and not, having grown fat, begin to grow wanton against the command of the mind. Let satiety always be far away, for nothing so inflames the body and stirs the genital members as undigested food and a belly hot with wine or beer. Hence Saint Jerome, admonishing Eustochium concerning temperance, the preserver of all virtues, says in a certain letter: Let the bride of Christ flee wine as poison; for wine and youth itself, more prone to gluttony, are weapons against adolescence. Avarice does not so shake adolescence, nor does pride puff it up, nor does ambition delight it, as do those [unclear] which seem to us innate in pleasure.

Omelia. XV. Fo. XXXVI. bis potuit novo. Quid enim damnavit prothoparentes nostros nisi malati transgressio: quoniam non fuit deo cura de cibo sed de obedientia. Nam si abstinuisset homo sicut ei preceperat omnipotens deus: certe per hanc obedientiam meruisset in sua innocencia fruitionem eterne felicitatis. Constat enim traditione scripturarum hominem sine merito liberti arbitrii non posse salvare: quoniam si gratia dei omnia operatur in omnibus: nemine saluabit sine cooperatione proprie voluntatis: exceptis duntarit in trinitatis nomine baptizatis infantibus: et qui liberum habere nequeunt vsu rationis. Nam sic ut arbitrium liberum nihil operatur ad salutem sine gratia salvatoris: sic dei gratia non saluabit adultum sine merito bone voluntatis. Primum autem homo in paradysco positus: mandatuniique dei per intemperantiam transgressus: meritum obedientie in bona voluntate non habuit: propterea miser et infelix proiecerit fuit. Sed omnipotenti dei miseratio collapsum ex infirmitate reformare ab eternitate statuit: quem deceptum invidia suggestione serpentes: potius quam propria malicia non ignoravit. Condonavit huc reatum passioni et morti vnigeniti filij sui in tempore nascentis de virgine: vt qui propria temeritate per intermediatoris obedientia reformaretur ad salutem. Imposibile nanque fuit perditum per inobedientiam genus humanum ad misericordiam creatoris pervenire: nisi per obedientiam talis mediatoris qui deus esset et homo: in quo et virtus esset potentie: et innocentia naturae. Eramus enim ceci per ignorantiam: et muti per taciturnitatem. Venit mediator dei et hominum christus iesus: destinatus ve illuminare omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum: dei mortalibus cognitionem tradivit: mortusque pro perditis maximam causam amoris redemptis consignavit. Intellectum erudivit per fidem qua deum cognoscimus: affectum concitauit per passionem: quo ipsum super omnia merito diligimus. Itaque si dominum redemporem nostrum integra sinceri cate diligimus: dignum est plane vt corpus nostrum pro eius amore castigem? Conducet enim nobis abstinentia nostra duplici ratione ad meritum: dum vi delicet feiunances per obedientiam statutis patrum sacrificium: et abstinentres per charitatem dei: nos redemptori nostro qui nostri causa mortem sustinuit gratos exhibemus. Abstinentia meruit aut gerit: obedientiam commendat: sapientiam et eruditionem prestat: affectum purgat: intellectum illuminat: victoriam contra demones tribuit: religionem perficit: veniam peccatorum impetrat: motus carnis illicitos domat: orationibus efficaci am conciliat: exemplum virtutis proximo declarat. Abstinentia mentem purificat: animam virtutibus ornat: infirmum corpusculum sanat. Qui diliget abstinentiam sapiens est: et qui iecium amat dominator fortis. Dens sobria domicilium sapientie: qui autem sectatur convivia: in egestate animi morietur. Difficile est hominem euader sapientem: qui vitam agit in delicis. Dauis contentatur naturae: et in modicis vite sanctas conseruat. Multis nocuit diutius continua voacitas: et plures crapula quam gladio perierunt. Consuetudo enim navaturam alterare videtur: et quanto diutius conualuit: tanto iam fortiter in quo liber negocia erit. Est apud Helueccios homo Nicolaus nomine cuius abstinentia totius germanie homines convertit in admirationem: et bodie sicue audiuitis in oceannium cum sanctitatis titulo nominatur. Is quondam ruricola in quodam Heluecciorum vico existens: mo re paganorum inter quattuordecim ius dicere consuevit altercantibus villanis. Contigit eum quodam tempore sententiam non posse reuocare sociorum quam putabat iniquam: metuensque salutis animae sue periculum: relictis domo: viro: filij: et cunctis mundi negocijs ac rebus solus in vicinum nemus pro dei secessis amore: in quo vitam solitarius agit. Et ecce annus bodie viceimus ex quo solitudinem ingressus abum non sumptis humanum. Omnibus notissima loquoz nec hominem in germania vivere putos qui famam buis miraculi non audieric Et ne quis forsitan in posterum simula tione deceptos nos credat: Heluecia nos vna cum prefulc Constanciensis ecclesie in testimonium citamus: qui mo res et vitaz eius curiosissime observant:

Homily XV. Fol. XXXVI.

[unclear] could [unclear] anew. For what condemned our first parents except the transgression of the commandment? For God’s concern was not with food but with obedience. For if man had abstained as almighty God had commanded him, surely through this obedience he would have merited, in his innocence, the enjoyment of eternal happiness. For it is established by the tradition of the Scriptures that man cannot be saved without the merit of free will, since, although the grace of God works all things in all, it will save no one without the cooperation of his own will, except only infants baptized in the name of the Trinity, and those who cannot have the free use of reason.

For just as free will accomplishes nothing toward salvation without the grace of the Savior, so the grace of God will not save an adult without the merit of a good will. But the first man, placed in paradise and having transgressed God’s commandment through lack of temperance, did not have the merit of obedience in a good will; therefore, wretched and unhappy, he was cast out. But the compassion of almighty God determined from eternity to restore him who had fallen through weakness, whom he knew to have been deceived by the envious suggestion of the serpent rather than by his own malice. He remitted this guilt to the passion and death of his only-begotten Son, born in time of the Virgin, so that he who had fallen by his own rashness might be restored to salvation through the obedience of the mediator. For it was impossible for the human race, lost through disobedience, to reach the mercy of the Creator except through the obedience of such a mediator, who would be God and man, in whom there would be both the strength of power and the innocence of nature. For we were blind through ignorance and mute through silence. The mediator of God and men, Christ Jesus, came, sent to enlighten every man coming into this world; he handed down the knowledge of God to mortals, and, dying for the lost, he sealed for the redeemed the greatest cause of love. He instructed the intellect through faith, by which we know God; he stirred the affection through his passion, by which we rightly love him above all things.

And so, if we love our Lord and Redeemer with the whole integrity of sincere charity, it is plainly fitting that we chastise our body for love of him. For our abstinence will conduce to merit for us for a twofold reason: namely, when by fasting, through obedience to the statutes of the fathers, we offer sacrifice, and when by abstaining through the charity of God we show ourselves grateful to our Redeemer, who endured death for our sake. Abstinence merits or bears [unclear]; it commends obedience; it supplies wisdom and instruction; it purges the affection; it enlightens the intellect; it grants victory against demons; it perfects religion; it obtains forgiveness of sins; it tames the unlawful motions of the flesh; it wins efficacy for prayers; it displays to one’s neighbor an example of virtue. Abstinence purifies the mind, adorns the soul with virtues, and heals the weak little body. He who loves abstinence is wise, and he who loves fasting is a mighty ruler. A sober mind is the dwelling-place of wisdom; but he who pursues banquets will die in poverty of soul. It is difficult for a man to become wise who lives his life in pleasures. [unclear] is content with the gifts of nature, and in modest things preserves a holy life. Continuous voracity over a long time has harmed many, and more have perished by gluttony than by the sword. For habit seems to alter nature, and the longer it has prevailed, the more strongly [unclear].

There is among the Helvetians a man named Nicholas, whose abstinence turns the men of all Germany to admiration, and today, as you have heard, he is named in [unclear] with the title of sanctity. He, once a farmer living in a certain village of the Helvetians, was accustomed, in the manner of the country people, to pronounce judgment among fourteen disputing villagers. It happened at one time that he could not revoke a decision of his companions which he thought unjust; and, fearing danger to the salvation of his soul, he left his house, wife, children, and all worldly business and possessions, and withdrew alone into a neighboring wood for the love of God, in which he lives a solitary life. And behold, today is the twentieth year since he entered the solitude without taking human food. I speak of things known to all, nor do I think there is any man living in Germany who has not heard the report of this miracle. And lest perhaps in future anyone believe that we have been deceived by pretense, we cite Helvetia, together with the prelate of the church of Constance, as witness; they observe his ways and life with the greatest care:

De abstinentia et ieiunio monachorũ. Acutissimus ingenio vir est: qui cū sit li- terarũ penitus ignarus: tn̄ quasi alter he- remita quondã anthonius sensum opti- me callet scripturaꝝ. Uidimus que diser- tissime cũ quodã disputauit magistro de sacramẽto altaris: que satis mirari nõ po- terit qui celestia ꝑ contemplatiõis studiũ minime gustauit. Hec ideo ĩtroduxeriin fratres quo intelligatis nihil esse tā diffi- cile: quod cōsuetudo multo tempore con- tinuata nõ efficiat leue. Sanctus iste ho- mo sicut ipse confiteť nõ subito ad huius abstinentie celsitudine peruenit: sed cum tempore successine p̃ gradꝰ: paulatim vi- delicet sibi de cibo subtrahens modicuʒ quousqƺ tandē abstinere potuit per totuʒ Abstinuit em̄ sicut diximus ab omni cor- ruptibili cibo iaʒ in annũ ferme vicesimu̇. Huiꝰ viri exemplo fratres mei vnusquis qʒ vestruʒ discat sibi quotidie alid de ci- bo et potu ꝓ dei amore subtribere: et assue scat corpori suo nõ quantũ pōt sedquan- tũ satis est ad nature sustentationem mi- nistrare. Paucis em̄ minimifqƺ boecio te- stante natura cōtenta est: cuius sacietateʒ si superfluis temptes vrgere alimẽtis: aut injocundũ fiet quod infuderis: aut noci- uũ. Multas egritudines: multa fercula pariunt:et ventris ingluuies mentē hebe tat et vitam cruciat. Dicit em̄ vir sapiens. Dulcis est somnus operanti siue parũ si- ue multũ comedat: saturitas aūt diuitis non sinit eũ dormire. Sine sacietate im- plendus est venter:et sine fastidio de men sa surgendũ: vt videlicet edamꝰ nõ quan tuʒ possumus: sed quantũ postulante na tura debemus. Monachis auteʒ maxi- me vitanda est ciborũ varietas: nam qui esculentis varijs vtitur: plus qͣ natura erigit ingerere stomacho temptans nõ si ne gule vicio epulatur. Uires em̄ corpo- ris nostri moderato et simplici sunt cibo reficiende: non aūt varijs et multis turpi- piter opprimende: quia non corpus pro- pter escam: sed esca propter corpus crea- ta est. Quod em̄ varios corpori morbos afferat ciborum varietas antiquorum tẽ perātia probamus: quos vniformis escu lentoꝛum simplicitas: in hac vita diutissi me conseruauit. Sanctissimus autem in stitutor noster principum monachorum omniuʒ modestissimus hierophantes be nedictus canonem nobis prescripsit sum ma discretione decoratum; in quo mensu ram ciboꝝ cupiens ostendere monachis dicit. Sufficere credinus ad refectionē quotidianã tam sexte quam none omni- bus menses cocta duo pulmentaria: p̃o pter diuersorũ infumi taes: vt qui forsi- tan ex vno nõ potuerit edere: ex alio resi- ciatur. Ergo duo pulmentaria cocta: om nibus fratribus sufficiãt. Et si fuerīt ibi poma: aut nascentia leguminũ: addatur et tertiuʒ. Si mentē legislatoris nostri fa ne intelligo: monachis duo pulmentaria cocta indulsit ybi necessitas expostulat in firmitatis: non ad sanorũ repletioneʒ ap peritus. Monachus em̄ qui sanꝰ est ab hac indulgentia merito excipitur: vt vno duumtaxat pulmentario cocto reficiatur. Infirmus aūt refici de vtroqƺ mea sentẽ- ria iure permittitur: cũ excessus in nullo timeatur. Uerũ cum non omnia possimꝰ equaliter oṁes: et vnus plus indige at ci borum: alius vero minus: impossibile est vnā abstinentie formā prescribere cūctis sed relinquitur vniuscuiusqƺ discretionis iudicio: vt tantũ sumat quantũ expostu- lat necessitas: non quantũ imperat appe- rentie voluptas. Hoc maxime cauenduʒ ne subrepat īmoderata ciborũ facietas: qͥ tunc animã cōma culat: cum aut fastidiu̇ refectionem sequitur aut grauis accidia mentē. Vomitus de saturitate p̃cedens: canũ est potius qͣ monachoruʒ. Religio christiana viruʒ maxime detestat᷑ epulo- nẽ: qm̄ delicie seruoꝝ dei: nõ esca et potus sed pietas et iustitia sunt: qua et deꝰ fideī puritate colitur: et vnicuiqƺ qđ suũ est in- ste ministrat᷑. Quisquis igitur deo place- re in toto corde tuo desideras: quicūqƺ ꝑ uenire ad eterne felicitatis gaudia festi- nas: ieiunandi modũ tibi mixta mensura viriũ tuarũ indicito: et curā adhibe maxi man: vt ieiunans sis in oratione continu us: in iudicijs iustus: in fraterna dilectio ne precipiuus: in iniurijs patiens: in in- crepationibus humilis: in sermone circũ spectus: in conscientia mundus: in amo- re dei feruidus: et in cunctis actionibus tuis comitante prudẽtia timoratus. Uer ba inutilia et ociosa fugito: et esto perfe- uerans in operibus bonis omnj tempo- re: habens in aduersis constantiam: in temptationibus vigilantiam: in refecti- one continentiam: et simplicem in coꝛ- de puritatem. Sint moderata et san- cta in omni mentis humiliitate ieiunia:

On the abstinence and fasting of monks.

He is a man of very keen intellect; although he is wholly ignorant of letters, nevertheless, like another Antony, the hermit of old, he understands the meaning of the Scriptures exceedingly well. We have seen how most eloquently he disputed with a certain master about the sacrament of the altar, a thing at which anyone who has not in the least tasted heavenly things through the pursuit of contemplation will not be able to marvel enough. I have introduced these matters, brothers, so that you may understand that nothing is so difficult that habit, continued over a long time, does not make it easy.

This holy man, as he himself confesses, did not suddenly arrive at the height of this abstinence, but over time, by successive degrees, little by little withdrawing a small amount of food from himself, until at last he was able to abstain altogether. For, as we have said, he has abstained from every corruptible food now for almost the twentieth year. By the example of this man, my brothers, let each of you learn daily to subtract something from his food and drink for the love of God, and let him accustom himself to provide for his body not as much as he can, but as much as is sufficient for the support of nature. For nature, as Boethius bears witness, is content with few and very small things; if you try to force its satisfaction with superfluous foods, what you pour in will become either unpleasant or harmful.

Many dishes beget many illnesses, and gluttony of the belly dulls the mind and torments life. For the wise man says: "Sweet is the sleep of the worker, whether he eats little or much; but the fullness of the rich man does not allow him to sleep." The belly is to be filled without satiety, and one must rise from the table without disgust, so that, clearly, we may eat not as much as we can, but as much as we ought when nature requires it.

For monks, however, variety of foods is especially to be avoided; for anyone who uses various dishes, attempting to put more into the stomach than nature raises up [unclear], feasts not without the vice of gluttony. The strength of our body is to be restored by moderate and simple food, not shamefully oppressed by many and various foods, because the body was not created for food, but food for the body. That variety of foods brings various diseases upon the body we prove from the temperance of the ancients, whom a uniform simplicity of foods preserved for a very long time in this life.

But our most holy founder, Benedict, the most modest hierophant of all the leaders of monks, prescribed for us a rule adorned with the highest discretion; in it, wishing to show monks the measure of foods, he says: "We believe that two cooked dishes are sufficient for the daily meal, whether at the sixth or the ninth hour, for all tables, because of the infirmities of different people, so that one who perhaps cannot eat from one may be refreshed from the other. Therefore let two cooked dishes suffice for all the brothers. And if there are fruits or fresh legumes there, let a third also be added."

If I understand the mind of our lawgiver correctly, he granted monks two cooked dishes where the necessity of infirmity requires it, not for the filling of the appetite of the healthy. For the monk who is healthy is rightly excepted from this indulgence, so that he may be refreshed by one cooked dish only. But in my judgment the infirm man is rightly permitted to be refreshed from both, since excess is feared in no respect.

Yet since not all of us can do all things equally, and one person needs more food, another less, it is impossible to prescribe one form of abstinence for everyone; but it is left to the judgment of each person's discretion, that he should take as much as necessity requires, not as much as the pleasure of appetite commands. This must especially be guarded against: that immoderate satiety of foods should not creep in, for it stains the soul when either disgust follows the meal or heavy sloth follows the mind. Vomiting that proceeds from satiety belongs to dogs rather than to monks.

The Christian religion especially detests a man who is a glutton, because the delights of the servants of God are not food and drink, but piety and justice, by which God is both worshiped in purity of faith, and to each person what is his own is administered justly. Therefore whoever you are who desire to please God with your whole heart, whoever you are who hasten to arrive at the joys of eternal happiness, impose upon yourself a manner of fasting with a measure mixed according to your strength, and apply the greatest care that, while fasting, you be constant in prayer, just in judgments, outstanding in brotherly love, patient in injuries, humble under rebukes, circumspect in speech, clean in conscience, fervent in the love of God, and, with prudence accompanying you, fearful in all your actions.

Flee useless and idle words, and be persevering in good works at all times, having constancy in adversities, watchfulness in temptations, continence at meals, and simple purity in heart. Let your fasts be moderate and holy, in all humility of mind;

Unde precoro nemo vestrũ simplicitate sermonis mei cōten- nat:nemo loquentẽ me grauiter ferat:qm̄ et si ad dicendũ non sum idoneus:tamen ratione cōmissi pastoralis cure officij ad monendũ vos coram deo me fateor obli- gatũ.Charitas mihi vr̄a loquendi p̃bet audaciã:et quanto vos prōptiores ad au diendũ ostenditis:tanto me amplius vt loquar prouocatis.Nec erit labor mihi grauis quantūlibet magnꝰ videat̉:quo salus animarũ vestraꝝ perficit̉.Uos me oꝛonibꝰ adiuuate:vt dñs iesus ĩ ore meo Ioquat̉: ꝯcedatqꝫ pusillo vires ingenio ꝓ ferēdi ad mediũ:quicqͥd in vobis ꝓduce re pōt sctī feruoris incremētiũ.Nā quātũ cupio ꝓdesse charitati vestre sermonibꝰ meis nequeo:ꝑterea quod cure rei secu laris nimiũ cōpellor occupari.Vn̄ festi[unclear]

Homily XV. Fol. XXXVII.

which so weaken the body that they do not lift up the mind into pride, lest the exercise of humility become material for vices. Fasting detests idleness; it does not love wordiness; it cherishes secrecy; it devotes itself to prayers and tears. Fasting, as Saint Ambrose bears witness, is the death of fault, the destruction of sins, the remedy of salvation, the root of grace, the foundation of chastity. By this step the righteous Moses came to God; by this gift Elijah, before he died, ascended into heaven in a chariot. Those who walk in the Spirit love fasting, and those who profess chastity necessarily flee an abundance of delights. For hunger is a friend to virginity, an enemy to wantonness. Fullness, however, betrays chastity and nourishes wantonness. For fasting extinguishes the burning arrows of the devil; the urgency of prayer restrains them; and the continuation of vigils in the love of Christ repels all the snares of demons. Hence Saint Leo the pope says in a certain sermon: What can be more effective than fasting, by the observance of which we draw near to God and, resisting the devil, overcome [his] alluring enticements? For fasting has always been food for virtue, and abstinence the nourishment of holy chastity. From abstinence, indeed, proceed chaste thoughts; it begets reasonable desires, and also modest counsels; and through voluntary afflictions the flesh dies to concupiscences, while the spirit is renewed in virtues. Let us therefore love fasting, my brothers, for love of virtue, on account of him who did not refuse to undergo death for us; and let us abstain not only from unlawful things but also, as far as can be done, from permitted ones, so that we who in many ways have offended against the commandments of salvation may, as recompense of satisfaction, henceforth restrain ourselves from every pleasure. Let us fast from every sin; let us take no food of malice; let us devour no banquets of pleasure, nor be made drunk with the wine of luxury. Let us fast from all perversities; let us abstain from evil works, and let us not speak harmful things; and let us always beware of hurtful and perverse thoughts, which separate us from God. Let us always keep most zealous watch in prayers to God, knowing that he whom we invoke with prayers is everywhere most present to us. Let his praise always be in our mouth; and since we cannot praise his magnificence in speech, let us adore him in the heart with the desires of a most chaste love. For then our fasts are pleasing to him, when they have been adorned with holy works and continual prayers. For the prayer of the righteous man, as sacred Scripture bears witness, penetrates the heavens, and it becomes the more effective, the more it is found adorned with charity and fasting. Let us join to it, as it were, two wings, fasting and charity, and it will obtain for us from the Lord whatever conducive to salvation we shall have asked.

On the Lenten fast of monks: Homily XVI.

Because, by the bounty of our Lord Jesus Christ, dearly beloved brothers, we have begun the Lenten fast, reason demands that we say something briefly about its observance. For although you have many writings of the holy fathers on this most sacred exercise of fasts, nevertheless, because I know by experience that my sermons among you are not wholly fruitless, I gladly impart to your edification what the Lord has granted. For, as blessed Jerome bears witness, the act of the living voice has within it a certain hidden operation, which in Greek speech he more elegantly called energy; and the discourse of a teacher, uttered by the mouth, is stronger for persuading. But I, set apart in your midst only by the name of pastor, confess that I am a young man, unlearned and lacking both the experience and the discretion necessary for the governance of souls; whence it happens that I speak with a certain blush and shame, a young man among elders, an ignorant man among the learned, a disciple among masters. Therefore I beg that none of you despise the simplicity of my speech; let no one take it ill that I speak, because even if I am not fit for speaking, nevertheless by reason of the office of pastoral care entrusted to me I confess that before God I am bound to admonish you. Your charity gives me boldness to speak, and the readier you show yourselves to hear, the more you move me to speak. Nor will the labor be burdensome to me, however great it may seem, by which the salvation of your souls is perfected. Help me with your prayers, that the Lord Jesus may speak in my mouth, and may grant strength to my poor little talent to bring forth in your midst whatever can produce in you an increase of holy fervor. For as much as I desire to benefit your charity by my sermons, I am unable to do so, because I am compelled to be too much occupied by the care of secular business. Whence

De quadragesimali ieiunio monachorũ. solum diebus et in ea parte noctis quam post laudes nocturnas ducere soleo in/ sonnem vobis exhortandis inferuio: in seedulis cõcipiens que mihi dicenda oc currunt. Itaqꝫ hodiernam collocutionẽ de regula sanctissimi patris nostri Bene dicti ĩtroducere volui: qui de quadrage/ sinali obseruatione sic dicit. Licet omni tempore vita monachi quadragesime de beat obseruationem habere: tamen quia paucoꝛum est ista virtus ideo suademus istis diebus quadragesime omni purita te vitam suam custodire: omnēs ꝙ pariter sordes et negligentias aliorum temporuꝫ his diebus sanctis diluere. Quod tūc di gne fit: si ab oṁibus viţi s temperemus orationi cum fl̓etibus: lectioni et compun ctioni cordis operam demus. Si paucor um est ista virtus vt omni tempore vitā obseruantie agant quadragesimalis: ma nifeste iam constat paucos in religione ui uere monachos ad euangelij puritatem: cum teneantur omnes qui christi profitẽ tur militiam ad perfectionis apicem co/ natum suum dirigere. Monachus enim iuxta nominis sui interpretationem soli/ tarius: in cenobio tūc recte vivere ad euā gelium et regulaꝫ quam professus est cre ditur: cum seculirebus atqꝫ honoribus p dei amore contemptis: in omni puritate cordis coram deo et hominibus conuer/ satur: in opere strennuus: in cogitatione mundus: in sermone parcus atqꝫ pacifi cus. Hec est vita monachi quadragesi malē in omni tempore habens obseruan riam: corpus pro dei amore castigare per abstinentiam: et mentem alere per inter/ nam compunctioneꝫ. Recte viuit qui iu ste viuit: qui deum diligit super omnia: qͥ summo studio: summaqꝫ diligentia ver/ bis et factis illius obseruat mandata. Il le enim christi verus est monachus: qui christum totis viribus imitatur. Si aūt volueris imitari christũ o monache: que sum dicturus diligẽtissime obserua. Fu ge mundũ et oṁia solatia carnis: vt vere solitarius esse merearis. Cogitatiōes va nas: inutiles: turpes: atqꝫ nociuas: nun/ quam in corde tuo morari permittas: sed cogita semper aliuid boni: et dominice passionis memoria de animo tuo nunqͣꝫ recedat: quo minus pendentem in cruce dominum quotidie cuꝫ gratiarum actio ne speculeris. Deuꝫ tibi presentem vbiqꝫ cõsidera: qui videt nouit et intelligit quic quid vel cogitaueris vl̓ operatus fueris quoniam nihil est illi occultũ. Cor mun/ dum custodi ab omni inquinamento pec cati: et purā habeto conscientiam semper in vero christi amore feruentem. Nulluꝫ tibi ociosum auolet tempus: sed in bonis operibꝰ semper inueniat te cogitatio im/ plicatuꝫ. Sommo ne torpeas multo: et ab omni tepor is accidia procul te facias ali enum. Ciborum et potus temperantiam capesce: et quanto licet parcius viuito: vt corpu s moder ate sustentatū spiritu sem/ per ĩ humilitate subseruiat: et ab minime cō/ tra rationis imperiū consurgat. Dox vt senseris in te aliquem oriri torporem: ad amarissime passionis domini iesu christi memorīa confugito: et quiicquid ac cidia depellere velocius potest: in iunctē reducito. Moras rumpito precor oṁes: quoniā torpor mentis subito crescit dissi mulatus: et accidia que nouio feruore mē tis nō statim extinguit̉: in graue animę ꝑ/ niciem confestim roboratur. Omniū em malorũ in monacho est pessimum: si per torpoꝛe et accidiam locuꝫ in corde suo p re stiterit seminario viciorũ. Et vobis o mo nachi non solum quotidie: sed omni hora atque momento contra hanc bestiam vi/ gilanduꝫ est: quoniam admissa in coꝛ nū quam sola ingreditur: sed ea mota con/ geries et scaturigo omnium viciorum com itatur. Non est perniciosioꝛ pestis mo/ nachi quam torpor accidie: per quem om nis feriuoꝛ deuotionis extinguitur: et pro fideli obsequio inter misso ignauia et ocio mens in foueam desperationis agitata precipitatur. A sanctitatis proposito ve/ lociter deficit: quisquis morā accidie per mittit. Quo contra Salomon te admo/ net in libro prouerbiorum dicens. Uade ad formicam o piger et considerat vias ei/ us: et disce sapientiam. Que cum non ha beat ducem: nec preceptorem: nec princi/ pem: parat in estate cibũ suu̓: et cōgregat in messe qd̓ comedat. Et iterū dicit. Desi deria occidunt pigrũ: qꝛ noluerūt quicqͣꝫ manus eius laborare. Nihil sanctitatis pro posituꝫ professis deterius est ocio: qꝛ non solum nihil boni accumulat: sed etiâ consumit et dissipat omnia prius accumu lata. Na̾ sancte deuotionis feruoꝛ ꝓ cessu gaudet ac proficit: cessatione vero torpe/ scit et paulatim ne dicaz subito euanescit,

On the Lenten Fast of Monks.

only by day and in that part of the night which, after the night lauds, I am accustomed to pass sleepless, do I devote myself to exhorting you, setting down on little sheets what occurs to me to say. And so I have wished to introduce today’s conference from the Rule of our most holy father Benedict, who says thus concerning Lenten observance: “Although at every season the life of a monk ought to have the observance of Lent, nevertheless, because this virtue belongs to few, we therefore advise that in these days of Lent they guard their life in all purity, and that all alike wash away in these holy days the stains and negligences of other times. This is then done worthily if we restrain ourselves from all vices, and devote ourselves to prayer with tears, to reading, and to compunction of heart.”

If this virtue belongs to few, that they should at every season lead a life of Lenten observance, it is now plainly evident that few monks in religion live according to the purity of the Gospel, since all who profess the soldiery of Christ are bound to direct their effort toward the summit of perfection. For the monk, according to the interpretation of his name, is solitary; and he is then rightly believed to live in the cenobium according to the Gospel and the rule which he has professed, when, having despised worldly possessions and honors for the love of God, he conducts himself in all purity of heart before God and men: vigorous in work, clean in thought, sparing and peaceable in speech. This is the life of a monk, having Lenten observance at every season: to chastise the body for the love of God through abstinence, and to nourish the mind through inward compunction. He lives rightly who lives justly, who loves God above all things, who with the greatest zeal and the greatest diligence observes his commandments in words and deeds. For he is the true monk of Christ who imitates Christ with all his powers.

But if you wish to imitate Christ, O monk, observe most carefully what I am about to say. Flee the world and all comforts of the flesh, so that you may deserve truly to be solitary. Never permit vain, useless, foul, and harmful thoughts to dwell in your heart, but always think something good, and let the memory of the Lord’s Passion never depart from your mind, so that each day, with thanksgiving, you may contemplate the Lord hanging on the cross. Consider God present to you everywhere, who sees, knows, and understands whatever you have either thought or done, since nothing is hidden from him. Keep your heart clean from every defilement of sin, and always have a pure conscience, fervent in the true love of Christ. Let no idle time fly away from you, but let thought always find you engaged in good works. Do not grow sluggish with much sleep, and keep yourself far removed from every sloth of tepidity. Embrace moderation in food and drink, and live as sparingly as is permitted, so that the body, moderately sustained, may always serve the spirit in humility and in no way rise up against the command of reason.

As soon as you perceive some sluggishness arising in you, flee to the memory of the most bitter Passion of the Lord Jesus Christ, and bring back [unclear] whatever can more swiftly drive away sloth. Break off, I beg you, all delays, since sluggishness of mind, when dissembled, grows suddenly; and sloth, which is not at once extinguished by the new fervor of the mind, is immediately strengthened into the grave destruction of the soul. For of all evils in a monk this is the worst: if through sluggishness and sloth he has offered a place in his heart to the seedbed of vices. And you, O monks, must keep watch against this beast not only every day, but every hour and moment, since, once admitted into the heart, it never enters alone; but when it has been stirred, a mass and spring of all vices accompanies it. There is no more destructive plague of the monk than the sluggishness of sloth, through which all fervor of devotion is extinguished; and, faithful service having been interrupted, the mind, driven by laziness and idleness, is cast headlong into the pit of despair. Whoever permits delay from sloth quickly falls away from the purpose of holiness.

Against this Solomon admonishes you in the Book of Proverbs, saying: “Go to the ant, O sluggard, and consider her ways, and learn wisdom. Though she has no leader, nor instructor, nor ruler, she prepares her food in summer and gathers at harvest what she may eat.” And again he says: “Desires kill the sluggard, because his hands have refused to work at anything.” Nothing is worse than idleness for those who profess the purpose of holiness, because it not only accumulates nothing good, but even consumes and scatters everything previously accumulated. For the fervor of holy devotion rejoices and advances by progress, but through cessation it grows sluggish and little by little, not to say suddenly, vanishes,

Om̄ia. XVI. Fo. XXXVIII. Radix enim desperationis est ignauia: et omnium mater ac nutrix viciorum. Nam sicut vestimentū tineam et generat et nutrit:ita perniciosissima peslis accidia et parit et fouet desperationem. Feminez hec bestia plus vexare cōsueuit:quā mo- nachos: et eos precipue qui vitam ducūt in solitudine abstracta. Cauendū ergo summopere vobis esto monachi:ab hoc hoste salutis animarum: et non fugiendo sed resistendo fortiter dimicandum:sedu loqꝫ cogitandum:quia torpore et ignauia nemo sanctitatis honoreꝫ consecutus est neqꝫ aliquis regnum eterne felicitatis si ne magno et continuo labore promeruit: Quotidianis igitur ac recentibus virtu- tū semper incrementis instauranda mēs est:et viuendi hoc periculosuꝫ iter non de transacto:sed potius de reliquo metien- dum. Nemo securitateꝫ sibi promittat in hac vita: que tota temptatio nominatur: tot periculis plena:quot sunt affectiones in anīa:sed caueat vnusquisqꝫ vt qui po- tuit fieri ex deteriore melior:nō fiat ex me- liore deterior. Et his sanctis maxime di ebus curemus omnes quantū possumꝰ fieri meliores:adijcientes nobis consilio diui preceptoris nostri aliquid ad solituꝫ pensum seruitutis nostre:orationes vide licet peculiares:ciborum et potus abstinē- tiam:vt vnusquisque super mensuram si bi indictam aliquid propria voluntate cū gaudio sancti spiritus offerat deo: idest subtrahat corpori suo:de cibo de potu de somno:de loquacitate:de securitate:et cū spiritalis desiderij gaudio sanctum pa- scha expectet. Parum enim religiosus alijs temporibus esse monachus conuin citur:qui sanctis diebus istis non religi- osior et in dei amore feruentior deuotior/ que inuenitur. Hinc diuus papa Grego- rius ait in quadam omelia. Quadrage- sima summā obseruatione est obseruan- da: vt ieiuonium in ea propter dies domi- nicos qui de abstinentia subtracti sunt:ni siquem infirmitas impe dierit:nullatenꝰ soluatur:quia ipsi dies decime sunt anni quas offerre domino iubemur. Sanctꝰ quoque Ambrosius dicit. Ille quadra- gesimaz facit: qui iejunando et vigilando ascendit ad pascha. Nam sicut reliquo tempore anni iejunare premium est: ita in quadragesima non iejunare peccatuꝫ. Illa enim voluntaria sunt ieunia: et ista necessaria:illa de arbitrio veniunt:ista ve ro delege. Ad illa inuitamur:ad ista con- pellimur. Et ergo qui constitutum nu- merū vna die manducando preterit:non vt violator vnius dei accusat̉: sed vt trās gressor totius quadragesime arguitur. Refrenanda sunt his sacris diebus om- nia desideria carnis: castigandum est per abstinentiā corpus:vt si forsan alijs tem- poribus minus temperate viximus: hoc quadragesimali ieiunio vtcunque recom- pensemus. Sequamus ergo monita san ctissimi patris nostri Benedicti fratres charissimi:et quanta possumus nos sedu litate in sanctis operibꝰ exercitemus: sub trahentes corpori nostro aliquid pro dei amore de cibo et potu quotidie:quatenus veros nos dei seruos cōprobemus.Con sequenter autem sanctus institutor no- ster subiungit diēs. Hoc ipsum tn̄ qd̓ vnusquisque offert:abbati suo suggerat: et cum eius fiat oratione et volūtate:quia quod sine permissiōe patris spiritalis fit. presumptioni deputabitur et vane glo- rie:non mercedi. Ergo cuꝫ voluntate ab batis: omnia sunt agenda: Aperta sunt verba sancti legislatoris nostri fratres:nē quis ad ignorantie velamen posset habe- re recursum. Nam si omnia cum volun- tate abbatis agenda sunt: ergo sine per- missione eius nihil omnino est facienduꝫ. Enimuero quanto bonuꝫ aliquid opus a pluribus decoratur virtutibus:tanto maioris apud deum esse meriti non erit dubitandum.Eum igitur monachus de licentia et benedictione sui abbatis corpo ri suo aliquid ciborum aut potus pro dei amore subtrahit: non solum de abstinen- tia ipsa mercedem promissam a domino recepturus est satietatīs eterne:sed etiam pro humilitate regnum:et pro sancte obe- didit: voluntatem suam christo in mani- bus abbatis resignauit:quam si arbitrio deinceps iterum suo vsurpauerit: chri- stuꝫ iam turpiter abnegauit. Quid enim aliud est monachus vsurpator volunta- tis proprie:nisi rei profefsor iniustus alie- nes? Sit ergo monachus abbati suo hu- militer subiectus pro christi amore sem- per in omnibus: nihil omnino presumat [unclear]

All things. XVI. Fol. XXXVIII.

For sloth is the root of despair, and the mother and nurse of all vices. For just as a garment both produces and nourishes the moth, so the most pernicious plague of acedia both gives birth to and fosters despair. This beast is accustomed to vex no one more than monks, and especially those who lead their life withdrawn in solitude. Therefore, monks, you must beware with the utmost care of this enemy of the salvation of souls, and it must be fought not by fleeing but by resisting bravely; and one must diligently consider that no one has attained the honor of holiness by torpor and sloth, nor has anyone deserved the kingdom of eternal happiness without great and continual labor.

Therefore the mind must always be renewed by daily and fresh increases of virtues, and this perilous journey of living must be measured not by what has passed, but rather by what remains. Let no one promise himself security in this life, which is named wholly a temptation, full of as many dangers as there are affections in the soul; but let each one take care that he who could become better from worse does not become worse from better. And especially in these holy days let us all take care, as much as we can, to become better, adding for ourselves, by the counsel of our divine teacher, something to the usual measure of our service: namely special prayers, abstinence from foods and drink, so that each one, beyond the measure prescribed to him, may offer something to God of his own will with the joy of the Holy Spirit, that is, may subtract from his body something of food, of drink, of sleep, of talkativeness, of ease, and may await holy Easter with the joy of spiritual desire.

For a monk is proved to be little religious at other times if in these holy days he is not found more religious, more fervent in the love of God, and more devout. Hence the divine pope Gregory says in a certain homily: Lent is to be observed with the highest observance, so that the fast in it, on account of the Lord’s days that have been subtracted from abstinence, unless sickness has hindered someone, is by no means relaxed, because these days are the tithes of the year which we are commanded to offer to the Lord. Saint Ambrose also says: He keeps Lent who by fasting and keeping vigil ascends to Easter. For just as at the remaining time of the year to fast brings a reward, so in Lent not to fast is a sin. The former fasts are voluntary, and these are necessary; the former come from choice, but these from law. To the former we are invited; to these we are compelled. And therefore he who passes beyond the appointed number by eating on one day is accused not as the violator of one day, but is charged as the transgressor of the whole of Lent.

In these sacred days all desires of the flesh must be restrained; the body must be chastised through abstinence, so that if perhaps at other times we have lived less temperately, we may in some way make compensation by this Lenten fast. Therefore, dearest brothers, let us follow the admonitions of our most holy father Benedict, and with as much diligence as we can let us exercise ourselves in holy works, subtracting something daily from our body, for love of God, from food and drink, so that we may prove ourselves true servants of God.

Next, however, our holy founder adds, saying: Yet this very thing which each one offers, let him report to his abbot, and let it be done with his prayer and will; because what is done without the permission of the spiritual father will be imputed to presumption and vainglory, not to reward. Therefore all things are to be done with the will of the abbot. The words of our holy lawgiver are plain, brothers, so that no one could have recourse to the covering of ignorance. For if all things are to be done with the will of the abbot, then without his permission absolutely nothing is to be done.

Indeed, the more a good work is adorned with more virtues, the more it must be considered of greater merit before God. Therefore, when a monk, by the license and blessing of his abbot, subtracts something of foods or drink from his body for love of God, he will receive not only from that abstinence itself the reward of eternal satiety promised by the Lord, but also the kingdom for humility, and for holy obedience: he has resigned his will to Christ in the hands of the abbot; and if he thereafter usurps it again by his own decision, he has now shamefully denied Christ. For what else is a monk who usurps his own will, except the unjust possessor of another’s property? Therefore let the monk be humbly subject to his abbot for love of Christ, always in all things; let him presume absolutely nothing

Quisquis ergo monachus cupit esse bo¬ nus: quisqͥs in ꝺomino vere vult esse ꝺe¬ uotus: abbatem suum vt vicariū in mo¬ nasterio iesu christi pura ꝺilectione semp̄ et vbiqꝫ veneretur:mandatis eius in om̄i¬ bus humiliter obediat: et ab eius ꝺirecti¬ one nullatenus recedat. Frustra enim ieiunabimus et nullū quo¬ dragesimalis obseruantie fructum inue¬ niamus:nisi omnes in vera charitate eccle¬ siastice vnionis coꝛam deo nō esse concoꝛ¬ des? On the Lenten fast of monks.

...to act against his command; let him omit or neglect nothing that has been enjoined on him by him. Let him beware of troubling or saddening his shepherd by a restless manner of life; nor let him murmur against him, nor disparage him, nor say any evil whatever against him. Rather, let him reverence him with the sincere affection of charity, as the vicar of Christ, and not sadden his spirit either by importunate or disorderly words or deeds. Moreover, let him aid his labors as much as he can, and intercede for him with continual prayers before God. Monks sin greatly against God who do not fear to sadden their abbot by their importunate disparagements and wicked behavior.

Therefore whatever monk desires to be good, whoever truly wishes to be devout in the Lord, let him always and everywhere venerate his abbot with pure love as the vicar of Jesus Christ in the monastery; let him humbly obey his commands in all things, and in no way depart from his direction. But let the abbot strive to show himself in all things a worthy shepherd to his monks, one who feeds the sheep of Christ entrusted to him by word and likewise by example, in all gentleness of charity. Let him not disturb the brothers without just and reasonable necessity; let him not be a despiser of the holy community; let him recognize himself as the steward of the monastery's goods, not their lord. Let him not be a mocker of his subjects, not turbulent, not importunate, not a tyrant, but their sincere lover, gentle in speech, mild and upright in conduct, holy in his way of life, clean in conscience, always devoted in mind to God.

Let him at all times bear solicitous care for the souls entrusted to him, and neglect nothing of those things which seem able to conduce to their salvation. Let him not therefore raise himself up on high because he has been placed as ruler of others, but let him remember that he must fear so much the more, inasmuch as he is most certainly bound to render account for all in the dread judgment of God. Let him correct the proud, rebellious, and contumacious as a lord; let him kindly cherish the humble, obedient, and governable as a most gentle father, and wisely distribute to each one his right without acceptance of persons. Let him always consider himself the mother and nurse of the monks; and therefore those whom he can bring back to better things by gentleness he ought not to exasperate with importunate words and harsh invectives. Let him always bear solicitous care for the weak, and provide for all in such a way that they have no just cause for murmuring. In his own weaknesses let him learn how he ought to have mercy on his subjects. For he cannot be a good shepherd of souls who disdains to suffer heartfelt compassion for the necessities of his ailing subjects.

But he can become a good abbot among monks who knows how to adapt himself to the persons of the weak in such a way that, whenever a brother asks something of him, taking upon himself the condition of the person asking, he says in his heart: What would I wish to be done to me in this matter, according to the right judgment of reason, if I were in the person of the one asking? Indeed, if the abbot imagines himself a subject, he will let no one go away from him saddened. We have now said, brothers, what sort of men it befits you to be toward us for the love of God, so that, existing as good monks, you may please the Lord Jesus in truth. You have nevertheless heard what sort of shepherd I ought to show myself to you; whether I do this or not, you yourselves will judge better than I.

For we shall fast in vain and find no fruit of Lenten observance unless we all are concordant before God in the true charity of ecclesiastical union. Or what good will it do to abstain from richer foods and defile the conscience with evil works or thoughts? For in order that the fasts we have begun may be pleasing to God, it is necessary that they be not only alien and remote from vices and sins, but also adorned with the fullness of all virtues. For holy Ambrose says: What profit is it to fast in the belly and to run riot in hunting, to abstain from foods and to wander in sins? Do you think, brothers, that he fasts who at first daybreak does not keep watch at church, does not seek out the holy places of the blessed martyrs, but rises in the morning, gathers his servants, arranges the nets, brings out the dogs, ranges through glades and woods, and, I say, drags along with him servants perhaps hastening rather to church? To his own pleasures he adds the sins of others, not knowing that he will be guilty both of his own fault and of the ruin of his servants. And Saint Pope Leo: The chief fast of ours does not consist in abstinence from food alone

[Homily?] XVI.

For food is by no means fruitfully withheld from the body unless the mind is recalled from all iniquity. Saint Jerome also says: What does it profit for the body to be made thin by abstinence, if the soul swells with pride? What virtue is there in not drinking wine, and being drunk with anger, hatred, and the other poisonous cups of the soul?

Therefore let none of you promise himself sanctity from abstinence from food alone, since whatever is required for true penitence is judged necessary also for fasting. For fasts profit unto salvation for those who are contrite for their sins in a true purpose of amendment, who fervently devote themselves to good and holy works. Hence all who fast from food and drink must also abstain from [unclear], so that the mind, adorned with the beauty of the virtues, may sweetly burn in the love of Christ and may in no way grow lukewarm from progress in inner conduct. For the virtue of abstinence is nothing if it has not been adorned with works of charity.

Therefore, monk, listen to my counsel: if you wish to make your fast fruitful before God, first cleanse your conscience from every stain of sin, so that no desire of evil may intervene; so that the mind may become fervent in the exercise of divine love and be laudably adorned with the remaining virtues. By the remedy of contrition and confession wipe away past sins, and by standing firm in prayers with tears strengthen your mind against all temptations with God’s help. Toward God, as much as you can, be fervent in the exercise of love; toward yourself, tranquil in a pure conscience; toward your brother, ordered in true charity. Always be foremost in humility, firm in constancy and obedience, shining in chastity of mind and body, pious in meekness, a monk in conduct, continually inflamed with desire for perfection. If you commend your abstinence by this kind of cleanness and purity, you will fast rightly.

Exercise your mind diligently in meditation on the passion of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, so that no day passes in which you do not run through his life and death at least once with thanksgiving. I will not say irreligious, but ungrateful, is the Christian who is so immersed either in temporal affairs or occupied with the pleasures of the flesh that he does not call to mind, at least once each day with thanksgiving, the most bitter passion of his Redeemer.

Fol. XXIX.

But the monk who forgets the benefits of our Lord Jesus Christ, who does not recall his passion once every day with thanksgiving, who does not meditate every day on the law of the Lord or on the Gospel, is rightly considered the most ungrateful of all men. Nothing is more powerful for him than that prayer which is offered to God the Father in union with, and in the power of, the Lord’s passion. Too justly is that spirit to be condemned which, though redeemed by the most precious blood of Christ, is led astray by the pleasures of its flesh so as not to remember such great benefits of God toward itself.

For there was no reason that the Son of God should become man except that he willed to justify us sinners: born in the world for us, suffering in the world for us, and cruelly dead on the wood for our crimes. That just one came into the world to justify us who were sinners; the pious one came to the impious, that we might learn piety, humility, and patience from him. The physician came to the sick, life to the dead, mercy to the desperate; it was not our merits that drew him down from heaven into the world, but our sins.

It is fitting, therefore, brothers in [unclear], that we celebrate with all devotion this Lenten fast dedicated to his most holy passion, who first deigned to do such great things for our salvation, who, in order to rescue us from the destruction of death, did not hesitate to give himself for us unto death. Let us do, for the love of Christ, whatever good we can; let us endure, in consideration of his passion and death, every adversity that happens to us in this world, since the Lord Jesus, who in charity willed to suffer for us, has truly shown himself most worthy that we love him with all our heart.

For if, brother, you recognize yourself as a sinner, Christ saves you by his death. Contemplate him as it is fitting, hanging on the cross, and you will be healed from every bite of sin. For nothing in this world is found more effective for cleansing and curing the wounds of conscience than meditation on Christ. For the most precious blood of the Lord, poured out, has become sufficient medicine for sin. Hence the holy bishop Augustine says: Brothers, that we who are wounded by sin may be healed, let us behold Christ crucified. For just as those who looked upon the bronze serpent in the desert did not perish from the bites of serpents, so those who

De quadragesimali ieiunio monachoru. de 7 deuotione intuentur morte iesu christi: sanatur a morbis peccatorum. Si autem iustificatum te confidis a peccato: eo magis ac ferventius tibi christus incruce pendens intuendus est: sine cuius merito passionis nemo vindit iustus in terra. Nam extra fidem christi non est iustitia. Quantumlibet homo vivat religiose, si non credit in dominum nostrum iesu christum, eternam nullatenus consequetur salutem: sed ira dei manet super eum: neecessario peribit in eternum. Dores christi ianuani salutis aperuit: per quam nemo alius potest ingrediendi qui in christum fideliter credit. Propterea eniz christus damnatione se mortis humiliter subdidit et credentes a iugo damnationis perpetue liberaret. O charitas infinita: o pie tas sine mensura: quis credenti in te ma iestas eterna: non miretur tam stupenda nobis indulta beneficia. Passio enim tua dominice iesu nostre salutis est precium: vt tinunt peccatorum refugium: infirmat mentium singularis remedium: fons ori go et finis omnium bonorum. Recolam? nunc igitur fratres charissimi et sedulo ad memoriai in reuocemus dominice passionis amaritudinez: vt quia necessario pe catores nos esse recognoscimus: iustificari tandem per meritum ipsius salvatoris nostri valeamus. Meditatio enim dominice passionis precellit omnia huius modi exercitia: si cum deuotionis intime fer uore diutius fuerit continuata. Mens il la monachi que studio divini amoris su censsa: passionis domini nostri iesu christi memoriam habere cum lachrymis quoti die ad horam saltem modicam consuevit demonum suggestionibus non facile pa tescit. Cor eteni illud quod amor iesu pos fidet: omnibus cogitatiõibus maliis sem per inaccessibile et clausum manet. Felix numirum ille monachus et nunquaz pre ter honorem nominandus: qui in doctrina et passione domini nostri iesu christi cu amoris studio meditatur die ac nocte: q salvatoris sui nunquam obliuiscitur: qui sine comedat sine bibat, sine alud quid fa ciat, semper dominum iesum in cruce pen dentez oculis mentalibus intuetur. Aul le versantur in eius corde perniciose cog rationes: verbum ex ore eius malum vel ociosum non procedit: nihil quam cruci fixum pro nobis iesum cogitat: et quicqd Omelia XVII. Fo. On the Lenten fast of monks.

[Unclear] with devotion beholds the death of Jesus Christ: he is healed from the diseases of sins. But if you trust that you have been justified from sin, all the more and more fervently must Christ hanging on the cross be contemplated by you; without the merit of his passion no one lives righteous on earth. For outside faith in Christ there is no righteousness. However religiously a man may live, if he does not believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, he will by no means attain eternal salvation; rather, the wrath of God remains upon him, and he will necessarily perish forever. The death of Christ opened the gate of salvation, through which no one else can enter except one who faithfully believes in Christ. For this reason Christ humbly subjected himself to the condemnation of death, that he might free believers from the yoke of perpetual damnation. O infinite charity, O immeasurable loving-kindness: who, believing in you, eternal majesty, would not marvel at such astonishing benefits granted to us? For your passion, Lord Jesus, is the price of our salvation, the refuge [unclear] of sinners, the singular remedy of infirm minds, the fountain, origin, and end of all good things. Therefore, now, dearest brothers, let us recall and diligently bring back to memory the bitterness of the Lord’s passion, so that, since we necessarily acknowledge ourselves to be sinners, we may at last be able to be justified through the merit of that very savior of ours. For meditation on the Lord’s passion surpasses all exercises of this kind, if it has been continued for a longer time with the fervor of inward devotion. That mind of a monk which, kindled by zeal for divine love, has been accustomed every day, at least for a little hour, to keep the memory of the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ with tears, does not easily lie open to the suggestions of demons. For that heart which the love of Jesus possesses always remains inaccessible and closed to all evil thoughts. Truly blessed is that monk, and never to be named except with honor, who meditates day and night with loving zeal on the teaching and passion of our Lord Jesus Christ; who never forgets his Savior; who, whether he eats or drinks or does anything else, always beholds with the eyes of the mind the Lord Jesus hanging on the cross. No pernicious thoughts have their course in his heart; no evil or idle word proceeds from his mouth; he thinks of nothing except Jesus crucified for us, and whatever

Homily XVII. Fo. XL.

he restrains: he calms avarice, [unclear] sloth, mitigates [unclear], uproots pride by the roots. Moreover, no passion of a carnal thing wearies the mind of a man whom the passion of Christ truly occupies. O how sweetly he burns whom the memory of Jesus’ passion sweetly inflames. O how blessed is the mind that embraces the continual meditation of Christ’s death. O good Jesus, my love of the cross, who are the salvation and health of faithful souls, grant us to keep continual memory of your passion; grant to your servants always to commend the fasts begun with good works, because then our abstinence will be most pleasing to your uncircumscribable majesty, when it has been adorned with meditation on your precious blood; who live and reign with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for all ages of ages.

Here ends Homily XVII.

On the sleep and wakefulness of monks. Homily XVII.

The monk who always thinks that he is going to die should permit his eyes to pass no time [unclear]. For Scripture says: “Remember your last things, and you will not sin forever.” Against the forgetful and uncertain, however, it is written: “A people without counsel and without prudence. Would that they were wise and understood and provided for their last things.” The remembrance of death brings watchfulness into the soul and extinguishes every disordered thought of the mind. He who rightly fears death never grows sluggish in good work. For the wise man says: “Whatever your hand can do, do it earnestly; for neither work nor reason nor wisdom nor knowledge will be in the lower world to which you are hastening.” For the monk who is a true worshiper of God spends no moment of time uselessly, but by nights and days, in the exercise of good work, always performs the watchfulness of the mind with the highest devotion; and while sleeping in body, steadfastly in [unclear] he says to the messengers of God: “I sleep, and my heart keeps watch.” Sleep is the image of death and the binding of the senses of the body; but he who is a true lover

On the sleep and wakefulness of monks.

[unclear]. For indeed they mercifully allowed monks in community a space of five hours before the night praises, and likewise added two, or two and a half, after matins for sleep. He for whom this time, namely seven hours, is not sufficient for rest shows himself a very sluggish and slothful monk. Hence we are admonished to keep watch not only in mind but also in body, since he who disdains to keep watch bodily in the service of God is scarcely able to preserve his body in true purity.

Let us keep watch, therefore, most beloved brothers, especially in these holy days of Lent, in which we have declared war on vices and are firmly prepared to conquer and overcome the ancient enemy, the devil. For you have heard the holy prince of the apostles admonishing in these words: “Brothers, be sober and keep watch.” Why did he give this warning? Because, he says, “your adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour; resist him, strong in faith.”

And so, my brothers, let us keep watch as long as we are set in battle, lest at any time, weighed down by drowsiness or idleness, we be overcome by the adversary of our salvation. For as long as we live in the flesh, it is necessary that by watchfulness and chastisement of our body we fight bravely against the enemy. Let the labor of the contest not frighten you, because although our adversary is troublesome, nevertheless he is so weak and feeble that he can overcome no one except one who is willing, and one who has utterly cast off all guard over himself.

But the Lord Jesus Christ is our strong helper and protector, who grants strength to those who fight eagerly and will bestow on the victors an unfading crown in heaven with all his saints. As dust is scattered by the wind, so our adversary the devil, confounded and terrified by the voice of those singing psalms with humble devotion, is driven away. Therefore let none of you, most beloved brothers, act negligently; let no one in the time of prayer grow dull through sluggishness of mind and drowsiness; let no one fear the contest with the devil with disordered fear.

Stand manfully for the perpetual salvation of your souls, fighting against a weak adversary, and hold your own flesh no less suspect than demons. For you know, as not only Scripture testifies but also long experience teaches, that the flesh desires against the spirit; and therefore the monk who is not harmed by the wantonness of his own flesh is rarely overcome by demons in the contest. Walk, therefore, in the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh.

Let him who is watchful and a strong fighter rouse the weaker brother, who is sluggish in devotion, and restore him as far as he can, both by words and by examples, to the holy fervor of the spirit. Let him who is spiritual among you not despise his disorderly brother, but rather bring him back through humble admonition to the pursuit of piety. For Scripture says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.”

For indeed, if, consenting together in brotherly love toward one another through faith in Jesus Christ, you have always been of one mind, without doubt you will easily conquer your adversary the devil. For where the true charity of Christ makes monks living in a monastery of one mind, there God is worshiped in all holiness; there the invisible presence of holy angels is believed to be present, through whom the rashness of malignant spirits is restrained. In such a congregation of saints God dwells, whom the army of the heavenly kingdom praises together with the voices of the monks singing psalms. A multitude of monks fervent in the love of God is the paradise of the delights of heavenly graces. A city adorned with a multitude of towers is a congregation of monks thinking the same thing in the Lord.

Keep watch, my brothers, I beseech you, keep watch in holy prayers, and especially at that time shake off drowsiness and dullness of mind when you stand in church before the Lord to sing psalms. For if, standing before God in psalmody, you are fervent in prayer, you will without doubt feel his grace present with you. For he is estranged in mind from the purpose of a monk who while praying thinks of something else, and offers his mind to be stirred not by divine things but by transient matters or occupations. For you know what our holy founder Benedict says in the Rule: “If,” he says, “we wish to suggest anything to powerful men, we do not presume to do so except with humility and reverence; how much more must supplication be made to the Lord God of all with all humility and devotion of purity; and let us know that we are heard not in much speaking, but in purity of heart and compunction of tears.” Since, however, for us singing psalms
