De vera humilitate monachorum. Humilitas mandatis dei placida volun- tate studiosa obsequitur: superbia prece- ptis altissimi reluctatur.Humilitas me- rita sempiterne felicitatis accumulat:su- perbia autē sibi grauissima inferni tormen̄ta parat. Humilitas securitateꝫ prestat in mortis articulo; superbia vero horribileꝫ metuꝫ et calamitatē affert morituro. Humilitas animaꝫ sui cultorīs in tremendo dei iudicio ab omni angustia liberat: supͣbia auteꝫ omnes elatos quos decepit in mundo corā iudice accusat. Humilitas dei seruos iudicis locabit ad dexterā: superbia vero damnandos constituet ad sinistram. Humilitas causaꝫ aget pro suis et obtinebit in iudicio: superbia autē nimiū cōfusa tradet elatos diabolo. Humilitas premiū eterne felicitatis suis rependet amicis: superbia vero tormēta perpe tua ꝺanationis omnibꝰ dabit elatis. Humilitas in celo sine fine coronabitur: suꝑbia autē apud inferos inestimabilē cruciatum cum demonibus perpetuo patietur.Humilitas coronata cum christo regna bit in celis:et superbia contempta cũ diabolo cruciabitur in penis:Humilitas lecta et gloriosa in eternum sedebit ad dextera ꝺei; superbia autē tristis et ignomini osa sine fine iacebit in tormentis inferni.Tunc humiles exultabūt in gloria:et superbi om̄es pre nimio dolore perpetuis temporibus clamabant in pena.Ibi stabunt humiles in conspectu dei et sanctoꝝ omniū in leticia magna et exultatiōe semipiterna: recipientes pro volūtaria huius vite inopia diuitias immarcessibiles:pro mansuetudine regnū:pro tristitia gaudiū pro dei amore imperium:pro contemptum mundi et carnis maceratione spontaneacelum. Uidentes aūt superbi et arrogantes in inferno constituti tantā gloriam humilium quos in mundo despexerunt miрабuntur in taꝫ subita mutatione sanctorum turbabunturqꝫ timore horribili premimia spiritus angustia gementes et dicētes in furore superbie.Hi sunt monachi pauperes et humiles quondā vilibus induti; sequestrati ab hominibꝰ: ab esu carniniū et omni spureicia carnis ahstinentes:quos habuimus aliqn̄ in derisum et finilitudinē improperij:nos insensatīr vltā illorū estimabantis insaniā:et fine illorū sine honore.Ecce qō inter filios dei computati sunt:et inter fauctos fors illorū est. Ergo errauimꝰ a via veritatis: et iustitie nobis lumen nō illuxit:et sol intelligentienō est ortus nobis. Quid nobis iaͣ pdest superbia qua runc inflati contempsimus humiles:et quid nobis confert habitain seculo diuitiarū iactantia? Preterieruntomnia:et nos ꝓ cōtunacia inter demonescōputati sumus:qm̄ humilitateꝫ odiosemꝑ habuimus:aefinefine patimur inestimabiles cruciatus.Humiles autē inperpetuū viuent:et apud dn̄m est mercescorū:et cogitatio illorū apud altissimum.Hee fratres mei semꝑ precogitate:qm̄ indubitanter ita futura funt;verāqꝫ ꝓpterea mētis humilitatē affluate: q̄tenꝰ eternep̄mia vite mercamini obtinere.Amen. De monachoru obe- dientia vera: Omelia. xx. HUmilitas monachoru fi vera et pfecta fuerit: omnē plenitudinē sanctarū virtutuꝫ parit.Quod sivirtutū splendoꝛe caruerit:vera in mente humili tas nuncqͣꝫ fuit.In primis etenim veramparit obedientiarū:et profundaꝫ in cunctispro dei amore subiectioneꝫ.Monachusem̄ qui vere humilis peregrinatur incunctesaluatoris nostri iesu christi studiosuꝫse in omnibus prebet discipulū: pro cuiueamore omni vtilitate et extremitate contētus:abbati suo in cunctis obediēs se gloriatur subiectum.Magna virtus est humnachi vera:que nō seruili metu sed interne charitatis affectu mandatis superioriimpenditur:que nō timore pene fed amorem iustitie vfqꝫ ad mortem perfeuerans ihilaritate mentis bonū operat. Due funteale mētis pulcherrime quibꝰ a terra monachus in celū auolat:quaꝝ altera humilitas dicit᷑;altera subiections obedientia nostat. Monachus qui his alīs ornatusnō fuerit:et nomē et meritū sue dignitatipsenitus amisit.Nec monachus est dicēdus fed me̓dax et fallacissimus apostata:quisqͥs ī cenobio viuit et cōuersat̉ sine hu [unclear]

On the true humility of monks.

Humility eagerly obeys the commandments of God with a peaceful will; pride struggles against the precepts of the Most High. Humility heaps up the merits of everlasting happiness; pride, however, prepares for itself the most grievous torments of hell. Humility affords security at the point of death; but pride brings horrible fear and calamity to the dying man. Humility frees the soul of its worshipper from every distress in the dread judgment of God; but pride accuses before the Judge all the haughty whom it deceived in the world. Humility will place the servants of God at the Judge’s right hand; but pride will set those to be damned on the left. Humility will plead the cause for its own and will prevail in the judgment; but pride, utterly confounded, will hand over the haughty to the devil. Humility will repay its friends with the reward of eternal happiness; but pride will give the perpetual torments of damnation to all the haughty. Humility will be crowned in heaven without end; but pride in the lower world will suffer forever with the demons an inestimable torment. Humility, crowned, will reign with Christ in heaven; and pride, despised, will be tortured with the devil in punishments. Humility, [glad?] and glorious, will sit forever at the right hand of God; but pride, sad and ignominious, will lie without end in the torments of hell.

Then the humble will exult in glory, and all the proud, because of exceeding pain, will cry out in punishment for everlasting ages. There the humble will stand in the sight of God and of all the saints in great joy and everlasting exultation, receiving, for the voluntary poverty of this life, unfading riches; for meekness, a kingdom; for sadness, joy; for love of God, dominion; for contempt of the world and voluntary chastening of the flesh, heaven. But when the proud and arrogant, placed in hell, see the great glory of the humble whom they despised in the world, they will marvel at so sudden a change of the saints, and they will be troubled with horrible fear, groaning under the very great anguish of spirit and saying in the fury of pride: “These are the poor and humble monks, formerly clothed in vile garments, separated from men, abstaining from the eating of meats and from all uncleanness of the flesh, whom we once held in derision and as a likeness of reproach. Senseless, we judged their life madness and their end without honor. Behold how they have been counted among the sons of God, and their lot is among the saints.

Therefore we have strayed from the way of truth, and the light of justice has not shone upon us, and the sun of understanding has not risen for us. What now does pride profit us, by which, then puffed up, we despised the humble? And what does the boastfulness of riches possessed in the world confer on us? All things have passed away, and we, because of obstinacy, have been counted among the demons, since we always held humility in hatred; and without end we suffer inestimable torments. But the humble will live forever, and their reward is with the Lord, and the thought of them is with the Most High.”

Always think on these things beforehand, my brothers, since without doubt they will be so; and therefore seek true humility of mind, so that you may merit to obtain the rewards of eternal life. Amen.

On the true obedience of monks: Homily 20.

If the humility of monks is true and perfect, it brings forth the whole fullness of the holy virtues. But if it lacks the splendor of virtues, there has never been true humility in the mind. For first of all it brings forth true obedience, and a profound subjection in all things for love of God. For the monk who in truth humbly sojourns shows himself in all things an eager disciple of our Savior Jesus Christ; for love of him, content with every advantage and extremity, he rejoices that he is subject to his abbot, obedient in all things. True [unclear] of the monk is a great virtue, which is rendered to the commands of superiors not through servile fear but through the affection of inward charity; which, persevering even unto death not from fear of punishment but from love of justice, performs good with cheerfulness of mind. There are two very beautiful wings of the mind by which the monk flies from earth to heaven; one of them is called humility, the other is marked as the obedience of subjection. The monk who has not been adorned with these wings has utterly lost both the name and the merit of his dignity. Nor should anyone be called a monk, but a lying and most deceitful apostate, whoever lives and dwells in the monastery without hu

Homily 20. Fol. XLVIII.

obedience of humble subjection. For a monk without obedience is a monster of the devil; and he who resists the commands of his superiors will inherit the punishments of hell. From the beginning the disobedience of the first man destroyed the way of eternal happiness, which the obedience of Jesus Christ restored. For he was made obedient to the Father for us, even unto death; and by his most innocent passion he restored to us the happiness we had lost. Hence the way to salvation is humble obedience, as our holy lawgiver Benedict cries out in the Rule: “Listen, my son, to the precepts of the master, and incline the ear of your heart, and willingly receive the admonition of a loving father and carry it out effectively, so that by the labor of obedience you may return to him from whom you had departed by the sloth of disobedience.”

Obedience is the tree of eternal salvation, which grows in the garden of monastic humility. Obedience is the dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit, and the quiet tomb of one’s own will. Obedience is the merit of heavenly happiness, and the sole lesson of monastic discipline. Obedience is the extermination of all pride and arrogance, and the persecutor of all vices. Obedience conquers every malice, and extinguishes every disordered pleasure of the flesh. Obedience makes the conscience pure and clean, and preserves true humility in the mind. Obedience is the remedy for the wound of the soul, and the foundation of all monastic observance. Obedience is the faithful guardian of all good works, and the discipline of a sincere mind. Obedience is the beginning of mortification, and the glorious ornament of monks. Obedience is the preserver of peace and concord, without which the vigor of monastic discipline perishes. Obedience always directs the edge of the mind toward God; and he who is truly mortified in spirit despises all the consolations of this world. Obedience makes a monk close to God, and far removed from all filth of soul. Obedience is the adornment of the soul and the garment of beauty; without it no one will come to the kingdom of eternal brightness. Obedience is the mother of victory; and whoever knows how, for the honor of God, to be subject in humility will obtain the crown of martyrdom in heaven. Obedience separates the monk from the world; and he who follows it with his whole heart will be great before the Most High. Obedience is the consummation of Christian perfection; in its humble workshop, the more a monk advances, the holier he becomes. Obedience is sure security at the hour of death; for a monk, when he is about to depart from here, will fly forth more securely the more ready he has been for obedience to commands. Obedience is the rewarder of the humble, and the chief emblem of merits. Obedience is the rule of Christian gentleness, and the strongest inner nourishment of charity. Obedience is the shelter of chastity, and the ornament of most pure innocence. Obedience is the wisdom of monks; and to acquiesce in the commands of prelates is the highest philosophy of cloistered men.

Obedience and humility are the wealth and riches of monks; and to possess continually in the mind the memory of the Lord’s passion is a sweetness greater than all the feasts of the world. Obedience and humility make the monk; but he who is rebellious and proud wears the monastic habit without cause. Obedience in the mind is the voluntary mortification of the members while they are alive; its merit is of such dignity that a man has nothing greater that may be offered in honor of God. Let each one offer for the love of God what he can: without doubt, he has offered more than all who has slaughtered his own will for God through obedience. It is indeed a great good to distribute one’s resources for Christ’s love to the uses of the poor, and to relieve by alms the want of the needy. But by as much as the whole outweighs the part, by as much as the free choice of the will is nobler than necessity, by as much as heaven stands apart from earth, by so much more has he offered who, for the love of God and by laying aside his will, has forever denied himself. For whatever temporal substance you have offered to God is not yours but another’s, and is of less value than what is proper to you, both in esteem and in reward. You have one thing proper to yourself which, offered to God, is pleasing above all things. What is this, if not free will, which the almighty Creator placed in your power? A good will is greater than all riches, for nothing richer can be offered to God, nothing will be judged more acceptable.

This most precious gift, my brothers, you once offered to God when, denying yourselves and all worldly things for Christ’s honor, you put on the monastic habit. I beseech you, be mindful of the prayers of your holy profession, and let that solemn promise never depart from memory, which each one of you made in the sight of God before us, saying: “I, brother Johannes, promise stability, and conversion of my ways, and obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, before God and his saints, in this monastery which was built in honor of blessed Martin, in the presence of lord Johannes, abbot.” Behold the bond by which we have voluntarily bound ourselves to obedience; behold

Sed hoc est verum, quia omnes peccati sunt communi causa mortis, et omnes boni sunt causa vitis; ergo si quis bonum faciet, sic etiam moritur, et si quis peccatuit, sic etiam vult. Et ideo dicitur apostolus, Qu

On the True Obedience of Monks.

...the warfare which we have professed. For these are the vows which our lips declared; these are the sacrifices of pious devotion which we offered to God. Certainly, my brothers, the things we have promised are great, and a greater necessity lies upon us to keep what we have professed. For unless we faithfully observe everything that the Rule of our blessed father Saint Benedict commands us, the justice of almighty God will judge us severely as perjured and impious transgressors. For it is very dangerous not to render to God what has been promised, and through forgetfulness of the holy institution to violate one’s purpose.

Therefore, to satisfy the duty of pastoral care, I am accustomed daily to admonish you to the observance of regular discipline; nor hereafter shall the necessary word of salvation ever be lacking to you, so long as my spirit remains in this prison of the flesh. But you, I pray, take care not to be fruitless hearers, since the matter concerns the soul, which, once lost, is never recovered. Therefore, all of you who have come together in the monastery to run the course of intellectual combat, all of you who for love of Christ have once renounced your own will and the world: take up holy obedience as the helmet of salvation, and you will carry off a sure victory over the enemy.

For obedience is the strongest armor of monks, which no adversities will be able to harm. For Scripture says: “He who keeps the commandment will experience no evil.” In Proverbs also it is said thus: “The obedient man will speak of victories.” Obedience makes a monk invincible in all temptations; and he who follows in all things the counsel of his elder will never suffer loss to the salvation of his soul. For obedience is a short and rough road, by which one quickly ascends to the summit of perfection. But the monk who is a true soldier of Christ never trusts his own judgment, but in all things follows and observes the direction of his pastor.

Indeed, he who is a true lover of Christ, the monk who wholly desires to be faithful, loves his abbot as the vicar of God, and, always obedient to his commands, counsels, and ordinances in all things, submits cheerfully. In order that a monk may be able to do this confidently, no boy, no unlearned man, no carnal man, no one lacking discretion, nor anyone light-minded or inexperienced in spiritual combats, is to be ordained abbot, but a man mature in character, learned in the divine Scriptures, walking in the spirit in the true way of life of holiness, pious, gentle, tranquil in mind, and discreet, one who knows how to show judgment to the wicked and mercy to the well-disposed.

For whenever a restless, turbulent, indiscreet, and inexperienced man is appointed abbot over monks, the integrity of regular discipline is at once shipwrecked. Subjection, and with it the obedience of humility, must perish when subjects cannot have firm confidence in their pastor. For if the abbot is a mocker of his brothers, or an over-harsh despiser of the weak, who will open to him any secret whatever of his heart? Therefore the greatest care must be taken at the beginning that such a pastor be appointed for sheep bereft of one, who seeks nothing other than the honor of God and the salvation of souls.

The monk who has obtained such a pastor should give thanks to God, for in these times of ours he rarely occurs who knows how to show himself in all things a worthy and suitable prelate. He is deservedly to be loved by all his subjects and, as the vicar of Christ in the monastery, honored with continual veneration. Let the thoughts of all be opened to him without fear, since he seeks nothing other than the progress of each one. If the physician of sick bodies must be prudent, experienced, and endowed with the highest discretion, how much more fitting is it that the abbot be an excellent man, since he is the physician of souls?

Blessed are the monks to whom God’s mercy has granted a useful and suitable pastor, provided that it has not also denied them the ability to understand this very thing. Otherwise a good pastor of bad sheep is not recognized in his uprightness, but rather, through the ingratitude of the depraved, is tormented with the Lord. For often the judgments of monks are blind whenever an opinion is sought about prelates; and those who by their conduct corrupt the integrity of the order rarely judge truly and rightly about pastors. Because of the ingratitude of subjects, rulers are very often changed for the worse; and monks who despise a good and useful pastor in the present life have received, by the just judgment of God, a foolish and useless successor.

Those who are subject in simplicity walk rightly, and those who truly imitate Christ do not pass judgment on the one presiding over them. For we have as the shepherd of faithful souls the one whom we should follow, our Lord Jesus Christ; looking faithfully toward him in spirit, we shall not rashly judge the visible pastor. “On the chair of Moses,” he says, “the scribes and Pharisees have sat; what they tell you, do; but what they do, do not imitate.” Hear these things, O monk, and [unclear]. But this is true: that all sins are the common cause of death, and all good things are the cause of life; therefore if anyone does good, [unclear], and if anyone has sinned, [unclear]. And therefore the Apostle says, “[unclear]”

FoxLIX. proprie salutis amator et studiosus for- man obediencie qua sequaris considera Abbas christi vicarii gerit i monasterio qui sine bonus sit sine malus: obediencie non suo merito sed christi nomine mere- tur omnium subditorum. Negentim de so- lis apostolis intelligimus dictu: qui vos audit me audit: & vos spernit me sper- nit: sed de quolibet in dei ecclesia prelato qui custos et rector constitut est anima. Ergo si abbatem habes bonum idoneum et sanctum: audi vocem eius tangi man- datum dei vicem gerentis: & quicquid ti bi precepterit esto obediens in omnibus. Si autem tibi doctrina eius norma vi- vendi: & conversatio sancta purioris insti- tutionis exempluz. Amicus enim dei est jesu christi vicarius: altero meretur ve diligas: altero vero vt in omnibus preci- pienti obediens. Quod si pastoret assecu- tus rudem: imperitum vel certe minus ido- neum: caueto peccare ne actiones eius te- mere velis discutere: sed cogita poti? q̄o peccata tua merentur pastorem inutiliern babere. Considera euiz non quod est sed quod dicitur: q̄ honora pastorem propter illius amorem et reuerentiam cuius vicar- iatu insignitur. Obedientiam quaz deo promisisti eius vicario pure et simpliciter exhibendam omni tempore memineris: quoniã si abbas in sua conversatione ma- lus fuerit: vicariatuz tamen christi nisi in re deponatur no amitter. Aec te absolvit a promissa religionis obedientia: pastoris reim reproba vita. Detuenda est visitati, p- uerbi nostri sententia. Monachi repro- bi: non merentur abbatem habere bonum Non de vobis hoc paradigma vibratuiz existimetis fratres charismi: negentim pastorem me malum confido: quanuis rudem et imperitum negare non possum: sed neç mali de vobis suspitione admisi- mus vnic: quippe qui nihil magis queri- mus et fraternam in omnibus nutrire et ampiare charitatem. Frequenter veniunt ad nos monachi vel cuz ratione vel sine causa peregrinantes: qui materiaz insta- bilitatis sue vt plurinnu retoquent in ab- bates. Ego aut qui vos ad omia quesan cta et utilia cupio esse instructos: charita- tes vestras paternu exhortor et moneo: vt bis circucelliõib? aures de cetero no por- rigatis: qui moribus pastorum suõi de- trabunt: & propria scelerà delationib? alie nis abscondere contendunt: Non est hec monastice institutiõis necessaria integri- tas: causã rebellionis et inobedientie sub ditozũ in capue retoquere pastoris. Qui verus est monachus aliena temere non judicat: & qui humilis obediëtiefilii est causas rebellionis non explorat. Qui au- tem passionibus carnis indulger consen- sum: nunquam potest quiescere: & qui vi- tam scrutinatur alienam: contemptor salu- tis est propriae. Monachus in dei amore fundatus non dijudicat mandatum seni- oris: & qui christum semper intuetur pre- sentem: summ ve angelum dei veneratur pastorem. Audacia monachum degenerat: & presumptrio multos in carcerem pre- cipitavit. Monachus petulas lascivius et protervus sanctitatis amise proposituz et nisi reuocetur ad mentem dura castiga- tione carnis pedem iam poluit ad infer- nũ. Qui mandatu senioris curiosa teme- ritate discernit no est obediens: & contra- sta ad imperiũ no est ver? christi discipu- lus. Vera nanci obedientia no murmuras no hesitat: no trista: no querit diverticu- lũ: no tardatno excusar: nec ostedit min- ni- mũ irresignatiõis signũ. Ad mandatu se- nioris p christi amore sempr exultat: occu- rit leta: & cum festinatione obedit bilari- ter. Quid enim aliud est monachus quae certator affiduus: qui virtutibus arma- tus humilitatis et obedientie semper in stadio certamis vigilar: & sub triplici acie victor contra semetipsum fortius pugnat. Beatus ille monachus qui vim sibi ipsi faciens: voluntatem carnis superare di- dicit: & per continuum spiritualis militia vsum: montem vere obedientie arduuz conscédit. Vere monachus ille beatus: qui cõtemptis omnibv mundi solacũs: se totũ in amore iesu christi reposuit: & nibil ia visibiliũ ampliõ cõcupiscit. No est mo- nachoru divitias: honores et voluptates in hoc mundo qrerere: nec decet militie christi aliud et christũ cogitare. O monachum ter quaterõ felice qui voluntate p christi amore pprĩa vsc ad vltimu vite mortifi- car: & invera obedientia humilis pleuerat Quantum sit bonum corae deo humilis obedientia: fratres mei nemo sufficienter porest edicere:iquam cunctis victimis div- uina prorestatio voluit preferre. Obedi- entia est q aiam deo recõciliat: & per effu- sionẽ languinis martyres coronat. De monachorum obedientia vera.

Homily XX. Fol. LIX.

O lover and student of your own salvation, consider the form of obedience which you are to follow. The abbot holds the place of Christ’s vicar in the monastery, whether he be good or bad; he deserves the obedience of all who are subject to him not by his own merit but in the name of Christ. For we understand the saying, “He who hears you hears me; and he who despises you despises me,” not only of the apostles, but of any prelate in the Church of God who has been appointed guardian and ruler of souls.

Therefore, if you have an abbot who is good, suitable, and holy, hear his voice as the command of God, since he bears God’s place; and whatever he commands you, be obedient to him in all things. If his teaching is for you a rule of life, and his holy conduct an example of purer instruction, then he is a friend of God and the vicar of Jesus Christ: in the one respect he deserves that you love him, and in the other that you obey him in all things when he commands.

But if you have obtained a shepherd who is rude, unlearned, or certainly less suitable, take care not to sin by wishing rashly to examine his actions, but rather consider that your sins deserve to have a useless shepherd. Consider him not as what he is, but as what he is called; honor the shepherd because of love and reverence for him whose vicariate marks him out. Remember at all times that the obedience which you promised to God must be shown purely and simply to his vicar; for if the abbot is bad in his manner of life, nevertheless he does not lose the vicariate of Christ unless he is deposed in fact. Nor does the shepherd’s wicked and blameworthy life absolve you from the obedience promised in religion.

The meaning of our word must be upheld. Bad monks do not deserve to have a good abbot. Do not think, beloved brothers, that this example is being hurled at you. For I do not think myself a bad shepherd, although I cannot deny that I am rude and unlearned; nor have we admitted any suspicion of evil about you, since indeed we seek nothing more than to nourish and enlarge brotherly charity in all things.

Frequently monks come to us, wandering either with reason or without cause, who for the most part turn the matter of their own instability back upon their abbots. But I, who desire you to be instructed in all things that are holy and useful, exhort and warn your charities in fatherly fashion that hereafter you not lend your ears to these wanderers, who slander the characters of their own shepherds and strive to hide their own crimes by accusations against others. This is not the necessary integrity of monastic life: to turn the cause of the rebellion and disobedience of subjects back upon the head of the shepherd.

He who is a true monk does not judge another rashly; and he who is a son of humble obedience does not investigate causes of rebellion. But he who grants consent to the passions of the flesh can never be at rest; and he who scrutinizes another’s life is a despiser of his own salvation. A monk founded in the love of God does not pass judgment on the command of his superior; and he who always beholds Christ present venerates his own shepherd as an angel of God. Boldness makes a monk degenerate, and presumption has cast many into prison.

A monk who is wanton, too lascivious, and insolent has lost the purpose of holiness; and unless he is recalled to his senses by the hard chastisement of the flesh, he has already set his foot upon hell. He who examines the command of his superior with curious rashness is not obedient; and he who resists an order is not a true disciple of Christ. For true obedience does not murmur, does not hesitate, is not sad, does not seek a byway, does not delay, does not excuse itself, nor does it show the least sign of lack of resignation. At the superior’s command, for the love of Christ, it always rejoices; it runs to meet it gladly, and obeys cheerfully with haste.

For what else is a monk than a constant combatant, who, armed with the virtues of humility and obedience, always keeps watch in the arena of struggle, and, victorious under a threefold battle-line, fights more strongly against himself? Blessed is that monk who, doing violence to himself, has learned to overcome the will of the flesh, and by the continual practice of spiritual warfare climbs the steep mountain of true obedience. Truly blessed is that monk who, having despised all the comforts of the world, has placed his whole self in the love of Jesus Christ, and now desires nothing further among visible things. It is not for monks to seek riches, honors, and pleasures in this world, nor is it fitting for the soldier of Christ to think of anything except Christ. O monk three and four times blessed, who, for the love of Christ, mortifies his own will until the end of life, and in true obedience has humbly [unclear].

How great a good humble obedience is before God, my brothers, no one can sufficiently declare; for the divine testimony wished to prefer it to all victims. It is obedience that reconciles the soul to God, and through the shedding of blood crowns the martyrs.

On the true obedience of monks.

96
Nachus enim qui se propter deũ spontanea voluntate ad perpetuam religionis obedientiam obligat: si iusta votus recte vivit prolixtum certe martyrium portat. Obedientia igitur est sine sanguinis effusione martyrium: et subjecere se homini propter deũ voluntarie carnis ingenis est to:metu. Aia q̄ humilitate tobedictiā veraciter diligit ad coronaz martiriī sine dubio perrigit. Arduum est opus tni mis laboriosum certamen liberuz hominem semipsum despiceret: et se totum voluntarem suam omnes sub imperio et po testate alterius perpetuo resignare. In tueamur autem fidelibus oculis huius mercedem certaminis: et reputabimus omnia dura et aspera huius vite quasi lu dum esse quendam puerilem: qui iam ad horam cernitur truṣç postea comparebit. Flam vi christi amatoris dicit apostolus: non sunt condigne passiones huius temporis ad superuentura gloria quae revelabitur in nobis. Coronaz quae sanctis martyriu p chris to q̄ndaz contulit: hodie veris christi amatoris humilis obedientia preparabit. Monachus enim pro christo vere humilis et obedientis sine paurose securus moritur: vt pote qui sub imperio senioris sui fideliter militans: ab omni rationis exactione liberatur. Flami qui ad nutum pastoris sui vivens in omnibus mā datis deirecte graditur: nihil potest com mittere quod ad iudicem deferatur. Ab batis em testimonio defenditur: ad cui9 directionem sine querela recte conversat. Considerate fratres legem obedientie se cundũ quam vivere promisistis: et scitote q̄n necessariuz fecistis quod voluntariũ fuerat: quado in sententia monasticae tra ditionis solenniter cōnsensistis. Non licet vobis iā a sancto proposito recedere: nec potestis votum semel emissum reuocare. Si feceritis omnia secundũ sancti euangelii christi et norma Benedicti patris q̄ voutis: non sit vobis hesitationis dubiũ beati eritis: et mercede sanctis debitam a dno recipietis. Si aut promissionum ve strarũ imemores: votus sancte puritatis deo factũ violaueritis: si cōversatione spi rituali cōtempra secundũ carnē vixeritis lá nunc denūcio vobis er lege vestra: q̄m certissime condēnandi estis a dno nto ieu chris to iudice oim quẽ irridēdo cōtem psiftis. Multo em melius est nibil pro/

For the monk who, for God’s sake, of his own free will binds himself to the perpetual obedience of religion, if he lives rightly according to his vow, surely bears a prolonged martyrdom. Obedience, therefore, is martyrdom without the shedding of blood; and voluntarily to subject oneself to a man for God’s sake is a great torment [of the flesh?]. The soul that truly loves humility and obedience undoubtedly advances to the crown of martyrdom. It is a hard work and an exceedingly laborious contest for a free man to despise himself, and to resign himself wholly, and all his will, perpetually under the command and power of another. But let us behold with faithful eyes the reward of this contest, and we shall reckon all the hard and rough things of this life to be like a certain childish game, which is now seen for an hour [unclear] will appear afterwards. Hence the apostle, speaking in the person of a lover of Christ, says: The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the coming glory that shall be revealed in us. The crown that martyrdom once bestowed on the saints for Christ, humble obedience will today prepare for the true lovers of Christ. For a monk who is truly humble and obedient for Christ dies secure, without fear, since, serving faithfully under the command of his elder, he is freed from every demand for an account. For he who, living at the nod of his shepherd, walks uprightly in all commands, can commit nothing that may be brought before the judge. He is defended by the testimony of the abbot, according to whose direction he has lived rightly and without complaint. Consider, brothers, the law of obedience according to which you have promised to live, and know that you have made necessary what had been voluntary, when you solemnly consented to the sentence of monastic tradition. It is no longer lawful for you to withdraw from your holy purpose, nor can you revoke a vow once uttered. If you do everything according to the holy Gospel of Christ and the rule of father Benedict, which you have vowed, let there be no doubtful hesitation for you: you will be blessed, and you will receive from the Lord the reward owed to the saints. But if, unmindful of your promises, you violate the vow of holy purity made to God, if you live according to the flesh in contempt of spiritual conduct, then I now denounce to you by your own law that you are most certainly to be condemned by our Lord Jesus Christ, the judge of all, whom you have mocked and despised. For it is much better to promise nothing /

Homily XXI.

[unclear]: for love of him you have set me, an unworthy man, over you as abbot. For I shall not be troublesome to you if you run well; but if anyone turns aside from the way of truth, I am compelled, even unwillingly, to meet him as best I can.

Let the monk always think on his entrance into the monastery, and never forget the first purpose of his profession. In all your works also, O monk, always consider that you are not long-lived upon the earth, but will shortly depart from this life, and that perhaps when you do not expect it, you will die. Therefore keep inviolate the purpose of holiness, and always be watchful in good works, so that when the Lord comes and calls you, he may find you prepared. Remember that you are a pilgrim on earth, and do not have here a lasting city; but just as a traveler hastens quickly toward the end of his journey, so death draws near to you daily without ceasing. Therefore, while you are healthy, set the house of your conscience in order, so that you may not fear death; for rarely does he die well who is not prepared as though he were to die daily.

How securely the monk departs from this life who, keeping his conscience clean in all purity, lives at all times, without reproach, according to the full integrity of the rule of our most holy lawgiver, even unto death. Let your mind continually hold in memory our Lord Jesus Christ as present, indeed as nowhere absent; and let no hour pass in which you do not think with thanksgiving of him suffering for you. Stand in humility and true obedience, and no adversities will ever prevail against you. Just as a tree sending many great roots into the earth is not easily torn from its place, so the monk who possesses charity and obedience in humility, together with the other virtues, is by no means overcome by demons. Obedience, brothers, is a great virtue, which brings the other virtues into the mind, and, once brought in, preserves them through the ministry of humility. May our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who became obedient for us unto the death of the cross, illumine your hearts by his grace, and sweetly inflame your minds at all times for the observance of regular life; who lives and reigns with God the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, unto all ages of ages. Amen.

On continence and true chastity: Homily XXI.

I would most earnestly wish, my dearest brothers, that I had obtained from God that grace by which I might be for you a worthy and suitable shepherd, both in deed and in speech. For I know, and it does not escape me, how perilous the governance of souls is for a young and inexperienced man such as I am, when one who has not yet learned to direct and govern himself according to the rule of justice presumes to approach the instruction of others. I blush to open my mouth among you to teach, since, having been a disciple for a short time, I am compelled before maturity to be a teacher. But since it so pleased you, and you wished to have me, a young man, as master, pardon me, because necessity compels me to fulfill, as best I can, the office committed to me.

Assist me with your prayers, I beg you, brothers, so that the mercy of God may grant the strength that the command of authority denies. For I desire you to walk before God in all purity of mind and body, so that you may please him to whom you handed yourselves over from the beginning. Having taken him as the leader of the journey to heaven, look upon our Lord Jesus Christ, who, born of the ever most chaste Virgin Mary, perpetually preserved the most perfect chastity of mind and body. Imitate this teacher, into whose service you have consecrated your hands, so that you may preserve not only in body the continence enjoined upon you, but also with a mind brighter than sapphire and carbuncle may perpetually guard chastity.

For chastity is a most beautiful virtue, especially fitting for cloistered men, so that under the yoke of reason it may restrain every assault of lust, and, the madness of vices being extinguished, the bearing of the body may preserve all honorableness. An incontinent and wanton monk, who follows the filthy lust of the flesh, is counted with the demons who withdrew from the Lord.

There are three things whose perpetual observance [unclear] our [unclear], without which no one among monks is to be judged worthy of being named. The first of these is the obedience of humble and true subjection; the second, the renunciation of all property, as the rule commands; the third, the inviolate guardianship of perpetual continence and chastity. Whatever one of these the monk violates, he corrupts the purpose of his order. Chastity is sustained by two companions: fasting, namely, and temperance; if it is ever deprived of these, it quickly, without doubt, collapses. The chastity of monks is the greatest ornament, by which, adorned, it will lead them into the fellowship of the angels.

On continence and true chastity: Homily XXI.

De continentia et vera castitate. Castitatem nihil est pulchrius: que conceptum de immundo semine facit munduꝫ de hoste quoqƺ efficit domesticũ: et de homine terreste angelũ. Castitas virtus est omnium virtutum speciosissima: que dũ pro chꝛisti amore vsqƺ ad mortem seruan da promittit̃: inestimabili premio remuneratur. Castitas angeloruꝫ societati est proxima: et summa chꝛistiane mentis me dicina. Castitas est iesu chꝛisti eterni regis amabile domncilii: et future ĩ corruptionis mirabile principiu. Castitas est ple nitudo celestis gratie: per quam redinte gratur om̄is corruptio nature. Castitas est virtus omniū potentissima: per quam in vase fragili mirabiliter certamine vincitur natura. Castitas vitam imitatuer angeli cam: et nescit in medio luti aliqnā macule conspersionem. Beatus homo qui vere donuꝫ castitatis a domino deo suscipere promeruit: et ipsuꝫ inuiolatũ vsqƺ ad morrem in humilitate christiana custodiiuit. Castus est qui amore iesu chꝛisti mente et corpore purus ab omni carnis coinquinatione se abstinet: qui feruore sancti spiritius in charitate dei dulciter ardet: qui nihil omnino concupiscit in hoc seculo: qđ esse et viuere semper desiderat euꝫ chꝛisto Castus est qui memor professionis miliarie spiritualis motus carnis ratione com primit: et om̄es prurientes libidinis scilillas mox a principio fortiter restringit. Castus est cui mox vt cogitatio carnalis mentem pulsare ceperit diuinum cuꝫ lachrymis implorat auxilium: nec quiescit a precibus: donec incendium prurientis ardoris penitus senserit extinctũ. Castus est qi fugit omnē materiam et occafionem luxurie: qui pepigit fedus cū oculis suis ne quidem cogitet de femina: et ponit custodiam sensibus suis ne quaingerantur feda vel impudica. Castus esth qui lasciuoꝝ declinat consortia: et semper auertit oculos suos ne conspiciat vana. Castus esh qđ omniuꝫ mulierũ detesta tur frequentiam: et qui suam fragilitateꝫ cum timore et vigilantia om̄i tempore habet suspectam. Castus quideꝫ est qui mēte et corpore naturam imitatuer angelicacet qui sanctis moribus nullam admittit corruptionem. Castitas donuꝫ est gratie et non opus nature vel industrie humane Castitas monachum humilē deo facitesse gratissimũ: quoniaꝫ qui viuit in carne mortali sine corruptiōe socius est angelo rum. Qui castitateꝫ assecutus est veram semper est humilis: et qui naturaꝫ eius intelligit: non sibi eius possessionē arrogat: sed domino qui dedit. Nemo enim castꝰ viribus suis: qm̃ naturam vincere homo fragillis nō sufficit: nisi dederit ille qui naturam et om̄ia creauit. Naꝫ quotiens na tura per castitatem vincitur: deus homini manifeste cooperatur. Habet aut̃ ipsa castitas in pubescentibus difficile princi pium: quo usqƺ motus illicite cogitatiōis duocatur in contemptu. Castitas fornicationē fugiendo porius quā concertando exuperat: qm̃ tot subtilibus armis luxuria circūcigitur: vt vltro sit declinanda priusqƺ congregiatur. Quotiens ergo cūqƺ animus luxurie motibus tangitur diuinũ sine mora auxilium inuocetur: non detur ĩmunde cogitationi deliberatiōis spaciũ: sed mox vt sentiri ceperit per obliuionis remedium ducatur in contemplu Cuꝫ hoste fraudulento et qui semper vti tur insidijs: nulla sunt penitus com̄iscen da colloquio: et cuꝫ ĩmundis cogitationibus carnis non sunt tractanda consilia. Enimuero nisi caput serpentis conteras labitur: et nisi motus luxurie mox compri mas a principio roborātur. Monet sanctus chꝛisti apostolus paulus cōtra que libet vicia pugnandum: fornicationē solā precipit fugiendã. Materiaꝫ contra nos victorie circūferimꝰ: propterea vult qđ hostem fugiamus. Castitas ieiunio alitura: gula naufragatur. Unde si castitateꝫ diligis ama ieiunium: vt necessariũ habe at alimentum. Qui castus est apis industriam sequitur: et qui vere est monachus quasi omnibus floribus exornatus cunctis virtutibus decoratur. Castus est nō omnis qui nescit luxuriā: sed qui in carne pura et mūda pro chꝛisti amore solius etiam mentis obtinet sanctitateꝫ. Alioquin quid prodest domicilij puritas: si habita tor sit fedus et ĩmundus? Habuit et virgines suas quondaꝫ veste sacrificantes ceça gentilitas: sed quia non deo vero pudi dicitiam corporū ĩmolarunt: nec fidem rectam mente tenuerunt: cum suis demonibbus quos coluerunt in profunduꝫ inferni descenderunt. Castus ess em̃ qui amorem creatoris et carnea ab omni cohibet luxuria: et mẽtē sanctis virtutibus ipsi deo ĩmolat omnifariaꝫ decoratam. Extra fi[unclear]

On continence and true chastity.

Nothing is more beautiful than chastity: it makes clean what has been conceived from unclean seed; it also makes an enemy into a member of the household, and an earthly man into an angel. Chastity is the most beautiful of all the virtues; when, for love of Christ, it promises that it is to be preserved even unto death, it is rewarded with an inestimable prize. Chastity is next to the fellowship of the angels, and the highest medicine of the Christian mind. Chastity is the lovable dwelling-place of Jesus Christ, the eternal king, and the wondrous beginning of future incorruption. Chastity is the fullness of heavenly grace, through which every corruption of nature is restored. Chastity is the most powerful of all virtues, through which, in a fragile vessel, nature is marvelously conquered in combat. Chastity imitates the angelic life, and, in the midst of mud, knows no sprinkling of stain.

Blessed is the man who has merited to receive from the Lord God the true gift of chastity, and has kept it inviolate, in Christian humility, even unto death. Chaste is he who, for love of Jesus Christ, pure in mind and body, abstains from every defilement of the flesh; who, by the fervor of the Holy Spirit, burns sweetly in the charity of God; who desires nothing at all in this age, but always desires to be and to live with Christ. Chaste is he who, mindful of the profession of spiritual warfare, restrains the motions of the flesh by reason, and at once, from the beginning, strongly checks all the itching sparks of lust. Chaste is he who, as soon as carnal thought begins to strike the mind, implores divine aid with tears, and does not cease from prayers until he has felt the fire of itching ardor wholly extinguished. Chaste is he who flees every material and occasion of lust; who has made a covenant with his eyes that he should not even think about a woman; and who sets a guard over his senses, lest foul or immodest things be brought in. Chaste is he who avoids the company of the wanton, and always turns his eyes away so that he may not behold vain things. Chaste is he who detests the frequent company of all women, and who at every time regards his own frailty with fear and vigilance as suspect. Chaste indeed is he who in mind and body imitates angelic nature, and who by holy morals admits no corruption.

Chastity is a gift of grace, and not a work of nature or of human effort. Chastity makes the humble monk most pleasing to God, since he who lives in mortal flesh without corruption is a companion of the angels. He who has attained true chastity is always humble; and he who understands its nature does not arrogate possession of it to himself, but to the Lord who gave it. For no one is chaste by his own strength, since frail man is not sufficient to conquer nature, unless he who created nature and all things has given it. For as often as nature is conquered through chastity, God manifestly works together with man. Chastity itself has, however, a difficult beginning in the young, until the motion of unlawful thought is brought into contempt. Chastity overcomes fornication by fleeing rather than by fighting, since lust is surrounded with so many subtle weapons that it must be avoided of one’s own accord before it is engaged.

Therefore, as often as the soul is touched by the motions of lust, divine aid should be invoked without delay; no space for deliberation should be given to unclean thought, but as soon as it begins to be felt, it should be brought into contempt by the remedy of forgetfulness. With a fraudulent enemy, and one who always uses ambushes, no dealings at all are to be joined in conversation; and plans are not to be considered with the unclean thoughts of the flesh. Indeed, unless you crush the serpent’s head, it slips away; and unless you at once restrain the motions of lust, they are strengthened from the beginning. The holy apostle of Christ, Paul, admonishes that one must fight against any vices whatever; fornication alone he commands to be fled. We carry about with us the material of victory against ourselves; therefore he wills that we flee the enemy. Chastity is nourished by fasting; by gluttony it is shipwrecked. Hence, if you love chastity, love fasting, so that it may have its necessary nourishment. He who is chaste follows the industry of the bee; and he who is truly a monk, adorned as if with all flowers, is decorated with all virtues.

Not everyone who does not know lust is chaste, but he who, in pure and clean flesh, for love of Christ alone, also obtains holiness of mind. Otherwise, what does the purity of the dwelling profit, if the inhabitant is foul and unclean? Blind paganism too once had its virgins, sacrificing in garments; but because they did not sacrifice the modesty of their bodies to the true God, nor hold the right faith in their mind, they descended into the depth of hell with their demons whom they worshiped. For he is chaste who, for love of the Creator, restrains even the flesh from every lust, and sacrifices the mind to God himself, adorned in every way with holy virtues. Outside fi

[unclear] of Jesus Christ, today there is no true chastity, nor any that is meritorious for eternal salvation. Although you live chastely, O monk, pure and holy, and as long as the spirit remains in the body, do not presume to have confidence in chastity from clay. The food of chastity is fasting and abstinence, and, in every action, the support of wholesome continence. But when you have attained all things, do not trust in yourself, because he whom we know to have eaten nothing fell from heaven. The mortification of the body is both very necessary and useful for preserving the beauty of chastity; but however much you have advanced in either, do not trust in yourself, but, always watchful and hoping in the Lord's help, be afraid. For unless you keep yourself continually and most earnestly in the fear of the Lord, the house of your conscience will quickly be overthrown. He runs in vain who presumes to guard chastity by his own strength. For unless the Lord causes the dwelling-place of chastity to be built, the one who builds the wall of abstinence labors in vain. And unless you become, with all your strength, a co-worker with divine grace, you will in no way obtain the beauty of chastity. For God will not make you chaste without your will, nor will you attain this great gift unless he, through his mercy, comes to the aid of your weakness. Therefore yours it will be, O monk, to offer the desire for chastity with good will, and, in humble confidence, to await certain increase from the Lord. Apply fasting, and the Lord's help will not be lacking. Chastity is a gift of grace, not of nature; and to live in the flesh as though beyond the flesh belongs to angelic strength, not human. Nevertheless it is not difficult for a man of good will to preserve chastity, especially one who is separated from the tumult of worldly people and lives solitary in the midst of monks. A monk, too, who, young and innocent, enters a monastery of good reform, if he keeps his mind continually occupied in the fear of the Lord, is less assailed by lust. For the experience of lust is pernicious, since, as someone truly said, it seeks to conquer souls, not to satisfy the veins. But a monk who is a lover of lust can easily extinguish the heat if, fleeing idleness and fullness, he is willing to occupy himself continually in spiritual exercise. For among all vices none assaults chastity more greatly and more dangerously than fullness and idleness. If a monk overcomes these two evils, he will easily preserve chastity. Hence the most holy princes of monks, wishing to cut away the causes of lust, established for us a spare and meager diet according to a fixed measure, by which the body is sustained for necessity and is not fattened for lust. They also decreed that scantiness of sleep was useful for monks, because immoderate rest expands the flesh no less than gluttony. But they wished idleness, as the most pernicious plague of the soul, to be far from cloistered persons, dividing the time most wisely so that a monk would never be found idle. Hear these things, brothers, and grasp them in your mind, you who carry a great treasure in a fragile little body. Always flee idleness; do something good, so that whenever the tempter, the devil, approaches, he may find you usefully occupied. For truly, he who is idle lies open to the snares of the tempter; but he who is occupied in good work has closed every entrance to snares. Therefore the mind must be occupied with continual exercise, so that it is never found idle. Blessed is that monk who occupies his mind at all times in good exercises and never sleeps in the sleep of torpor and sloth. Blessed is the spiritual soldier of Christ who always keeps watch in the fear of the Lord and immediately restrains, from the beginning, all the disordered motions of the flesh. For it is not enough to guard true chastity unharmed, if someone plays with unclean thoughts as though deliberately. It belongs to strong men to [unclear] the first motions of wicked [unclear], because where delay creates danger, one must fight strongly at once. There must always be vigilance against the adversary of our salvation, who is never conquered more quickly than if he is choked off immediately from the beginning. Naz fornicationis vìciũ consuetudine diuturna conualescens defacili non vincitur: nisi cōtrarijs remedijs per violentiã emendetur. Facilimum est a statu rectitudinis in quodlibet viciusz cadere: quam roboratum consuetudine peccatũ emēdare. Nam vt veraciter quidam ait gentilis, facilis est descēsus auerni: sed re uocare gradũ supaqƺ euadere ad auras: hic opus hîc labor est. Consideremus illos qui foueam hanc turpissimaz incide runt: et postea maiorum auctoritate ad penitentiam compulsi sunt quemadmoduz in medio fratrũ conuersantur. Vere com punctionis non habent signa: sed in ariditate coꝛdis vitam agunt inquietã. Nul la mentis deuotio apud eos conspicuitur: sed carnis vbiqƺ solatia sequunt̃. O quaꝫ raro ad interni amoris dulcedinẽ cōuertitur: quisquis in lacuʒ fornicationis semel precipitatut. Qui ergo gulosus ad satietatem manducans et bibẽs vincere spiritum fornicationis desiderat quasi oleum ad incendiuʒ portat. Et qui cum sola abstinentia luxurie motus contentit extinguere: similis est homini qui cum vna manu in medio fluctuum cernitur natare. Coniungatur abstinence continua ad deum oratio: et in naui sancte hũmilitatis secure nauigabitur. Semper sit in ore monachi oratio: et memoria passionis et mortis domini iesu christi. Quotiens ergo motum carnis inordina tum sensueris: quotiens hostem a dessesse inuisibilem ad nocendum perceperis: mox ad pendentez in cruce filium dei confugito flexiqƺ in terram genibus talis ad eũ formetur oratio. On continence and true chastity.

to God, by whose words you have sworn; and so live that you do not fear to appear at his judgment.

You are monks, set apart from the world for the service of our Lord Jesus Christ by a voluntary promise; hence, under necessity of salvation, you must lead a life higher and holier than the rest of your fellow Christians, and overcome every depravity of flesh and soul. For you must always be most chaste in mind and body alike, and stained by no filth of corruptible flesh. An incontinent monk is an apostate; and he who defiles his flesh with the filth of women is like one violating an oath. Lust is a lake of hell, and despair is always very near to incontinence. A monk who once slips into the pit of the flesh is rarely kindled to true compunction of heart. For the vice of fornication, strengthened by long habit, is not easily conquered unless it is corrected by force through contrary remedies. It is a matter of greater difficulty to rise again after a fall of the flesh to true chastity than to remain in continence once possessed. It is very easy to fall from the state of uprightness into any vice whatever, rather than to amend a sin strengthened by habit. For, as a certain pagan truthfully says, easy is the descent to Avernus; but to recall the step and escape upward to the breezes: this is the work, this is the labor.

Let us consider those who have fallen into this most shameful pit and afterward, by the authority of their superiors, were compelled to penance: how do they live among the brothers? They do not have the signs of true compunction, but pass a restless life in dryness of heart. No devotion of mind is seen in them, but everywhere they follow the comforts of the flesh. O how rarely is one converted to the sweetness of inward love who has once been cast down into the lake of fornication. For unless, before he comes into this misery, he has been grounded in the fear of the Lord, when fallen he returns with difficulty to true compunction.

Therefore live soberly, dearest brothers, and always keep watch in holy prayers, since unless you walk most cautiously in all things, you will by no means be able to escape the snares of demons. Love abstinence; guard humility above all things. For no one can suppress the movements of his flesh who has disdained to subdue gluttony and pride. The insolent demon of fornication is never better conquered than if true humility of heart is preserved in the fullness of all virtues. For just as almighty God, resisting the proud, gives grace to the humble, so the devil, fleeing the humble, casts the proud down into fornication. Therefore he who, being gluttonous, eating and drinking to satiety, desires to conquer the spirit of fornication, is as one carrying oil to a fire. And he who strives to extinguish the movements of lust by abstinence alone is like a man who is seen swimming in the midst of waves with one hand. Let continual prayer to God be joined to abstinence, and in the ship of holy humility one will sail securely.

Let prayer always be in the mouth of the monk, and the memory of the passion and death of the Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore whenever you feel a disordered movement of the flesh, whenever you perceive the invisible enemy to be present to do harm, immediately flee to the Son of God hanging on the cross, and, with your knees bent to the ground, let such a prayer be formed to him: O crucified Jesus, my love, through the pain of your wounds have mercy on me; through the outpouring of your most holy blood help me in this struggle, and through the power of your most innocent death free me from every contagion of mind and body.

Nothing is more salutary than this manner of prayer, in which the memory of Christ’s passion is cherished and petitions are strengthened in the power of the Savior of all. Nothing weakens the snares of the ancient enemy more; nothing more quickly enfeebles the forces of his malignity, than if a devout servant of Christ humbly perseveres in meditation on the most bitter passion of the Lord. Just as some thief flees before the face of a pursuing judge, so the devil quickly vanishes from the sight of a monk who attentively meditates on the passion and death of the Savior. He quickly extinguishes the movement of wicked thought when the bitterness of Christ’s passion is recalled to mind. Just as snow melts when the sun grows warm, so the devil is driven away by meditation on the Lord’s passion.

The greatest protection of chastity is always to invoke divine aid. And unless immediately at the beginning of temptation you run back to the Lord, you will little by little incur harm from delay. For if you admit delay in pernicious thoughts, demons soon cast a perceptible blindness into the mind.

All Things XXI. Fol. LII.

[unclear]. For unless the mind has first been blinded, the will does not yield to the demon. The spirit of fornication first gravely darkens the mind; afterward it fights until it has hurled it, blinded, into sin. But afterward, when it has cast the monk into the mire of unspeakable crime, it sets two means in the way, lest he rise again to repentance. For either it subtly tries to make light of the gravity of the sin, so that he may not fear a great penalty; or it brings back to the fallen man’s memory the severity of judgment, so that he may fall into the pit of despair. By these snares the sinful soul is caught; and the longer it has lain in the depth of misery, the more hardened it is rendered.

Flee idleness, O cloistered men, and avoid gluttony and the excess of the belly with the greatest care, because the monk who stuffs his belly with food and drink provides the demon of fornication with matter for doing harm. Put on true contrition of heart, and restrain the illicit motions of the flesh through tears of prayer. For no one is able rightly to conquer his body who has not first taken up the goad of contrition. But he cannot attain to the grace of holy contrition who [unclear] has perfectly despised himself to deny himself. Whoever, however, has perfectly denied himself for the love of Christ, already overcoming the assault of the flesh, will more easily [unclear] contrition. For he who has been mortified in will desires nothing carnal, nothing base.

But who among us, brothers, is there who would dare say that he has arrived at this grace of mortification? Which of us does not feel himself weak? We run in the arena of spiritual warfare, and in daily combat we fight against vices. We have received no confidence of peace, even if at times we have peace. The more familiar to us is the weakness of the flesh, the harder are the battles of chastity. Here we must be especially watchful, since we carry about a familiar enemy and sustain, as it were, a domestic instigator of evil. Therefore, so long as we live in this mortality, let us always fear the most relentless enemies of chastity. Let us beware of everything that arouses lust; as much as we can, let us flee sloth and idleness. For fullness of bread and idleness are the strongest enemies of true chastity; unless they have been driven far away by abstinence and the labor of salutary exercise, they threaten immediate shipwreck to chastity.

Keep your hearts with divine guard, O most dear [unclear], and always keep watch in spirit against your adversary. Arm yourselves with the breastplate of perfect faith in Jesus Christ, so that in deed and belief you may be true Christians. Always be of one mind in brotherly charity, and united without pretense in the true observance of regular discipline. Love fasting and continence; pray without ceasing. Flee idleness as the pernicious plague of the soul, and continually exercise yourselves in holy works. Love silence, and do not flee monastic solitude, if you desire to obtain true purity of mind and body. Keep continual guard over your eyes, ears, and speech, lest through the windows of the body [evil] enter into the soul. Flee conversations with women, and avoid even the touch of holy women as the burning of fire. No one safely looks willingly upon what brings the sting of death to the desirous man. Always behold with faithful eyes of the mind, through love, our Lord Jesus Christ dying for you; occupy yourselves daily in salutary fashion with his evangelical teaching; give humble thanks for his passion and likewise for his death. If you do these things with continued perseverance in true simplicity of heart until death, we trust that you will be rewarded with the fellowship of the saints.

On Brotherly Charity and the State of Monks. All Things XXII.

Let us hear, my dearest brothers, our Lord Jesus Christ commanding in the holy Gospel: Whatever you wish men to do to you, do the same also to them. This is indeed a brief but solid commendation of brotherly charity, without which no one can ascend to the love of God. For no one can love God who is shown not to love his fellow Christian. Hence the blessed apostle John says: Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that every murderer does not have eternal life abiding in him. Hence, if anyone has said that I love God, and hates his brother, he is a liar. Therefore Paul, the holy lover of Christ, exhorts us, saying: Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ. And Peter, prince of the apostles, admonished us thus: Before all things, he says, having continual mutual charity among yourselves, because charity

Fo. LIII.

On the brotherly charity of monks.

It covers a multitude of sins. How necessary brotherly charity is for salvation, the Lord of all, Jesus Christ, revealed, saying: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the first and greatest commandment. The second is like to this: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets.” For whatever is commanded anywhere in the whole course of the Scriptures is without doubt referred to these two commandments.

By “neighbor” here we understand not one joined by closeness of blood, but every human being by the fellowship of reason, and especially the Christian, whom each person is commanded to love as himself, with whom he is seen to await eternal salvation. But it is especially fitting for you, brothers, to love one another in the true charity of the Savior Jesus Christ, since monastic profession enjoins you to strive with all your strength toward the height of perfection. For just as covetousness is the root of all evils, so charity is the root of all goods. In the first place you ought to love God above all things with a pure heart for his own sake, because he is the highest good, and then to love your neighbor with sincere charity for the Lord’s sake. These two precepts of charity are joined by the authority of Christ, so that one can in no way be fulfilled without the other. For he who truly loves God cannot hate his neighbor. If he hates his neighbor, he does not truly love God. The love of God begets in him love of neighbor, and through love of neighbor the love of God is nourished. If one of the loves is lacking, the other by no means grows strong. For he who certainly does not love his neighbor shows himself empty of the love of God. Therefore we truly love God when we love our neighbor, that is, every Christian human being, more diligently with sincere intention.

For brotherly charity is the bond of peace, which alone nourishes concord in the dwelling and preserves Christian unity among brothers. Charity is the begetter of meekness and the noble mother of Catholic piety. Brotherly charity is fearsome to demons, since it makes victorious all whose inner chamber of the heart it embraces. Charity extinguishes the fire of lust and covers every multitude of sins. Charity renders good people most dear to God and makes them companions of the holy angels. Charity preserves the Church in the unity of the saints, outside which no one obtains eternal salvation. Brotherly charity orders the morals of cloistered men and makes God dwell in the midst of monks. Charity does injury to no one, but supplies help to all through compassion. Charity drives out every vice, because it is the sole nurse of all virtues. Charity preserves the reform of brotherhood in vigor among cloistered men and works a great salvation of souls. Mutual charity confirms obedience and makes brotherly correction fruitful. True charity nourishes concord among brothers and preserves a sweet-smelling chastity of both minds and bodies. Charity makes monks of one mind in the house of God, and laudably concordant in every good work. Mutual charity lightens the rigor of the order, and all things that seem hard and harsh to the carnal it changes through custom into nature, as though they were something very gentle. Charity is the most beautiful beauty of monks, adorned with all virtues. Charity utterly drives hatred and envy out of the monasteries of God’s servants, and by its presence puts to flight far away the remaining crimes of death. The charity of brothers is a fitting dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit and a fortress of serene conscience. Charity is the handmaid of justice and the sole preserver of regular discipline in a monastery. Charity keeps the mind innocent of cruelty and provides for all a peaceful lightness of spirit. Brotherly charity seeks the salvation of all, and does not allow the one who has it to grow sluggish in idleness. Charity does not loathe poverty, but for love of the brothers is ready to endure every poverty. Charity is the water of heavenly sweetness; if anyone drinks it in the fervor of the Holy Spirit, he does not fear the perpetual thirst of hell. Brotherly charity does not seek the enticements of the flesh, but directs pure, holy, and unstained affections toward the neighbor. Charity has the name of chaste beauty, which cannot be shared with things or actions of most impure pleasure. Charity loves purity and cleanness, and admits no impurity. Charity, in the working of love, considers not the flesh of the neighbor but the soul, which it does not doubt was created in the image of God. Brotherly charity raises up a delinquent neighbor with pious admonitions, and keeps all its own actions pure and innocent of every malice. Charity walks in peace and tranquility of mind, and saddens the neighbor neither by word nor deed nor sign. Charity humbles itself as much as it can in all things, and ministers most lovingly to an infirm neighbor as to a son of God. Cha

tas neinme tencire indicat: sed peccantes proximâ mansuetissimis admonitionibus humiliter emendat. Charitas terribilis metuenda est reprobis, sed pia et benigna mansuetis. Charitas aliena incómodo da veluti propria computat, et pro fratri tribulatio quasi patiát ipse ploeat. Charitas omnibus in necessitate positis com paritur: et non inimis pro inimis alienis quam pro suis contristatur. Charitas primi nihil impoperat: sed infirmitates omnium pro dei amore semper equanimiter portat. Charitas in bonis operibus est affida: et quam diu manet in corde nun quam est oeciosa. Charitas nihil eorum ad quod obligatur neglit: sed omnia qua di ligentissime custodit. Charitas fraterna legis est consummatio: quoniam quicquid post dei cultum precipitur: ad dilectiones proximi referitur. Hinc sanctus christi amor dicit. Qui dilegit proximum: leges implevit. Nam non adulterabis, non occides, non furaberis, non falsum testimonium dices, non concupisces rem propriam cui, et si quod est aliud mandatum: in hoc verbo instauratur: dileges proximum tuum sicut teipin. Dilectio proximi malu nó operatur. Plenitudo ergo legis est dilectio. Itaque fratres mei charissimi rogamus vos per dominum et salvatorem nostrum christum qui iudicaturus est vivos et mortuos, quaten? fraternalis charitatem semper custodiatis illeá: sine qua nec Deus veraciter potestis dilegere: nec alió modo datú eius adimíplere. Tazem necessaria est vobis ad salutem fraternalis charitatis custodia: qua corporis ad vitam conservandam ciboy et potus alimenta. Corpus namque sine nutrimento necessario moeritur: et omnes animae virtutes sine fraternali charitate dissipantur. Charitas etenim fraternalis multitudinem monachorum conservat in unitate spus: quin sine vinculo dilectionis mutue, nullus claustralium perseverat sine perturbatione contentus. Monachus qui fratrem suum odio persequitur: Deus charitate procul elongatür. Dicit enim sanctus evangelista iohannes. Qui odit fratrem suum in tenebris est in tenebris ambulat: et nescit quo eat: quia tenebre obce cauerunt oculos eius. Amator autem proximi castus et prudens in lumine spus sa eti securus ambulat: et nec ipse perturba tur ab alio: nec quemquam alium per turbat. Est enim proximi verus amor mitis dulcis ac piemissimus: et in omni con vietú suo mansuetus pacificus et tranquillus. Dirigit tamé vigor discipline à pudicis rectoris mansuetudinem: et clemetia fraterne considerationis pulchre tempat vigorem. Oportet enim ut sic alterum te percuter ex altero: quatenus nec vigor sit rigidus: nec amor dissolut? Amator fraterne charitatis viam iusticie non deserit: qui recte diligit proximum suum: nihil corruptionis interponit. Verus namque p rimus amor: nec aurum concupiscit nec ministrii requirit obsequia: sed contentus omnibus que animi statum subvertere posset: solius animae sectatur incremente. Non enim sincera est charitas propter mores dona corruptis appetere: aut mo te puerus propter munusculo: ut distributiones concurrentem affectu similitudinis amare. Monachorum amicitia in ter bonos eiusdem propositi zelatores debet esse communs: et procul remora ab omni affectione carnis. Si pura, simplex, recta et sine cuiusquá iniuria durabilis: nec babeat in se quicquam suspecte conspirationis. Non est bec norma fraternalis charitatis privata consolationis interdicta coventicula querere: et sine benedictione pri oris furtivis immo prohibitis locutionibus vacare. Amoré vestri proximo nó re cete et potégnitiose impeditis: quotiens cótra norma regularis observáne ad carnis solatia conveniétis. Dilectio monachi debet esse solida et ab omni transgressione discipline regularis remotissima: quoniam nisi charitas multa fuerit a colloquii car halibus signé in se non habet divini amoris. Examinate nunc fratres vestra colloquia: si corde habeatis etiam in vera charitáte radicata. Charitas enim que consolationes spiritui nocentes vel dat proprió, vel recipit: nüquam sincera fuit. Eu rate igitur méritis oculum non ad carnis pulchritudines sed potius ad animae contemplatione dirigere: si recte volitis proximis mutui et laudabiliter amare. Caro enim cum sine respectu animae diligitur: non sincera sed carnalis et impura dilectio generatur. Considera fratrem tuum anima tibi babere colimilez: et semper cogita qui felicitate ambo exspectatis aequalis. Dente sine anima intelligimus: anima non co porre immortales sumus. Quod immor

Charity judges no one rashly, but humbly corrects erring neighbors with the gentlest admonitions. Charity is terrible and fearsome to the reprobate, but tender and kindly to the meek. Charity reckons another’s misfortune as its own, and weeps over a brother’s tribulation as though it suffered it itself. Charity suffers with all who are placed in necessity, and is no less saddened by others’ adversities than by its own. Charity imputes nothing evil first, but for the love of God always bears the infirmities of all with equanimity. Charity is diligent in good works, and as long as it remains in the heart it is never idle. Charity neglects none of the things to which it is bound, but guards all things most diligently. Brotherly charity is the fulfillment of the law, since whatever is commanded after the worship of God is referred to love of neighbor. Hence the holy love of Christ says: He who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the laws. For, You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, you shall not covet another’s property; and if there is any other commandment, it is renewed in this word: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Love of neighbor does not work evil. Therefore the fullness of the law is love.

And so, my dearest brothers, we beseech you through our Lord and Savior Christ, who is to judge the living and the dead, that you always keep brotherly charity unharmed, without which you can neither truly love God nor in any other way fulfill his commandment. The keeping of brotherly charity is as necessary for your salvation as the nourishment of food and drink is for preserving the body’s life. For the body dies without necessary nourishment, and all the virtues of the soul are scattered without brotherly charity. For brotherly charity preserves a multitude of monks in unity of spirit; for without the bond of mutual love, no cloistered man perseveres content without disturbance. The monk who persecutes his brother with hatred is far removed from God’s charity. For the holy evangelist John says: He who hates his brother is in darkness and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because darkness has blinded his eyes. But the chaste and prudent lover of his neighbor walks safely in the light of the Holy Spirit, and he is not disturbed by another, nor does he disturb anyone else. For true love of neighbor is gentle, sweet, and most tender, and in all its intercourse meek, peaceable, and tranquil.

Yet the vigor of discipline directs the meekness of a chaste ruler, and the clemency of brotherly consideration beautifully tempers vigor. For one must be struck from the other in such a way that vigor is not rigid, nor love slack. The lover of brotherly charity does not abandon the way of justice; he who rightly loves his neighbor introduces no corruption. For true first love neither covets gold nor requires the services of ministry, but, content with all things that could overthrow the condition of the mind, pursues only the increase of the soul. For charity is not sincere when it seeks gifts because of corrupt morals, or [unclear] a boy because of a little gift, so as to love with an affection of likeness one who runs together for distributions. The friendship of monks among good men who are zealous for the same purpose ought to be common, and far removed from every affection of the flesh. Let it be pure, simple, upright, and durable without injury to anyone, and let it have in itself nothing of suspicious conspiracy.

This is not the rule of brotherly charity: to seek forbidden private gatherings for consolation, and without the prior’s blessing to be occupied with furtive, indeed prohibited, conversations. You do not rightly and [unclear] hinder love of your neighbor whenever you come together for the comforts of the flesh against the rule of regular observance. A monk’s love ought to be solid and very far removed from every transgression of regular discipline, since unless charity has been much [unclear] by the signs of carnal conversation, it does not have within itself the mark of divine love. Now examine your conversations, brothers, to see whether you have them rooted in your heart even in true charity. For charity that either gives or receives consolations harmful to the spirit was never sincere. Therefore take care to direct the eye of the mind not toward the beauties of the flesh, but rather toward contemplation of the soul, if you wish rightly and laudably to love your neighbors mutually. For when the flesh is loved without regard for the soul, not sincere but carnal and impure love is generated. Consider that your brother has a soul like yours, and always think that you both equally await happiness. [unclear] without the soul we understand; in soul, not in body, we are immortal.
