Epistola. IOannes Tritemius abbas monasterij Spanhemẽsis licet indi gnus: reuerẽdo patri dño Ioãni de colenhausen abbati Selgẽ- stattensi quondã uero Spanhemensi antecessori meo charissi mo cum orationibus animũ complacendi promptũ atque pa ratum. Miseram nuper ad te preceptor uenerande libri meũ exhortationũ ad monachos primum quinque &; uiginti continentẽ Omeli as: quem postea quam tuo examine comprobatum intellexi: etiam hunc se- cundum quem nunc mitto nomini tuo duxi cõfidenter inscribendũ. In illo ad institutionem fratrum omelias.xxv.quas coram eis habueram compor- taui: in isto sermones numero secundum ordinem quo dicti sunt in eorundem presentia ordinaui. Examen paternitatis tue subire non uereor: quoniam te preceptorem semper mansuetum habui: &; ueritatis syncerum amatorem dudum expertus sum. Ingenio quippe uiges &; miti &; profun- do: qui facile inter uerum &; falsum potes discernere: &; ubi requirit neces- sitas omnia sufficienter emendare. Vnde secundum innatam tibi mansue- tudinem pacienter feras ingenij mei ruditatem precor: qui &; in scientia scri pturarum sum paruulus: &; in ordine prelatorum nouicius. Dabit mihi si- cuti confido in scripturis exercitatio usum:&amp;; continuata sollicitu- do profectum.Occũpatio rei familiaris et amp; inopia loci sepius me a salutari stu dio retrahunt: &amp; animum contra uoluntatis propositum aliorsum transpo nunt.Diebus tantùmmodo festis atque dominicis mihi ad scribendum cõ- ceditur ocium:in quibus ob dei reuerentiã nullas soleo admittere causas ru- sticorum.Interdum etiam post decantatas ex consuetudine laudes matuti- nas quod reliquum est noctis studio literarum soleo impendere: &amp; aliquid pro fratrum meorum institutiõe pro ut possum lucubrare.Cupio enim tua in omnibus sequi uestigia: &amp; laudabilem docẽdo esse sollicitus.Sermones istos examini tuo subiijcio:quos ut magisterij tui lima corrigat humili supplicatione expostu- lo.Paucos e pluribus comportaui in ordinem: quoniam nec omnes cõmen daui literis:nec uidebatur mihi nimia libri extensio uel necessaria uel utilis. Festis enim diebus quando feriamur a tumultu negociorum mundialium: lectioni uacamus iuxta regulam scripturarum.Et nefrustra locum uidear occupare pastoris:quod noctibus lucubraui soleo post nonas loco regularis studij dicere:&amp;; coram fratribus in conuentu ex cartula recitare.Exterior enim quod hec sollicitudo mea non solum fratribus ad edificationem profi- cit:sed etiam mihi ad dictandi pericium conducit.Vale preceptor uene- rande:&amp;; ora pro nobis. Ex Spanheim duodecimo die mensis Septembris. Anno christianorum.Millesimo quadringentesimo octuagesimo sexto.

Letter.

John Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of Sponheim, though unworthy, to the reverend father Lord Johannes de Colenhausen, abbot of Seligenstadt and formerly of Sponheim, my most dear predecessor: with prayers, a spirit ready and prepared to give satisfaction.

Recently, venerable teacher, I had sent to you my first book of exhortations to monks, containing twenty-five homilies. After I understood that it had been approved by your examination, I judged that this second book also, which I now send, should confidently be inscribed to your name. In the former I collected, for the instruction of the brothers, twenty-five homilies which I had delivered before them; in this one I have arranged the sermons in number according to the order in which they were spoken in their presence. I do not fear to undergo the examination of your paternity, since I have always had you as a gentle teacher, and long ago found you to be a sincere lover of truth. For you are vigorous in intellect, both gentle and profound, able easily to distinguish between true and false, and, where necessity requires, to amend everything sufficiently. Therefore I pray that, according to the gentleness innate in you, you may patiently bear the rudeness of my talent, for I am both a little child in knowledge of the Scriptures and a novice in the order of prelates. Exercise in the Scriptures will give me practice, as I trust, and continued solicitude will give progress.

The occupation of household business and the poverty of the place very often draw me back from salutary study, and carry my mind elsewhere against the purpose of my will. Only on feast days and Sundays is leisure granted me for writing; on these, out of reverence for God, I am accustomed to admit no cases of the country people. Sometimes also, after the customary chanting of matins, I am accustomed to spend what remains of the night on the study of letters, and, as far as I can, to work by lamplight on something for the instruction of my brothers. For I desire in all things to follow your footsteps, and by teaching to be solicitous for what is praiseworthy. I submit these sermons to your examination, and with humble supplication I beg that the file of your mastery may correct them. I have collected a few out of many into order, since I neither committed them all to writing, nor did an excessive extension of the book seem to me either necessary or useful. For on feast days, when we have respite from the tumult of worldly business, we devote ourselves to reading according to the rule of the Scriptures. And lest I should seem to occupy the place of shepherd in vain, what I have worked out by night I am accustomed after none, in place of the regular study, to say and to recite from a small sheet before the brothers in chapter. For I consider that this solicitude of mine not only profits the brothers for edification, but also conduces to my skill in composition. Farewell, venerable teacher, and pray for us. From Sponheim, on the twelfth day of the month of September, in the year of the Christians one thousand four hundred eighty-six.

116
Germo.I. Fo.LIX. In nomīe domini no liri isu christi incipit liber exhortationū ad monachos secundus. Ioannis Trite mij abbatis Spanhemensis postea pea- politani. Quam caute fit monachis viue̓dum: Sermoprimus. MUta quidē sūt fratres di lectissimi vobis ad cōside rationē in hac vita neces- saria: si ad eterne salutis gloriam cupitis ꝑuenire. Scitis em̄ scriptura testāte qm̄ aduersarius vester diabolus sicut leo ru giens circuit querēs quē deuoret: cui magna vigilantia in fide dn̄i nostri iesu christi ꝑ charitatis opera nouimus resistendū. Nemo īgitur de suis viribꝰ p̄sumat: ne in vanitate ꝯfidat: qm̄ nisi vos intimore dn̄i humiliter contineritis: cito in laqueū diaboli cadetis. Quanto magnꝰ es (scriptura precipit) humilia te in omībꝰ qm̄ deus resistit supbis: et graciā cōcedit humile̓: et verū huius mundi cōtemptorem. Monachū oportet in obseruantia regularis disciplīe semꝑ esse sollicitū: et ī timore dn̄i cōtinue studiosū. Monachū opor tet castū et pudicū esse mente simul et corpore: vt deo seruiat quēadmodū promissit in om̄i puritate. Monachus nō debet viuere secundū voluntatē propriā: sed secudū regulā et pastoris sui conformē norme institutionis cenobitice directionē. Monachus negociosum et sanctū debet amare silentium: et mentē sua occupare vtiliter in lectione scripturarū. Monachus om̄i tēpoꝛe vsqƺ ad mortē debet esse sollicitus quatens in obseruantiam mandatorū dei et regule sit ꝑfectus. Ut aūt sciatis q̄ vobis in sancta religione cōuersantibꝰ ad ꝑfectionem sint necessaria: describā vobis quendā virtutū tramite̓: ꝑ quem ad regnū celoꝝ viā oporret dirigere. Uirtutes aūt oīes mutuo coherent necessitudinis glutino: vt qui vnā ꝑfecte possidet omnes habere videat̉: et qui vel vna caret nullā penitus dicatur possidere. ¶ Omniū virtutū pri- ma ad salutē necessaria est sanctissima fides catholica: ab om̄i errorū et heresū pollutio segregata: et in doctrina dn̄i nostrieisu christi originaliter radicata. Nā scriptura testante sine fide impossibile est pla cere deo: et qui nō credit in vnigenitū filiū dei: iam iudicatus est et ira dei manet super euꝫ. Omniū ergo virtutū origo fides est: de qua om̄ia salutis studia oriuntur. Fides in deū vera et recta timorē domini generat: qm̄ si deū credimus iustuꝫ: merito confitebimur esse time̓duꝫ. Fides recta spem parit et confidentiā: quia dū miseri cordē deū credimus: mox de bonitate illius salutē nos posse consequi speramus. Fides charitatē generat: quia si deū essefummmū bonū credimus: ipsuꝫ sine dubio amamus. Quis em̄ non amaret quod sūme bonū non dubitar? Fides est substantia rerū sperandarū argumentuꝫ non ap- paretiuius. Fides deo coniungit animam: et facit eam medio charitatis eterni regis amicam. Dicit enim sanctissimus presul Augustinus. Nulle maiores diuitie: nulli thesauri: nulli honores: nulla huiꝰ mūdi maior est substātia: quā est fides catholica: que peccatores homīes saluat: ceocos illumiat: infirmos curat: cathecuminos baptizat: fideles iustificat: penitentes reparati: iustos augmentat: martyres coromnat: virgines: viduas et coniugales castopudore conferuat: clericos ordinat: sacerdotes cōsecrat: credētes cū sanctis angeslis in eterna hereditate celoruꝫ collocat. Ubi aūt sana fides nō est nō potestesse iustitia: qƺ iustus exfide viuit: et qui carer iustitie merito portionē nullā habebitur cumchristo. Fides est humane salutis initiuꝫsine qua nemo ad numerū filiorū dei postest pertingere: nec partē aliquā in regno dei possidere. Fides fundamentū virtutmum est omniū: q̇cqͥd extra fidem agiturprocul dubio ad ie hennam edificatur. Fides christiana lampas est pulcherrima illuminans animā: et per obseruantiam mādatorum introducens eam ad felicitatezeternā. Fides in primis mentem reducitad dei scientiā: postea dat precepta viuen- di ad obedientiā: et cum homo dei mandata custodierit spes cōsequende salutis etigitur: deinde charitas in cordibus firmaetur. Fides cognitioneꝫ dat anime: cognitione: quia dumi fides recta heresum falsitate corrumpitur: ad salutis portum actione nulla peruenitur. Sit ergo infide k iij

Sermon I. Folio LIX.

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begins the second book of exhortations to monks, by Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, afterwards of [unclear]. How cautiously monks must live: Sermon One.

Many indeed, most beloved brothers, are the things necessary for you to consider in this life, if you desire to arrive at the glory of eternal salvation. For you know, Scripture bearing witness, that your adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour; and we know that he must be resisted with great vigilance in the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ through works of charity. Therefore let no one presume on his own powers, lest he trust in vanity; for unless you humbly keep yourselves in the fear of the Lord, you will quickly fall into the snare of the devil. “The greater you are,” Scripture commands, “humble yourself in all things,” for God resists the proud and grants grace to the humble, and to the true despiser of this world.

A monk must always be solicitous in the observance of regular discipline, and continually zealous in the fear of the Lord. A monk must be chaste and modest in mind and body alike, so that he may serve God just as he promised, in all purity. A monk ought not to live according to his own will, but according to the Rule and according to the direction of his pastor, conformed to the norm of cenobitic institution. A monk ought to love busy and holy silence, and usefully occupy his mind in the reading of the Scriptures. A monk must at all times, even unto death, be solicitous that he be made perfect in the observance of the commandments of God and of the Rule.

But so that you may know what things are necessary for you, living in holy religion, for perfection, I shall describe for you a certain path of virtues, by which one must direct the way to the kingdom of heaven. All the virtues, however, cohere with one another by the bond of kinship, so that he who possesses one perfectly seems to have them all, and he who lacks even one is said to possess none at all.

The first of all virtues necessary for salvation is the most holy Catholic faith, separated from every pollution of errors and heresies, and originally rooted in the doctrine of our Lord Jesus Christ. For, as Scripture bears witness, without faith it is impossible to please God; and he who does not believe in the only-begotten Son of God is already judged, and the wrath of God remains upon him. Therefore faith is the origin of all virtues, from which all pursuits of salvation arise.

True and right faith in God begets fear of the Lord, for if we believe God to be just, we shall rightly confess that he is to be feared. Right faith brings forth hope and confidence, because when we believe God to be merciful, soon we hope that by his goodness we can attain salvation. Faith begets charity, because if we believe God to be the highest good, without doubt we love him. For who would not love what he does not doubt to be the supreme good? Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not appearing. Faith joins the soul to God, and through the mediation of charity makes it the friend of the eternal King.

For the most holy prelate Augustine says: There are no greater riches, no treasures, no honors, no substance of this world greater than the Catholic faith, which saves sinful men, enlightens the blind, cures the sick, baptizes catechumens, justifies the faithful, restores penitents, increases the just, crowns martyrs, preserves virgins, widows, and married persons in chaste modesty, ordains clerics, consecrates priests, and places believers with the holy angels in the eternal inheritance of the heavens.

But where sound faith is not, there justice cannot be, because the just man lives by faith; and he who lacks the merit of justice will have no portion with Christ. Faith is the beginning of human salvation, without which no one can reach the number of the children of God, nor possess any share in the kingdom of God. Faith is the foundation of all virtues; whatever is done outside faith is without doubt built for Gehenna. Christian faith is a most beautiful lamp illuminating the soul, and through the observance of the commandments leading it into eternal happiness.

Faith first brings the mind back to the knowledge of God; afterward it gives the precepts of living unto obedience; and when a man has kept the commandments of God, hope of attaining salvation follows; then charity is made firm in hearts. Faith gives knowledge to the soul, knowledge [unclear]; because when right faith is corrupted by the falsehood of heresies, by no action is one brought to the harbor of salvation. Therefore let it be in faith

Fidē habere sine operibꝰ charitatis est imitari demones: qui cū ab om̄i charitate procul sint alieni: deū tamen esse iustū et credunt et cōtremiscūt. Hinc de credulis qui opera non exhibent charitatis: dn̄s loquitur per prophetā Esaiam et postea per semet ipsum in sancto euangelio dicens. Populus hie labijs me honorat: cor aūt eoruz longe est a me. Qui christū ore laudat si ne oꝑe: quasi vir qui dubitat in fide. Naz si veraciter crederet: deū vtiqƺ timeret. Fides sine operibus quasi corpus sine spiritu mortuū: quod a viuorū sublatum consensus spectibus absconditur in sepulchruz. Si bene credis et male viuis: proprio te gladio perimis: quia scientibonū et non facienti peccatuʒ est illi. Cauete fratres meine que errorē admittatis in fide: et curate summopere vt nulla sit nequicia in opꝑati one. Sequamini fideʒ quam nobis sancta commendate ecclesia: agite vitā sicut euangeliū precipit et norma cenobitica. ¶ Dein de spem habeatis in dei manifestationē om̄i tempore certissimā: sed nūcqƺ a timore domini alienā. Spes est futurorum bonoꝝ certa per graciam miserentis dei expectatio: et merendi per charitatis exercitiū institie coronaz sollicitudo. Spes est certae expectatio future beatitudinis: quam gracia dei operatur in nobis comitante rectitudine bone volūtatis. Spes est qua qͥs venire ad vitā eterne felicitatꝭ sperat quam desiderat: et mediante gracia dei suā etiā voluntatē in occursum componit et aptat Spes est bonorū: arduorū: futurorum et possibiliū: quibꝰ nemo sperat contrariuʒ. Neqƺ em̄ malū quis sperat necqƺ leuerneqƺ quod presens est siue p̄teritū: negignoramus sem nō esse impossibiliū. Spes moderatrix laborū est omnium: et vnica cōsolatrix in medio tribulationum. Spes em̄ furutorū bonorū laborantibꝰ pro christo in hac vita parit requiem: sicut in agone certantibꝰ mitigat dolorē vulnerū corone expectatio per continuā victoriā. Spes ī tormentis roborauit martyres: et fecit eos in virtute christi omnijs persecutoribꝰ fortiores. Spes eterne beatitudinis cōseruat ecclesiā: et dedit sanctis confessoriibus atqƺ virginibꝰ verā in christo charita teʒ. Spes deiectū merore fortiter erigit animū: et quanto se per amoreʒ altius su stulerit: tanto minus contraria huius mū disentit. Beatus vir qui confidit indn̄oquia spes non cōfundit sicut sanctus promisit apostolus: qua saluti facti sumus. ¶ Ut aūt spes non crumpat in presumptione timor domini ad saluteʒ nobis est necessarius: vt quē piū et misericordē creditmus: iustū etiā et rectuʒ non dubitemus. Dicit em̄ beatiissimus papa Gregorius. Nobis nihil securius quam sub spectimere ne incauta mens vel desperando se in profundū viciorū deiꝭciat: vel extollendo dedonis presumptuosa ruat. Nas quāto ante oculos districti iudicis sub spe humili us trepidat: tāto in illo robustius stat. Timor dei mentē corrigit: et puram ab omnimalicia custodit. Timor domininitiū est sapientie: qm̄ in via dei a timore incipitur vtpaulatin ad charitatis fortitudinē peruenciatur. Timor domini componit monachū: et facit eum in obseruantia regularis discipline studiosum. Timor domini custodit regulā: et seruat verammentis corporis puritatē. Timor dn̄i nihil eoruʒ que precepta sunt negligit: sed om̄ia solliciti sunt muri. Urbs sine muroꝝ custodia cito ab inimicis capitur: et monachꝰ qui non habet dei timoreʒ facile a demonibꝰ superatur. Solus enim dei timor est qui mentes corrigit: fugat crimina: innocentes seruat: et facit monachū in sanctitatis proposito perseueranteʒ. ¶ Ex timore paulatim oritur charitas: que cuʒ iuuan te deo veraciter in mente radicata fuerit: seruilem timorem superans iam foras miruit. Radix omniuʒ bonorum est charitas: quoniam quicquid in hac vita boni agitur: vt deo placeat per solam charitatem temperatur. Charitas omnium virtutū est maxima: sine qua nihil sunt cūcta mortallium facta. Dicit enim sanctissimus christi apostolus. That monks must live cautiously.

[unclear], uprightness and truth; in action, justice and sincerity; and no iniquity will have dominion. For faith without works is dead, and earns nothing toward the salvation of eternal happiness. To have faith without works of charity is to imitate the demons, who, though they are wholly estranged from all charity, nevertheless both believe that God is just and tremble. Hence concerning believers who do not show works of charity, the Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah, and afterward through himself in the holy Gospel, saying: This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. Whoever praises Christ with his mouth, without work, is like a man who doubts in faith. For if he truly believed, he would certainly fear God. Faith without works is like a body dead without the spirit, which, removed from the sight of the living, is hidden in the tomb. If you believe well and live badly, you destroy yourself by your own sword, because for one who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin. Beware, my brothers, lest you admit any error in faith, and take the utmost care that there be no wickedness in action. Follow the faith which holy Church commends to us; live the life prescribed by the Gospel and by the cenobitic rule.

Then have hope in the manifestation of God at all times most certain, but never divorced from fear of the Lord. Hope is the certain expectation, through the grace of the merciful God, of future goods, and solicitude for deserving the crown of justice through the exercise of charity. Hope is the certain expectation of future blessedness, which the grace of God works in us, accompanied by the uprightness of a good will. Hope is that by which a person hopes to come to the life of eternal happiness which he desires, and, through the mediation of God’s grace, also disposes and prepares his own will to meet it.

Hope concerns good things, difficult things, future things, and possible things; in these no one hopes for the contrary. For no one hopes for evil, nor for something trivial, nor for what is present or past; nor are we ignorant that hope is not of impossible things. Hope is the moderator of all labors, and the sole consoler amid tribulations. For hope of future goods gives rest to those laboring for Christ in this life, just as expectation of the crown, through continual victory, softens the pain of wounds for those contending in the contest. Hope strengthened the martyrs in torments, and made them, in the power of Christ, stronger than all persecutors. Hope of eternal blessedness preserves the Church, and gave the holy confessors and virgins true charity in Christ. Hope strongly raises up the soul cast down by grief; and the higher it has lifted itself through love, the less it feels the contrary things of this world. Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, because hope does not confound, as the holy Apostle promised, by which we have been made saved.

But so that hope may not break out into presumption, fear of the Lord is necessary for our salvation, so that we may not doubt that he whom we believe merciful and compassionate is also just and upright. For the most blessed Pope Gregory says: Nothing is safer for us than to tremble humbly under hope, lest the incautious mind either cast itself into the depth of vices by despairing, or fall presumptuously by being exalted. For the more humbly it trembles before the eyes of the strict judge under hope, the more robustly it stands in him. Fear of God corrects the mind and keeps it pure from all malice. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, because on the way of God one begins from fear, so that little by little one may come to the strength of charity. Fear of the Lord orders the monk, and makes him zealous in the observance of regular discipline. Fear of the Lord guards the rule and preserves true purity of mind and body. Fear of the Lord neglects none of the things that are commanded, but is solicitous in all things. Walls are [unclear]. A city without the protection of walls is quickly taken by enemies, and the monk who does not have the fear of God is easily overcome by demons. For the fear of God alone is what corrects minds, drives away crimes, preserves the innocent, and makes the monk persevering in the purpose of holiness.

From fear there gradually arises charity; when, with God’s help, it has truly been rooted in the mind, overcoming servile fear, it now casts it out. The root of all goods is charity, since whatever good is done in this life is ordered by charity alone, so that it may please God. Charity is the greatest of all virtues; without it all deeds of mortals are nothing. For the most holy Apostle of Christ says: If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. Sermon I. Folio LX.

“... so that I might move mountains, but if I have not charity, I am nothing. And if I should distribute all my goods as food for the poor, and if I should hand over my body so that I burn, but have not charity, it profits me nothing.” Consider carefully, now, my brothers, your own selves, and ask your consciences whether you have the true charity of God, without which all other things avail nothing for salvation. For you have heard the clear judgment of the Apostle, by which he says that charity is necessary for salvation. Let no one put confidence in the wisdom of this world; let no one vainly exalt himself over the natural gifts he has received; let no one presume upon bodily continence, since, if charity is lacking, the observance of the other things contributes nothing to salvation. But lest anyone presume a false opinion of himself, the holy Apostle set forth certain signs and operations of charity, saying: “Charity is patient, is kind. Charity does not envy, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, and does not seek what is its own; it is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices together with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never fails.” Have the charity of God in you, my brothers; unless you keep it, you labor in vain by striving.

Humility is very necessary for you, and often so: it is not only a great virtue, but also the nurse of the other virtues and the foremost guardian of them all. For Pope Gregory the Great says: “He who gathers virtues without humility carries dust into the wind.” For the greatest virtue of monks is humility, since they are bound to be so much humbler than others living their life in the world, as by profession they are bound to strive and tend toward greater perfection. Humility is the stable foundation of the virtues; whatever is built upon it will be overturned by no whirlwind of tempest. Through pride the devil fell from heaven; through humility man ascends. In vain are we called monks if we have not been humble, for just as fire is extinguished if it lacks the fuel of wood, so a monk without humility is judged very unworthy of his name. By Christian humility the devil is conquered, and, as if struck by a nail, is overcome as he flees. No more splendid jewel is seen in monastic adornment than humility; if a monk has despised it, he has denied both his profession and the humble Christ.

Prudence follows upon humility; it always directs all things to the standard of reason and does nothing except what is right, honorable, and praiseworthy. Prudence knows what it ought virtuously to seek, and knows well what, according to the right judgment of reason, it ought to avoid. True and perfect prudence is that by which we seek that highest, unchangeable good, and order all things to their due and right end. Prudence preserves the observance of regular discipline stable in vigor, and brings wandering monks back to the complete restoration of their lost purpose. Prudence directs the monk in the right way of salvation, and does not allow him to decline to either side. Prudence preserves peace and concord among brothers, and orders right action in each matter. Prudence, O my brothers, is very necessary for you; by it you will know in every action what things are to be undertaken by you, and what in turn are to be fled. True prudence, not of the flesh but of the spirit, teaches you to despise the world, and to desire only those things that are future and eternal. Prudence teaches a man to stand firm in himself, and neither in prosperity nor in adversity to decline from the purpose of holiness. Prudence teaches how to order present things beautifully; it brings past things back to memory for instruction; and it foresees future things, lest anything happen unexpectedly. Prudence corrects offenders usefully and fruitfully, and composes all that it either does, says, or thinks, according to the judgment of reason, toward its due end. Therefore be prudent as serpents and simple as doves, because prudence without goodness is malice, and simplicity without rational prudence is called foolishness. For the most holy Paul, Apostle of Christ, says: “The prudence of the flesh is death.” Be prudent, lest you be circumvented by the deceit of others, but simple, lest you circumvent anyone. For this is the duty of the prudent man: neither to be capable of being deceived, nor to wish to deceive anyone. [unclear] By foreseeing, indeed, one is called prudent.

Justice accompanies prudence; it is the most splendid of all the virtues. For without justice all the remaining virtues are nothing. Justice is the preserver of religion, the mother of grace, the nurse of observance, the nourisher of truth, the begetter of peace, and the origin of piety.

Quod caute sit monachis viuendum. Iustitia est virtus que distribuit et conseruat vnicuiqꝫ qd̓ suū est: que propriā vtilitatē negligitur vt cōmunē seruet vtilitatē et equitateꝫ: sine qua nulla res publica diuin pace pōt subsistere. Dicit em̄ in ecclesiastico vir sapiens. Regnū a gente ingente transfertur ꝓpter iniustitias: et iniurias et ꝯtumelias ac diuersos dolos. Ordo iustitie primū respicit deū: deinde patriā: ex inde parentes: postea oēs in cōmuni secūdū distinctiones graduū: et merita dignitationū. Deo ī pͥmis iustitia dictāte debemꝰ religionē: fidē: cultuz: deuotionē et gratiarū actiōes: et verā ex toto corde subobedientia dilectione. Nobis deinde puritas tē mentis et corporis cōtinentiā cũ studio perfectionis: quo ad illū nobis ꝑ obedien arū redire liceat a quo creati sumus. Terzio loco patric debemus cōmodū: honorē et defensionē: eiusqꝫ quantū possumus cū ipsa iustitia procurare vtilitateꝫ. Quarto parentibꝰ tenemur honore et obedientiaꝫ: et in eorū necessitate curā et omnimodā sutationē. Quinto prelatis doctrinā et pabuluꝫ subditis: correctionēqꝫ delinquētibꝰ. Septimo aut̄ loco tenemur maioriꝝ et principibꝰ horent: et sine crimine pro dei amore subiectione. Octauo debemus venerabilibꝰ personis reuerentiam: et sacerdotibꝰ honorem. Cōsequenter equalibus tenemur amiciciaꝫ: inferioribus dignatione: bn̄factoribus visitudinem: amicis cōmunitate: inimicis pacientiam: pauperibus misericordiam: miseris consolationem: omnibus charitatem. Hec aut̄ est vera iustitia: qua deū ex toto corde propter seipsum diligimus: et proximum nostrum in deo sit nosmetipsos: inimicos aut̄ propter deū distribuētes vnicuiqꝫ quod sibi iure debetur omniū vtilitatipro uidentes. ¶ Sed cũ nimia iustitia facile incurrat peccatum: temperantia in omībus vobis necessaria est: que sola perfectorios facit. Est aut̄ temperātia virtus rati one discernens et vincēs animi motus et omnē libidinē: ne impetus in agēdo excelat legis equitatē. Temperantia virtus optima voluptatibꝰ imꝑat: et oīa in ordine debito cōseruat. Om̄ibꝰ actionibꝰ verbis quoqꝫ et cogitationibꝰ vestris adhibete tēperātiā: et necessariā virtutibꝰ discretione. Quicqd boni cũ discretione feceritis vir tutis merito vocabulū accipit: qd̓ autem fit sine discrezione viciū est dicenduz. Discretio moderatrix virtutū est onnium: et maximum prudentie ac iustitiiornamentum. Discretio non solū prelatis sed etiam subditis est necessaria: quoniam ipsa virtuentibus dat ordinem: affectionibus confert modestiam: et cunctis hominū consisti lijs tribuit decorem pulcherrimū et honestatem. Hinc quidam sapiens dixit. Estmodus in rebus sunt certideniqꝫ fines: quos vltra citraqꝫ nequit consistere rectū ¶ Ad hoc animi fortitudo vobis necessarria est fratres: per quam non solū ꝯstantes efficiamini in aduersis: sed etiam prompti et alacres in arduis. Quis em̄ sine animifortitudine maxime: hunc mundū cũ suis voluptatibꝰ possēt cōtemnere: et in sanctareligione monastica sub obedientie legibꝰ vsqꝫ ad mortē perseuerare. Fortitudo animivires de charitate christi suscipit: et cōstans nō minus in aduersis qͣꝫ in prosperis virtutis desiderio cōsistit. Fortitudovia rectitudinis absqꝫ timore graditur: ethostibꝰ quadāsancta superbia terribilissans autem videtur. Fortitudo animerisformidāda videt̉. Fortitudo paruuloꝝ cōtemnit iniurias: et omnes facilesuperat carnis voluptates. Fortitudoinpacien latet in aduersitate ostendit̉: et manifeste ꝑ paciemīa declarat̉. Animo fortisest nō qui vindicat iniurias sibi illatas sedqui pacienter tolerat: et si acceperit in potestatem aduersariū: potuisse vindictamputat. Monachorū fortitudo est mundū contēnere: carnē vincere: omnes mudi honores et voluptates spermere: et insoluꝫdeū spē omnē et cōfidentiā collocare. Mēsurafortitudinis est necessimū esse necaudaceā: qm̄ recta incerdēs via neqꝫ addextera declinat neqꝫ adsiniram. Monachꝰ illefortis est iudicādꝰ: qi tēperas est in omībus: moderatusqꝫ et iustus. Hinc dicit sactissimiꝰ papa gregorius. Iutorū fortitudoest carnē vincere: ꝓprijs voluptatibuscōtraire: delectationē vite presentis extinguitum roborant: terrena despiciunt: celestiaappetunt: occidi possunt: flecti nō possuntnecsustinere falsa. Per infirmitatemmetuunt: nec lesi vnqͣꝫ a veritate ꝯticescunt.

That monks must live cautiously.

Justice is the virtue which distributes and preserves for each person what is his own; by it private advantage is neglected so that it may preserve the common advantage and equity, without which no commonwealth can subsist in divine peace. For the wise man says in Ecclesiasticus: “A kingdom is transferred from one nation to another because of injustices, and injuries, and insults, and various deceits.” The order of justice looks first to God, then to the fatherland, thereafter to parents, afterwards to all in common according to the distinctions of ranks and the merits of dignities. To God, in the first place, at the dictation of justice, we owe religion, faith, worship, devotion, and thanksgivings, and true love from the whole heart with obedient submission. Then to ourselves, purity of mind and body, continence with zeal for perfection, so that through obedience it may be permitted us to return to him by whom we were created. In the third place, to the fatherland we owe advantage, honor, and defense, and, insofar as we can, to procure its benefit together with justice itself. Fourth, we are bound to our parents by honor and obedience, and in their necessity by care and support of every kind. Fifth, to prelates [unclear], to subjects teaching and nourishment, and correction to those who offend. In the seventh place, however, we are bound to give honor to elders and princes, and, without fault, subjection for the love of God. Eighth, we owe reverence to venerable persons, and honor to priests. Consequently we are bound to equals by friendship, to inferiors by condescension, to benefactors by reciprocation, to friends by fellowship, to enemies by patience, to the poor by mercy, to the wretched by consolation, to all by charity. This, however, is true justice: by it we love God from the whole heart for his own sake, and our neighbor in God as ourselves, but enemies for God’s sake, distributing to each person what is owed to him by right and providing for the advantage of all.

But since excessive justice easily incurs sin, temperance is necessary for you in all things; it alone makes men more perfect. Temperance is the virtue which by reason discerns and conquers the motions of the soul and every lust, lest impulse in acting exceed the equity of the law. Temperance is a most excellent virtue: it governs pleasures and preserves all things in due order. Apply temperance to all your actions, words, and also thoughts, and the discretion necessary to the virtues. Whatever good you do with discretion receives the name by the merit of virtue; but what is done without discretion must be called vice. Discretion is the moderator of all virtues, and the greatest ornament of prudence and justice. Discretion is necessary not only for prelates but also for subjects, since it gives order to those exercising virtue, grants modesty to affections, and bestows on all human counsels most beautiful grace and honorableness. Hence a certain wise man said: “There is a measure in things; there are, finally, fixed limits, beyond and short of which the right cannot stand.”

For this, brothers, strength of soul is necessary for you, through which you may become not only steadfast in adversities but also ready and cheerful in difficult things. For who, especially without strength of soul, could despise this world with its pleasures, and persevere in holy monastic religion under the laws of obedience even unto death? Strength of soul takes its powers from the charity of Christ, and stands constant, no less in adversities than in prosperity, in desire for virtue. Strength walks the way of uprightness without fear, and to enemies it appears terrifying with a certain holy pride. But strength of soul seems fearful of [unclear]. Strength despises the injuries of the small and easily overcomes all the pleasures of the flesh. Strength lies hidden in patience, is shown in adversity, and is openly declared through patience. Strong of soul is not the man who avenges injuries brought upon him, but the man who patiently tolerates them; and if he has received his adversary into his power, he thinks that he has been able to take vengeance. The strength of monks is to despise the world, to conquer the flesh, to spurn all the honors and pleasures of the world, and to place all hope and confidence in God alone. The measure of strength is to be necessary, neither rash nor [unclear], because, walking on the right way, it declines neither to the right nor to the left. That monk must be judged strong who is temperate in all things, and moderate and just. Hence the most holy pope Gregory says: “The strength of the just is to conquer the flesh, to oppose their own pleasures, to extinguish the delight of the present life [unclear] strengthen; they despise earthly things, seek heavenly things; they can be killed, they cannot be bent, nor can they endure falsehoods. Through weakness they fear [unclear], nor, when harmed, do they ever keep silent from the truth.”

120
Donachus ergo qui vera virtute fortis est: nec temere auder: nec incōsulte timet. Regia em̄ via est fortitudo simul atqꝫ cōstantia: a qua temerarius et ꝑtinax declinar ad dexterā: timidꝰ vero pusillanimis pauidusqꝫ ad sinistrā. Donachus anīo ꝯstans et fortis nūqͣꝫ recedit a sanctitatis ꝓposito: sed nec aduersis deprimit̉: nec ꝓsperis eleuat̉. Unde et sanctissimus presul ambrosius. Stultꝰ īquit vt luna mutat̉ Sapiens aūt metu nō frangit̉: potestate nō mutatur: nō extollit̉ prosperis: nō mercuritur tristibꝰ. Ubi em̄ sapientia et virtꝰ: ibi cōstantia est et fortitudo animi. Sapiēs ergo semꝑ idē est animo: non minuit̉ nec auget̉ mutationibꝰ rerū: nec vt paruulus fluctuat vt circūferatur omni vēto doctri ne: sed manet perfectus in christo: fundatus charitate radicatusqꝫ in fidei prefectione. ¶ Postremo fratres mei charissimi ꝑfeuerātiā erit. Tolle perseuerātiā et neqꝫ virtꝰ habebit premiū: nec mercedē obsequiū: nec gratiā meretur beneficiuꝫ. Sola etenim ꝑseuerauerit vsqꝫ in finē: saluus erit. Nullū vir¬ tus habet meritū: cui perseuerātia nō deductur incrémentū. Nō incipientibꝰ bonū sed perseuerantibꝰ in bono vsqꝫ ad morteꝫ re¬ gnū externe felicitatis repromittitur: quia nō mane nō meridie: sed cū sero factū esset laborātibꝰ in vinea denarius reddebat̉ Nō em̄ qui bene cepit laudandus est: sꝫ qui bene continuauit vsqꝫ ad finē honorācius ē. Quo circa fratres mei sedulo vos admonere soleo nec vnqͣꝫ debeo cessare: quatenus diligenter attendatis vocatio ne vestrā et caute ambuletis in omī religione: sanctitate queadmodū iuratos de¬ cet milites christi. Nunc em̄ tempus est bn̄faciēdi: quia cū mortis hora aduenerit omnē facultatē oꝑandi funditꝰ amputabit. Et ideo qͣꝫ diu viuitis sani et incolumes bñfacite: futurā retributioneꝫ semꝑ cogitate: et quotidie ex ꝓfectu spiritali crescite: Querite dn̄m dū inueniri pōt. Christi saluatoris vita sit imitatio vr̄a: quē sequitur viribꝰ nō gressibꝰ pedū sꝫ similitudine affectionū: ex institutionis vꝛ̄e fundante tenemini. Caute in om̄ibꝰ ambula¬ te: timorē dei in vera humiliter semꝑ animentis intuitū ponite. Magna em̄ puritate vobis est opus: qui mente et corpore in sanctā christi militiam consensistis. Ad vos nūc pertinet o fratres mundū etomnia que in mūdo sunt propter deū perpetua fortitudine contemnere: omnes carni liū voluptatū motus vincere: peccatū fugere: in bonis et sanctis operibus vos ingiter occupare. Uita quoqꝫ vestra quaītuꝫ fieri humanam infirmitas sinit puritatē debet iustitiari angelicā: et omnē fugere ac detestari angeli aūt sancti nunquās sunt ociosi: sꝫ in laudibꝰ dei semꝑ absque fatigatiōe vl̓ tedio solliciti. Angeli sancti deū suꝑ oīa diligunt: et ab eius charitate nec momentanee quidē recedūt. Horum imitatiōe monachus in obsequio christi debetur esse assiduus: et semꝑ in bonis operibus secundū euangeliū et regulā occuperatus. Monachꝰ dei charitatē debetur habere feruentissimā: et proximi veraꝫ ordinarium est syncerā dilectioneꝫ. Amor etenim seruens in deū perficit monachū: et non sinit esse ociosum. Dicit enim quater sanctissimus papa Gregorius. Amor dei nūqͣꝫ est ociosus. Operatur enim magna si est: qui si operari rennuit: verꝰ dei amor nunquam fuit. Nam si de carnali amore verum poeta dixit insanus: qui non vult fieri desidiosus amet: quanto fortius castissimus dei amor mentem ad atdua impellit quam possidet. Amate deū fratres in toto corde quantum se desiderij foritur do potest extendere: et omnia que vobis precepta sunt facilime potestis observare. Nihil em̄ amāti difficile: sed omīa du¬ra: omnia grauiae ardua: ardens facilia facit amor. Que fit ordinatio vi¬re monastrice bona: Sermo secundus. Egimus institutionē sanctissimi patris nostri Bñdicti quā visitato vocabulo religionem siue ordinē appellamꝰ: in prōncipio fundatiōis sue claruisse scitissimā: et ꝑ totā latinorū ecclesiam valde et multipliciter fuisse dilatatā. Unde annis qͣꝫ plurimis in hoc ipso ordīe multi claruerūt viri sapiētes eruditi atqꝫ sanctissimꝰ

The monk, therefore, who is strong with true virtue neither ventures rashly nor fears imprudently. For fortitude together with constancy is the royal road; from it the rash and obstinate man turns aside to the right, but the fearful, faint-hearted, and timid man to the left. The monk, constant and strong in spirit, never withdraws from the purpose of holiness, but is neither cast down by adversities nor lifted up by prosperities. Hence also the most holy bishop Ambrose says: “The fool is changed like the moon. But the wise man is not broken by fear, not changed by power, not puffed up by prosperities, not overwhelmed by sorrows.” For where wisdom and virtue are, there is constancy and fortitude of spirit. Therefore the wise man is always the same in spirit; he is not diminished or increased by changes of affairs, nor does he waver like a little child so as to be carried about by every wind of doctrine, but he remains perfect in Christ, founded in charity and rooted in the perfection of faith.

Lastly, my dearest brothers, there must be perseverance. Take away perseverance, and neither will virtue have a reward, nor service a recompense, nor a benefit merit grace. For he alone who has persevered to the end will be saved. No virtue has merit if perseverance does not bring it to its increase. The kingdom of eternal blessedness is promised not to those who begin the good, but to those who persevere in the good even unto death, because not in the morning, not at midday, but when evening had come, the denarius was paid to those laboring in the vineyard.

For it is not he who began well who is to be praised, but he who continued well to the end is more honorably regarded. Therefore, my brothers, I am accustomed earnestly to admonish you, and I must never cease, that you should diligently attend to your vocation and walk cautiously in all religion and holiness, as befits sworn soldiers of Christ. For now is the time for doing good, because when the hour of death has arrived it will cut off entirely every capacity for working. And therefore, as long as you live sound and unharmed, do good; always consider the future repayment, and daily grow from spiritual progress. Seek the Lord while he can be found. The life of Christ the Savior should be your imitation; you are bound, from the foundation of your institution, to follow him not by bodily steps, but by your powers, by likeness of affections. Walk cautiously in all things; always place the fear of God before the gaze of your mind in true humility. For great purity is needed by you who have consented, in mind and body, to the holy warfare of Christ. It now belongs to you, O brothers, to despise the world and all things that are in the world for God’s sake with perpetual fortitude; to overcome all motions of fleshly pleasures; to flee sin; to occupy yourselves constantly in good and holy works. Your life also, as far as human weakness allows, ought to be made righteous in angelic purity, and to flee and detest every [unclear]. But the holy angels are never idle, but are always intent, without weariness or tedium, upon the praises of God. The holy angels love God above all things, and do not withdraw from his charity even for a moment. In imitation of them the monk ought to be assiduous in the service of Christ, and always occupied in good works according to the Gospel and the Rule. The monk ought to have most fervent charity for God, and it is proper that he have true and sincere love of neighbor. For burning love toward God perfects the monk and does not allow him to be idle. For the four-times most holy pope Gregory says: “The love of God is never idle. For it works great things if it exists; but if it refuses to work, it was never true love of God.” For if the mad poet spoke truth concerning carnal love, “let him love who does not wish to become idle,” how much more powerfully does the most chaste love of God drive the mind that it possesses toward arduous things. Love God, brothers, with the whole heart, as far as the strength of desire can extend itself, and you will be able most easily to observe all things that have been commanded you. For nothing is difficult to one who loves; but all hard things, all grave and arduous things, burning love makes easy.

What the ordering of a good monastic life is: Sermon Two.

We have set forth that the institution of our most holy father Benedict, which by the customary term we call religion or order, shone forth as most excellent at the beginning of its foundation, and was very greatly and manifoldly spread throughout the whole church of the Latins. Hence for very many years in this same order many wise, learned, and most holy men flourished.

II. Fo. LXII.

What the good ordering of monastic life is.

who magnificently illuminated the whole Church. For there are some who write that from this monastic religion of ours fifteen thousand six hundred, men as well as nuns, have been entered in the catalogue of the saints. The multitude of these saints in the order, brothers, is set before us for imitation, not for vain glorying. What can their multitude contribute to our salvation, if we do not imitate the manner of life in which they went before us? Whenever we desire profitably to praise the most holy men of our order, let us hasten by holy conduct to come into their fellowship. For then we shall glory fruitfully in the multitude of the saints of our order, if, living rightly, we earnestly strive to increase their number. Therefore indeed we set before you so great a multitude of saints, so that, when you see that many before you in this very order conquered the world and the flesh, you may at last rise up from your lukewarm manner of life. The virtue that God’s mercy granted to them he will not deny to you, if you ask in true charity.

They conquered the world because they loved Christ with entire devotion, despising all things for love of him. They despised all things, and the Lord Jesus provided for them whatever seemed necessary to them for the sustenance of life. This fervor of devotion among monks endured after the first institution of the order for many years with great constancy, and converted the souls of many thousands of people to the Lord. But nothing among human things is stable; nothing among perishable things is everlasting. Holy religion brought riches upon the monks, until in time the daughter suffocated the mother. For, as Scripture says, all those who wish to become rich fall into the temptations of the devil. The beloved grew fat and kicked back; made fat and enlarged with earthly possessions, he abandoned the holy pursuits of the first institution, went after vanities and false madnesses, and an abundance of temporal things made him needy and wretched in spiritual riches.

This pitiable deformity of our order began almost two hundred years after the passing of the divine father Benedict, and with time it grew more and more, until at last the harmful poison spread through the whole order. But this deformity occupied the order not suddenly, but through the succession of many years, until it had taken over almost the whole of it, although almighty God never left it wholly without good men, but always reserved for himself some who had by no means bent their knees to Baal. For men of mercy arose, whose righteous deeds will never be handed over to oblivion; pitying the ruin of the order, they put their shoulder under the labor and, the Lord generously granting aid, restored it in many places.

Indeed many varied particular reformations flourished often in the order at different times, but there was never any general one that brought the whole order back to the integrity of regular observance. Finally, we now see that the particular restorations, which we have said were many, have almost all collapsed again. Most recently, however, namely in the year of the Christians one thousand four hundred and twenty, when the general council was being celebrated at Constance, a certain new and, up to now, last particular reformation took its beginning in Germany. It took its name from a certain monastery in the regions of Saxony, then indeed the poorest of all, which is called Bursfelde.

The first author and leader of this most holy reformation was Johannes Rode, abbot of the distinguished monastery of Saint Matthias at Trier. Having been appointed general visitor of the order by the aforesaid Council of Constance, lest, while preaching to others, he himself should be judged reprobate, he first displayed reformation in himself. For first of all he reformed both himself and the monks of the said monastery; he issued constitutions conforming to the Rule; he obtained confirmation of the holy work from the apostolic see. But among all the monasteries of the order, Bursfelde, a humble and rather poor monastery, first received this reformation, which it afterwards extended to Reinhausen and to a few monasteries of Saxony neighboring it.

When at last Johannes Rode, abbot of Saint Matthias and leader of our reformation, had died, since in that place no suitable successor was found for extending the undertaking that had been begun, Johannes de Hagen, abbot of Bursfelde, who had already reformed certain monasteries, a holy man and very zealous for the order, was elected at the urging of Jacob, archbishop of Trier. Content with his poverty, he did not consent to leave Bursfelde, lest he seem to have preferred riches to poverty. He therefore remained in his own monastery, and another was appointed in the place of the first reformer. Since he seemed comparable to his predecessor neither in learning nor in zeal, he was able to accomplish little for the continuation of the undertaking begun, nor to enlarge the reformation among many. Meanwhile it happened that Nicholas of Cusa, presbyter cardinal of the holy Roman Church

apostolice sedis legati venire in Germania: qui cu zelo magno ferueret ordinis nostrum multa pro illius reformatione constituit et indulgit: Audiens aut prefati abbatis in Burkfeldia fama bonâ et feruen- tissimâ regularis discipline propositum: vocatu ad se generali ordinis reformato rem constituit: & plura per eum industria nobia reformatum. Hac tandez occasione capitulâ annale pro conservatione reformationis instituit: praesidentiaz de sancto mathia in Burkfeldiam transulit: cõfor- nari omnia que p bono reformationis in sticuerat per sedé apostolica imperauit. Primus aut Burkfeldie abbas in refor- matione fuit Ioannes monachus de rein hausen institutus: secundus Ioannes de hageniam dictus: tertius vero theoderi- cus que vidimus: & quartus Ioannes qui nunc est in regimine noviter institutus. Re- formationis nostre origines fratres cha- rissimi propterea breuiter perstringimus ut quâto ceperit labore cognoscatis: & vt ad morte in sancta observantia regulâ constantes perseveretis. Inter omnes reformationes ordinis nostri que pre- cesserunt nulla fuit vnâ regulâ divi patris benedicti magis conformis et consen- tanea: & a peregrinis adiumentioniby ma- gis aliena. Omniâ aliarû penere reformati onû statuta legimus: sed nulla plus qua nostra colentanea regulâ ad puritate inte- tiohie benedicti epistimanus. Hec est re- formation burkfeldensis in ordine saucis- fina: que vera et docer obedientiâ et custo- dit in humilitate subjectionem. Vivût in hac sancta religiâ paupes et sine peculio monachi: viuût humiles: viuût obedienti- tes: viuût casti. Q veneranda monacho- ru vnio: in q charitas gemiâta impat: obe- dientia militat: humilitas obtéperat: oza- tio vigilar: pleuerâtia pugnat: castitas la- cta triumphant. Hec est schola discipline regularis: instituitx christiane humilita- tis: q mores ad rectitudinem dirigit: & car- nis vicia restringit. Hemo in hac virtutâ palestra voluntate: priâ sequi cõtra regu- laz pmittit: memâ bïfacere prohibet. Ad puritâtë regulie in hac sancta vnione vui- tur: & si quispias a semitare rectitudinis de- viare ceperit: seniôr industria mor ad ob- seruantiâ iustitie reuocat. Regula sa ncti- fini patris benedicti ter publice in anno le- git: vt neino sub ignorantie typole de ob servâcia excusare moliaç. Duo sunt q mihi spé magnâ de pseuerantia huius sancte re- formatiôis pollicent: annale vis capitulâ 7 bienal diligês visitatio monachop. legate of the apostolic see to come into Germany; and since he burned with great zeal for our order, he established and granted many things for its reformation. Hearing, moreover, of the good reputation of the aforesaid abbot in Bursfelde and of his most fervent purpose of regular discipline, he summoned [him] to himself [unclear], settled the matter, and through his diligence [unclear] many things reformed. On this occasion at last he instituted an annual chapter for the preservation of the reformation; he transferred the presidency from Saint Matthias to Bursfelde; and he commanded, through the apostolic see, that all things which he had established for the good of the reformation be confirmed.

The first abbot of Bursfelde in the reformation was Johannes, a monk appointed from Reinhausen; the second, Johannes called de Hagen; the third, Theodericus, whom we saw; and the fourth, Johannes, who has now lately been installed in the government. We briefly touch upon the origins of our reformation, dearest brothers, for this reason: that you may know with how much labor it began, and that unto death you may persevere steadfast in the holy observance of the rule. Among all the reformations of our order that preceded it, none was more conformable and agreeable to the one rule of the divine father Benedict, and none more alien from foreign aids. We have read the statutes of nearly all other reformations; but we judge that none cleaves more than ours to the rule, to the purity of Benedict’s intention. This is the Bursfelde reformation, most holy in the order, which teaches true obedience and preserves subjection in humility. In this holy religious life the monks live poor and without private property; they live humble; they live obedient; they live chaste. O venerable union of monks, in which charity reigns doubled, obedience serves, humility complies, prayer keeps watch, perseverance fights, glad chastity triumphs. This is the school of regular discipline, the institute of Christian humility, which directs morals to rectitude and restrains the vices of the flesh. No one in this arena of virtue is permitted by his own will to follow [unclear] against the rule; no one is forbidden to do good. In this holy union one lives according to the purity of the rule; and if anyone begins to stray from the path of rectitude, the diligence of the elders immediately recalls him to the observance of justice. The rule of the most holy father Benedict is read publicly three times in the year, so that no one may try to excuse himself from observance under the pretext of ignorance.

There are two things that promise me great hope for the perseverance of this holy reformation: namely, the annual chapter and the diligent biennial visitation of the monks. But if either of these is neglected, the reformation will soon be in danger. Consider now, dearest brothers, and take the most diligent care you can, that you do not occupy this monastery of the divine bishop Martin uselessly under the title of so venerable a reformation; for unless you live according to the rule and the statutes of the order, purely, holily, and blamelessly, you trust in the name in vain. We shall say to you a few true admonitions for salvation, through which the zealous observance of our Bursfelde reformation will possess its name by merit and dignity.

First of all, before all things, direct the whole power of your striving and your whole desire toward monastic perfection; and as often as you feel it growing lukewarm, renew it by the intent remembrance of the Lord’s passion and most innocent death. For although we are not bound to that perfection by necessity of salvation, nevertheless we are bound to strive for perfection with all our desires. The monk who casts aside the striving to be perfected falls into the pit of failure. The second thing which the sacred custom of our reformation has established for you to keep preserves strongly the striving for perfection in its first desire. Therefore when, awakened, you rise for Prime, do these things in secret. Examine and discuss the course of the coming day; prudently consider what useful thing stands before you to be done. Set in your hearts in what caution you wish to live the whole day, and arm your spirits with patience against all things that might occur as adversities. Whatever you do, perform it in the fervor of charity, and always order all words and deeds to the praise of God. The third thing we judge useful and necessary for you is that, with most devout prayers, you always strive to implore the help of divine aid in all things. And it seems very fitting to us, as we have often said and always admonish, that each of you at least once a day make remembrance of the Lord’s passion, and for the many benefits received from God say an act of thanksgiving one time. That this may be done uniformly by each one of you, listen to this brief form which we have arranged; if you wish, write it out for yourselves.

I adore, praise, bless, and glorify you, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, savior and life-giver of the souls of all the faithful; and I give thanks to you from the innermost part of my heart for your most holy incarnation and nativity from the most pure virgin Mary; for your circumcision; for your flight into Egypt; for your seven-year exile there; and for

Ago tibi gratias dulcisime domine ieu: laudo: bündico: t adoro te: p cunctis laboizibus: itineribus: t fatigatio nibus tuis: pro fame: siti: frigoze: nudita te: paupertate: t inopia: t pro necessitati bus imurijs: cōtumelījs: irrisiombus et detractionibus quas in omni vita tua su stimuisti pro nobis voluntarie non coact? Et quoties manu mouisti ad operanduz pedem ad ambulandũ: vel quotiens ape ruisti os tuũ ad loquendũ: tociens te be nedico: laudo: glorifico: humiliter gado ro: t ex omib cordis mei virib? tibi sem per gratias ago mediator: de t hominuz ieu christe dulcisime. What the good ordering of monastic life is.

... by your return afterward into the land of your temporal birth. I give you thanks, most sweet Lord Jesus; I praise, bless, and adore you for all your labors, journeys, and weariness; for hunger, thirst, cold, nakedness, poverty, and want; and for the necessities, injuries, insults, mockeries, and slanders which throughout your whole life you willingly, not under compulsion, endured for us. And as often as you moved your hand to work, your foot to walk, or as often as you opened your mouth to speak, so often I bless you, praise you, glorify you, humbly adore you, and with all the powers of my heart always give thanks to you, mediator of God and men, most sweet Jesus Christ.

I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, most merciful king of the heavens, for your most holy teaching, for the establishment of your faith and of the evangelical sacraments, for the calling of the nations, for the justification of sinners, and for all your wondrous acts and virtues, and for all your benefits, which either you have bestowed upon me in particular or upon all others together with me in general.

I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, most benign savior, for your charity which you had toward the human race, and for your whole most bitter passion, and all the pains which you endured on account of us wretched ones. I give you thanks, Lord Jesus; I praise, bless, and adore you for the grief and sorrow of your most innocent heart which you endured for us at the time of your impending passion, when you said to your disciples who were following you: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death.” I beseech you, by this sorrow of your heart, O God, have mercy on me now and in the hour of my death, and take from me all melancholy and disordered grief, granting me at all times a salutary sorrow for my sins.

I give you thanks for the sadness of your most holy heart, when, placed in agony, you prayed to the Father a second and third time that he would take away from you the chalice of the passion; and, pouring forth sweat in marvelous anguish, you resigned yourself wholly to his will for us. I give you thanks, O king of heaven and earth, for your captivity, for the insults, injuries, and mockeries which you endured throughout the whole time of the passion on account of the salvation of us all.

I give you thanks, O Lord Jesus; I praise, bless, and adore you, bound to the column, for the most harsh scourging of your most tender body, and for the shedding of your most sacred blood from the wounds, with immeasurable pain. I adore you, Lord Jesus Christ, crowned with thorns, and I give you thanks for the piercings and pains of your most holy head, for the blows, spittings, and all the mockeries cruelly inflicted upon your majesty by the wicked. I adore you, Christ Jesus, Son of the living God, bearing the very heavy weight of your cross; I adore you, stripped of your garments before the multitude; I adore you, stretched out by hands and feet with iron nails upon the cross and very cruelly fastened to it.

I adore you, Jesus Christ, everlasting king, hanging and dying on the cross for me; and I give thanks for the pains of your wounds, I give thanks for the shedding of your most precious blood, I give thanks for your most innocent death which you willingly endured for our sins and the sins of the whole world. I give thanks to your boundless goodness, because you called me, your own, to the faith; because you caused me to be baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity; and because you deigned to call me away from the vanity of the world, to serve you in true tranquillity of mind, into this holy congregation.

I beseech you by your most holy name, O most sweet Jesus, mediator of God and men; I beseech you by the pain of your wounds and by the merits of your most bitter passion; I beseech you by the shedding of your most holy blood and by the power of your most innocent death: grant me indulgence of all my sins; pour into my heart the sweetness of your most fervent love; give me, with progress in all virtues, perseverance; and have mercy on me now and in the hour of my death, guarding me today and at all times, in your mercy, loving Jesus, from every sin and danger of mind and body. In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

And which of you, brothers, is there who cannot say this short prayer, or one like it if he has a better, once each day? It is not long nor is it wrapped in foreign words, but short and plain, gathering the life and passion of Christ in a compressed summary. A Christian person, and especially one in the cloister, is exceedingly ungrateful to God if he does not at least once in the day recall the Lord’s passion to memory, devoutly rendering acts of thanks. But if to any of you this prayer has seemed too lengthy, in the eighth homily of our exhortations to you we recently set down a shorter one, to which the weary man can have recourse. Above all, take care, I beg you, that among so many benefits of God you not be ungrateful for even one. Let this be done...

Dico em̄ qđ verū testatū efficaciores: qͣꝫ illas que cū dn̄ice passionis memoria et gratitudine deo patri offerunt̉. ¶ Quartū qđ vobis ꝓ regulari obseruantia iudicauimus neces- sariū est: vt in custodia sensuū vigiletis ex teriorū: qꝛ nemo ciuitateꝫ cordis sui bene custo dire sufficit: qͥ portas claudere contē nit. Amate silentiū: et fugite omneꝫ huius seculi tumultū. Prudentiā sanctā cūctis adhibete que facitis: et secretū amate qui etis. Monachus em̄ qͥ publicū et vagos discursus diligit: verus obseruantie ama tor nun fuit. ¶ Quinto monemus vt p̄- niciosum anime fugiatis ociū: qm̄ hoc pe stiferū virus grauissima nutrit vicia: et ẜe¬ per īmundas parit cogitationes. Quicū qꝫ igitur virtutū amator propriā salutem diligit: quicumqꝫ peruenire ad eternā seli citatē concupiscit: quasi a facie diaboli fu giat ociū: si cupit declinare peccatū. ¶ Se xto ad puritatē obseruantiē regularis de salutis necessitate requiritur: vt proprie¬ tatis abdicatio vsqꝫ ad mortē ab omnibꝰ inuiolata custodiatur. Monachus enim babēs peculiū: iter sibi parat ad infernuꝫ Qui aut̄ pecunias recipit et exponit in ce nobio minister sit publicus: nemo id pre¬ sumere audeat priuatus. Diuitiarū pos- sessio nō decet monachos: qui dn̄m iesuꝫ in paupertate spiritus imitari iubentur. Audiamus sanctū christi apostolū dicen tē. Habentes victū et amictum his contē tisumus. Prouidemus vobis deo mise¬ rante necessaria: non quantū postulat in¬ ordinate voluptatis cōcupiscientia: sꝫ qn̄ tū cōtenta paucis requirit natura. Itaqꝫ sicut vobis habere aliquid sine consensu abbatis non est licitū: ita cū ministremus om̄ia necqꝫ necessariū. ¶ Septimū quod facit monachū: est humilē obedientia p̄¬ ceptorū. Non em̄ verus monachꝰ esse po test qui cōtemnit obedientiā: et negat su¬ perioribꝰ suis quā promisit humile subie ctionē. Hic inobedientie morbus ex ela¬ tione et superbia mentis oritur quēadmo duꝫ ex malo vlceres anies generat̉. Sed qͥd ait scriptura? Odibilis corā deo et ho¬ minibꝰ est superbia: et omnis transgressio nis initiū. Militia monachorū est initia¬ cio christi: qui patri obediuit vsqꝫ ad moꝛ tem. ¶ Octauum locū exornaꝝ virtus pul cherrima castitas: qua cōtempta necesse iā est regularis vt om̄is naufragetur inte- gritas. Monachus em̄ de necessitate sa¬ lutis sue vsqꝫ ad morteꝫ iubetur caste vi¬ uere: et ab omni pollutione venerea ꝑpe¬ tuo abstinere. Hec em̄ tria sint vota mo¬ nastice cōuersationis principalia: cōtra qͦ¬ rū obseruantiā viuere monachorū est dā¬ natio certa. Monachorū etenim profes¬ sio sub eterne damnationis sententia p̄ci¬ pit eos viuere sine proprio: sub obedientia pastoris: et in ꝓpetua castitate. Uno ex tri¬ bus his ablato: integritas monastica vio¬ lata est: et damnat transgressio cōtemnen¬ tē. ¶ Nono igitur loco admonemus om¬ nē hominē deo dicatū quatenꝰ tan ser¬ pentē venenosum: propriā semper caueat voluntatē: qm̄ nisi eā om̄i tempore supe¬ ctā habuerit: facile in foueā damnationis cadit. Attendite regulā: q̄ monachis nec corporis nec voluntatis ꝓprie ꝑmittit vo¬ luntatē. Nemo peccat inuitus. Si volū¬ tatē tuā deo et abbati tuo in omnibꝰ perfe¬ cte submisseris: peccatū facile declinabis. ¶ Decimū quod integratē obseruantie regularis cōseruare pōt in vobis fratres mei charissimi: est vt in omnibꝰ aduersis et contrarijs pacientiā habeatis cōstantif simā propter amoreꝫ dei. Est em̄ paciētia virtut magna quā tolerantiā alio nomīe vocamus: sine qua nemo tentationū sua¬ rū victor euadet. Propterea dixit in san¬ cto euā gelio dn̄s. In paciētia vestra pos¬ sidebitis animas vestras. Quid est paci¬ entia nisi et suorū iniurias et cetera queqꝫ aduersa pro dei reuercentia et amo¬ re eqͣnimiter tolerare? Credite mihi fra¬ tres sententiā apostoli dico: pacientia vo¬ bis est valde necessaria: vt voluntatē dei facientes reportetis repromißionē. Sit vobis paciētie dn̄s iesus viuū exemplar: queꝫ totis viribꝰ sequamini. ¶ Undecimo fratres mei cauete nec corda vestra graue¬ tur in crapula: qꝛ monachus nō debet ad sacietatē manducare et bibere: sed abstinē¬ tie amore semꝑ cū qͦdaꝫ appetitu et esurie cessare. Dicit em̄ vir sapiens. Qui diligit epulas in egestate erit: et qui amat vinū et pinguiā nō ditabitur. Amate ieiuniū: ab¬ stinentiā diligite: in omnibꝰ cōtinentiā et parcimoniā seruate. Hec arma sunt clau¬ straliū: hec īsignia spiritualis militie mo¬ nachorū

thanksgiving after matins, because it is a most fitting time for prayer, and the silence of the night’s rest is wont to increase devotion. For I say that [unclear] testify [unclear] more efficacious: than those which they offer to God the Father with remembrance of the Lord’s Passion and gratitude.

Fourth, what we have judged necessary for you for regular observance is that you keep watch in the guarding of the outward senses, because no one is able to guard well the city of his own heart who disdains to close the gates. Love silence, and flee every tumult of this world. Apply holy prudence to all that you do, and love the secrecy of quiet. For a monk who loves public life and wandering excursions was never a true lover of observance.

Fifth, we admonish you to flee idleness, destructive to the soul, because this pestiferous poison nourishes the gravest vices and always begets unclean thoughts. Therefore whoever, as a lover of virtues, loves his own salvation, whoever desires to arrive at eternal happiness, let him flee idleness as from the face of the devil, if he desires to avoid sin.

Sixth, for the purity of regular observance there is required, by necessity of salvation, that the renunciation of property be kept inviolate by all until death. For a monk having private possessions prepares for himself a way to hell. But whoever receives and disburses money in the monastery, let him be a public minister; let no private person dare to presume this. The possession of riches does not befit monks, who are commanded to imitate the Lord Jesus in poverty of spirit. Let us hear the holy apostle of Christ saying: Having food and clothing, with these we are content. By God’s mercy we provide you with necessities: not as much as the desire of disordered pleasure demands, but as much as nature, content with little, requires. And so, just as it is not lawful for you to have anything without the abbot’s consent, so, since we minister all things, not even what is necessary [unclear].

The seventh thing that makes a monk is humble obedience to commands. For he cannot be a true monk who despises obedience and denies to his superiors the humble subjection which he promised. This disease of disobedience arises from elation and pride of mind, just as from evil matter pus is generated in ulcers. But what does Scripture say? Pride is hateful before God and men, and is the beginning of every transgression. The warfare of monks is the imitation of Christ, who obeyed the Father even unto death.

The eighth place is adorned by the most beautiful virtue, chastity; when this is despised, it is now necessary that all integrity of regular observance suffer shipwreck. For a monk, by the necessity of his salvation, is commanded to live chastely until death and to abstain perpetually from every venereal pollution. For let these be the three principal vows of monastic conversion: against the observance of which to live is certain damnation for monks. For the profession of monks, under sentence of eternal damnation, commands them to live without property, under obedience to a pastor, and in perpetual chastity. If one of these three is taken away, monastic integrity has been violated, and transgression condemns the one who despises it.

In the ninth place, therefore, we admonish every person dedicated to God that he always beware his own will as a venomous serpent, because unless he has held it suspect at all times, he easily falls into the pit of damnation. Attend to the rule, which permits monks neither the will of the body nor that of their own will. No one sins unwillingly. If you have perfectly submitted your will to God and to your abbot in all things, you will easily avoid sin.

The tenth thing, my dearest brothers, that can preserve in you the integrity of regular observance is that in all adversities and contrary things you have most steadfast patience for the love of God. For patience is a great virtue, which by another name we call endurance, without which no one will come forth victor over his temptations. Therefore the Lord said in the holy Gospel: In your patience you shall possess your souls. What is patience, if not to bear with equanimity both the injuries done by one’s own people and all other adversities whatever, out of reverence and love for God? Believe me, brothers, I speak the sentence of the Apostle: patience is very necessary for you, so that, doing the will of God, you may receive the promise. Let the Lord Jesus be for you the living example of patience, whom you should follow with all your strength.

Eleventh, my brothers, take care that your hearts not be weighed down in gluttony, because a monk ought not to eat and drink to satiety, but, from love of abstinence, always to cease with a certain appetite and hunger. For the wise man says: He who loves feasts will be in want, and he who loves wine and rich foods will not be made rich. Love fasting; cherish abstinence; preserve continence and frugality in all things. These are the weapons of cloistered persons; these are the insignia of the spiritual warfare of monks.
